operator_plays.name: GIS Landlocked-Parcel Spite-Strip & Access-Easement Assemblage Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Combine GIS parcel geometry with recorded access rights to option overlooked strips and negotiate voluntary easement assemblages; mapped boundaries alone do not establish legal access.
inputs: County GIS parcel and road layers
Recorded plats, deeds, and easement instruments
workflow: 1. Flag apparently landlocked parcels and narrow connecting strips in GIS
2. Verify boundaries, existing rights, and easement-by-necessity exposure with surveyor and counsel
3. Secure contingent options and negotiate voluntary access agreements without obstructing existing access
4. Record approved easements and close the assembled sale through title escrow
metrics: Verified access gaps per screened parcel
Net assemblage margin after survey and title costs

platform_risks.failure_mode: GIS false positive or unenforceable access premium
platform_risks.trigger: Unmapped easement, boundary error, or preexisting legal right of access
platform_risks.impact: Option expiry or acquisition with no incremental assemblage value
platform_risks.detection_metric: Survey and title exceptions per shortlisted parcel
platform_risks.fallback: Exercise diligence contingencies and offer survey-backed voluntary access services instead

operator_plays.name: Forced-Pooling Docket & Non-Consent Mineral Lease Curve-Jumping Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Use public pooling applications and drilling schedules to identify unleased mineral interests before election deadlines, pricing royalty upside against title defects and non-consent cost exposure.
inputs: State pooling dockets and election orders
Mineral ownership chain and lease abstracts
Operator development plans and local lease comparables
workflow: 1. Monitor pooling applications and map affected mineral tracts and hearing dates
2. Verify net mineral acres, ownership authority, and election consequences with specialist counsel
3. Negotiate disclosed lease or option terms and fund obligations before applicable deadlines
4. Assign permitted interests or administer royalty receipts with division-order reconciliation
metrics: Net royalty or assignment proceeds per invested dollar

platform_risks.failure_mode: Missed election or unexpected non-consent penalty
platform_risks.trigger: Stale docket feed or misread state-specific pooling order
platform_risks.impact: Delayed royalties and unbudgeted development-cost exposure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unverified order changes and days remaining to election
platform_risks.fallback: Stop acquisitions pending counsel review and choose only timely, fully understood permitted elections

operator_plays.name: Fractional Heir-Share Acquisition & Tenancy-in-Common Partition Buyout Forcing
operator_plays.mechanism: Acquire documented fractional heir interests at a discount reflecting illiquidity, then seek consensual buyouts or counsel-supervised partition subject to heirs-property protections and co-owner rights.
inputs: Probate files and verified heirship records
Title chain, occupancy facts, and independent appraisal
Applicable partition and heirs-property protection rules
workflow: 1. Establish ownership fractions, probate authority, and encumbrances before contacting sellers
2. Provide transparent offers with independent-advice opportunity and modeled partition costs
3. Seek voluntary co-owner buyouts or an agreed market sale before considering litigation
4. If unresolved, use counsel-led statutory procedures honoring notice, appraisal, and buyout rights
metrics: Net proceeds after carrying and legal costs

platform_risks.failure_mode: Heirs-property protections defeat assumed forced-sale economics
platform_risks.trigger: Mandatory co-owner buyout, partition-in-kind preference, or defective heirship
platform_risks.impact: Long holding period and lower realizable value
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unresolved heirs and statutory buyout conditions per property
platform_risks.fallback: Renegotiate voluntary exits or retain the interest without threatening unavailable remedies

operator_plays.name: Cell-Tower, Rooftop & Billboard Perpetual Easement Strip-Out Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Separate assignable site-access and rent rights from underlying real estate for specialist buyers, pricing tenant termination rights and the permanent burden left on the residual property.
inputs: Tower, rooftop, and billboard leases and amendments
Title, lender consent, and zoning documents
Specialist easement-buyer bids and residual property appraisals
workflow: 1. Identify leased sites and reconcile actual rent receipts with termination and renewal terms
2. Verify assignment rights, mortgage restrictions, maintenance duties, and required consents
3. Compare easement sale proceeds against lost rent and residual property impairment
4. Close approved conveyances through escrow and record access, utilities, and rent-allocation rights
metrics: Net easement proceeds versus retained rent value

platform_risks.failure_mode: Nonassignable lease or excessive permanent property burden
platform_risks.trigger: Missing tenant or lender consent or easement scope exceeding valued rights
platform_risks.impact: Failed closing or reduced refinancing and resale value
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unresolved consent conditions and residual appraisal discount
platform_risks.fallback: Retain the lease or negotiate a narrower term-limited assignment with all required approvals

operator_plays.name: FERC / ISO Substation Interconnection Queue & Powered-Land Option Flipping
operator_plays.mechanism: Overlay public interconnection queues with land-use and substation data to option potentially useful sites, treating queue position and nearby infrastructure as signals rather than guaranteed deliverable power.
inputs: ISO and utility interconnection queues and study results
Parcel zoning, transmission corridors, and substation maps
Utility service estimates and developer site requirements
workflow: 1. Match queue activity and infrastructure constraints to suitable parcels
2. Verify site control requirements, zoning, environmental limits, and utility capacity assumptions
3. Negotiate assignable diligence-contingent options within capped carrying-cost budgets
4. Assign approved options to qualified developers with explicit disclosure of unresolved power and study conditions
metrics: Option cost per qualified developable acre
Net assignment proceeds after study and option costs

platform_risks.failure_mode: Queue withdrawal or prohibitive network upgrade cost
platform_risks.trigger: Restudy, milestone failure, or capacity estimate unsupported by utility commitments
platform_risks.impact: Option expiry and unrecoverable diligence spending
platform_risks.detection_metric: Study cost revisions and unresolved interconnection milestones
platform_risks.fallback: Let contingent options lapse or reposition land for independently viable uses without claiming secured power

operator_plays.name: TCPA Serial-Plaintiff Docket Scraping & Real-Time Litigator-Scrub Firewall Tollbooth
operator_plays.mechanism: Offer consent-first outbound compliance screening using lawful docket-derived risk signals alongside mandatory do-not-call and revocation checks; plaintiff matching neither authorizes contact nor replaces TCPA compliance.
inputs: Permitted public docket data with identity confidence scores
Consent provenance, revocations, and suppression lists
Applicable calling rules and customer retention policies
workflow: 1. Ingest permitted docket records with source dates, minimization, and human identity review
2. Check consent, do-not-call status, revocations, and calling restrictions before optional risk enrichment
3. Suppress noncompliant contacts and route uncertain matches to review without planting honeypots or provoking claims
4. Serve auditable screening decisions with correction, deletion, and retention controls
metrics: Contacts blocked for missing consent or suppression match

platform_risks.failure_mode: False identity match or false assurance of permission to call
platform_risks.trigger: Stale docket data or treating absence from a plaintiff list as consent
platform_risks.impact: Unlawful outreach, privacy complaints, and customer liability
platform_risks.detection_metric: Consent-audit failure rate and upheld identity correction requests
platform_risks.fallback: Disable uncertain enrichment and require independently verified consent and authoritative suppression checks

chapters.question_prompt: How does the land flipping business model actually work end to end, and what does it take to build it into a real business?
chapters.title: The Land Flipping Business Model
chapters.subtitle: Buying below value and reselling near market, the land flipping life cycle and 7-step process, first-year profit breakdowns, full A-to-Z blueprints, why land is not passive, practitioner lessons from Seth Williams and Alex Reese, replacing a W-2, land acquisition fundamentals, and where the industry is heading
chapters.executive_summary: Land flippers agree on the core trade: buy vacant parcels from apathetic, free-and-clear owners, often inherited or absentee, at a deep discount and resell to builders, investors, or retail buyers. REtipster's Seth Williams teaches buying at 5% to 30% of value, while Clayton Hepler offers 50% to 55% and Ron Apke now buys near 80% and manufactures margin by subdividing. The street mechanics are numeric: counties with at least 200 land sales a year, days on market under 90 to 120, parcels scrubbed of the 40% to 50% with wetlands, flood, slope, or bad access, and offers built from median price per acre minus agent, closing, and lender costs. Texting beats mail for Landon Bleau, roughly 9x versus 3x return on ad spend. Disagreements remain over mail versus texting and over assigning contracts versus taking title.

key_metrics.label: First-Year Land Flipping Profit
key_metrics.value: About $700K profit in year one
key_metrics.context: Ron Apke and their brother started the land company in 2020, cleared about $700K in year one, then scaled to 50, 75, or 100 deals per year.

key_metrics.label: Texting vs Mail Return on Ad Spend
key_metrics.metric: Texting vs Mail Return on Ad Spend
key_metrics.value: About 9x for texting, about 3x for mail
key_metrics.context: Landon Bleau runs about 50K texts a week plus 10K to 20K handwritten mailers a month; texting produces 60% to 70% of deals.

key_metrics.label: Marketing Volume Per Deal
key_metrics.value: 6,000 to 8,000 mailers or 30,000 to 40,000 texts per deal, about $25K average profit
key_metrics.context: Clayton Hepler's benchmarks per closed deal, with cold calls at about 6 weeks per deal and a 5 to 10x return on ad spend.

key_metrics.label: Minimum County Land Sales
key_metrics.value: At least 200 land sales per year
key_metrics.context: Thomas only pulls lists in counties with at least 200 land sales a year and fewer active listings than sold listings.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator in this lane runs the same core arbitrage: buy dirt from an owner who no longer cares about it, at a price far below what a retail buyer or builder will pay, then resell fast. Seth Williams of REtipster frames the classic spread as offering 5% to 30% of market value and reselling at 50% to 80%, a 'win-win-win' where sellers who refuse that range are 'probably not the right person' [Zu8LEqQ-L0w @ 00:01:15]. At REWBCON, Williams widens the buy band to 10% to 40%, arguing the property is worth more the day you buy it [pBstDNy9IuM @ 00:08:18]. The spread has compressed as the market matured. Clayton Hepler on the DealMachine Podcast offers 50% to 55% of expected sale price on flips and 65% to 70% on double closes, with a $25K minimum, aiming to double the money [HE45qWS8txg @ 00:13:00]. Ron Apke has pushed further into a project model, buying around 80% of market value and manufacturing the margin by subdividing or adding a mobile home before selling above market [Z_ZynszdCFo @ 00:02:33]. The consensus is not one fixed percentage; it is that the margin lives in the gap between an apathetic seller's price and a motivated buyer's, and the operator's job is to sit in that gap.

The practitioners agree on who sells and why the asset class still works. Williams points out that banks rarely finance vacant lots, so most owners hold free and clear with no lender forcing a price, and that only about 6% of US land is developed [pBstDNy9IuM @ 00:06:52]. On Launch Control, Williams describes the 'seasoned' owner: someone who bought a dream parcel 20 to 30 years ago, inherited it, or is tired of paying the taxes, and who 'just don't care about it anymore' [4xzZ7rKlL4E @ 00:06:50]. Thomas, who reports a $63,000 month, describes the same seller as an inherited or absentee owner paying roughly $600 a year in taxes, someone who trades price for speed and certainty the way a driver accepts $5k from a dealer instead of $8k selling privately [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 01:25:05]. Hidden Money flags the identical signals for list building: delinquent taxes, out-of-state owners, decades of ownership, and estates [hWcjM0400as @ 00:00:52]. Thomas adds that land sellers carry less emotion and sign simpler contracts than house sellers, and puts the competition gap bluntly: 'for every 99 household sellers, there's one land flipper,' and most of those flippers only use the builder exit.

None of these operators sells land as passive income. REtipster's short take is blunt: 'This is not a passive process at all,' because acquisitions demand zoning, title, survey, and environmental work, many sellers decline deep discounts, and even owned lots need mowing, drainage fixes, and trespasser control, though it stays '10 times easier' than houses [WmRK4kG81e4 @ 00:00:47]. Ron Apke tells operators to plan for five years, not six months, to distrust 30-day promises, and to treat the business as a plan executed with consistency, since 'if you turn off your marketing, your leads are going to get turned off as well' [Z_ZynszdCFo @ 00:06:09]. Hepler dates the shift: the 2020 to 2022 market 'forgave bad underwriting,' and now operations and capital stacks decide who survives, with weak operators selling below what they underwrote [HE45qWS8txg @ 00:04:15]. Thomas lists who should stay out: anyone who won't pick up the phone, needs money within two weeks, avoids volume, or wants to get rich quick, and calls the role being 'an operator of a machine' that must run at least five days a week [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 00:33:03]. The shared baseline is a disciplined, volume-driven acquisitions machine, not a side bet.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Market selection is the first gate, and the screens are numeric. Apke goes rural, two to three counties outside a metro, and wants real transactions, days on market under about 120, a healthy sell-through rate, limited inventory, and county population density under 500 [Z_ZynszdCFo @ 00:04:04]. Hepler runs the same play on Zillow: sell-through above 100% a year within an acreage band, 25 to 250 or 300 active listings, tight pricing, and days on market under 90 rated good, 90 to 120 middling, and over 120 slow; 30 listings with one sale is unhealthy [HE45qWS8txg @ 00:07:59]. Thomas ignores days on market entirely because agents post lazy land listings, and instead demands at least 200 land sales a year, fewer actives than solds, and a sell-through target of 60% at six months and about 120% at one year [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 01:56:40]. Pitt County, NC, at 172 active versus 272 sold with reasonable price per acre, is 'absolutely' a market to spend in, while Harris County at 2,700 active versus 800 sold and Wake County's savvy, builder-saturated owners get rejected; median price per acre typically runs $10k to $50k [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 02:01:22]. Thin data lies: one Georgia county hit its sell-through targets on just eight sales and was still cut.

List quality is where land splits from house wholesaling. Thomas pulls 0.2 to 100 acres, 10-plus years of ownership, no corporate owners, no landlocked parcels, a minimum of roughly 30 feet of road frontage, plus wetland and flood limits, inside a land-specific tool like Land Insights or Land Portal, warning that skip tracing at 'less than a penny' buys junk data [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 02:05:04]. Hepler expects 40% to 50% of raw parcels to be bad, wetlands, flood plain, slope, flag lots, and scrubs them first; benchmarks run 6,000 to 8,000 mailers, about six weeks of cold calls, or 30,000 to 40,000 texts per deal at roughly $25K average profit and 5 to 10x return on ad spend [HE45qWS8txg @ 00:09:38]. Landon Bleau sends about 50,000 texts a week and 10,000 to 20,000 handwritten blind-offer mailers a month; texting produces 60% to 70% of deals at roughly 9x return versus about 3x for mail [Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:38:55]. Thomas's own funnel: 20,000 texts a month yields 57 offers and one to three qualified leads a week, about 10% of which close within 30 days, run through Smarter Contact with a simple 'Are you open to an offer?' opener [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 04:32:27].

The offer math is explicit. Thomas comps by median price per acre within acreage bands: a 5.7-acre sale at $61k gives $10,700 an acre, times 8.8 acres is $94,500, discounted about 10% to an $85k resale; after a 7% agent fee, $2,500 closing, and a $950 transactional lender, a 70% offer of $59k leaves roughly a $16k spread, and the seller gets texted a range near 60% to 65% [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 02:41:01]. Exit choice follows the deal: assign to a builder when the spread is thin, like $100k in and $105k out on a Nashville lot, or double close same day through a transactional lender on MLS deals and fat spreads, since the lender fee kills a $2k to $3k margin [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 01:07:08]. Hepler's two-call close targets doubling the money, offering 50% to 55% of expected sale for a flip, so a $60K property gets a $31K offer, after checking acreage band, proximity, characteristics, price, utilities, survey, deeded access, and buildability [HE45qWS8txg @ 00:13:00]. Hidden Money's beginner version: offer $6K cash on $15K land, budget $500 to $1,000 for title, close in about two weeks, and list slightly below market at $12,999 [hWcjM0400as @ 00:02:46].

callout.title: Small Tweaks the Operators Say Move Conversion
callout.body: Wording, list size, buyer intel, and template tracking are where these operators find extra deals without extra spend.
items: Cut outbound texts to roughly 100 characters; Landon Bleau's reply rate climbed from 13% to 15% up to nearly 20% [REtipster — Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:43:33]
If a county list comes out under 1,000 texts, bundle it with neighboring counties so the campaign does not burn out fast [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 02:01:35]

Keep owner names visible on sold comps to spot LLC builders; Perfect Deed Homes LLC paid $30k per lot in Ocala, and the buyer's agent can be paid about 3% to bring them in [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 03:26:43]
Stamp each mailer template with a reference number, track conversations had and cash collected per template, and double down on the winner [Olufemi Ajose — tF_EbilAGj4 @ 00:14:48]

sop_steps.title: Screen the County
sop_steps.action: Pull active listings, sold listings, and median price per acre for each candidate county.
sop_steps.detail: Require at least 200 land sales a year, fewer actives than solds, and sell-through near 60% at six months and about 120% at one year, with median price per acre roughly $10k to $50k [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 01:56:40]

sop_steps.title: Pull and Scrub the List
sop_steps.action: Filter parcels inside a land-specific data tool, scrub the junk, then skip trace.
sop_steps.detail: Use 0.2 to 100 acres, 10-plus years owned, no corporate owners, no landlocked parcels, about 30 feet of frontage, and wetland and flood limits; expect to scrub 40% to 50% of raw parcels [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 02:05:04] [DealMachine Podcast — HE45qWS8txg @ 00:09:38]

sop_steps.title: Run Volume Outreach
sop_steps.action: Send short opener texts at volume, tag every no, and comp only the hand-raisers.
sop_steps.detail: Open with 'Are you open to an offer?', tag no replies for later follow-up, and treat it as a funnel; texting runs about 9x return on ad spend versus about 3x for mail [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 02:15:37] [REtipster — Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:38:55]

sop_steps.title: Comp, Offer, Contract, Exit
sop_steps.action: Price by median price per acre, back out costs, sign a protected contract, and let the deal pick the exit.
sop_steps.detail: Comp in acreage bands, subtract agent, closing, and lender costs, offer 60% to 70%, sign with $100 to $500 earnest money held by title and fully refundable through the inspection period, then choose assignment or double close [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 03:03:27]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Practitioners split hardest on how deep to buy. Ron Apke has moved to a project model, buying at about 80% of market value and then manufacturing the margin by subdividing or adding a mobile home before selling above market [Z_ZynszdCFo @ 00:02:33]. Clayton Hepler runs a tighter flip formula: offer 50% to 55% of expected sale price for a straight flip and 65% to 70% when a double close covers the spread, with a $25K profit floor, so a $60K property gets a $31K offer [HE45qWS8txg @ 00:13:00]. Seth Williams sits at the opposite pole, teaching offers at 5% to 30% of market value and resale at 50% to 80%, and stating that sellers who refuse that range are probably not the right person [Zu8LEqQ-L0w @ 00:01:15]. Landon Bleau shows how the number drifts with the market: offers ran 40% to 45% of value in 2024 and now climb to 70% on subdividable land, while average gross profit per deal rose from $18K to $28K and the minimum purchase sits around $30K to $40K [Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:35:47]. The practical read: deep-discount offers fit small, fast cash flips, while high-percentage offers only work when the operator adds value through splits, entitlements, or a double-close spread.

The lead-channel fight is just as sharp. Thomas runs a text-first machine and says flatly, "I don't mess with any direct mail," pushing beginners to SMS because "money loves speed" and reporting roughly 120,000 texts across 61 lists in Smarter Contact [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 01:47:02]. Landon Bleau still mails 10,000 to 20,000 handwritten blind offers a month, but the scoreboard favors phones: about 9x return on ad spend from texting versus about 3x from mail, with texting producing 60% to 70% of deals [Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:38:55]. Olufemi Ajose builds the opposite case, crediting $1M in profit to direct mail and arguing that branded envelopes, a logo, QR code, headshot, and investment-firm copy aimed at lawyers, doctors, and portfolio holders unlock six-figure spreads; the rule is to mail weekly for 6 to 8 months instead of blasting 12,000 to 15,000 pieces once [tF_EbilAGj4 @ 00:15:19]. Seth Williams lands in the middle, calling direct mail the most competitive and expensive channel while listing texting, cold calling, ringless voicemail, and email as cheaper alternatives [4xzZ7rKlL4E @ 00:14:34]. The split tracks deal size: Ajose's mail hunts big-asset owners, while Thomas and Bleau chase volume and speed.

Exit structure and sourcing draw a third set of disagreements. Thomas treats assignment and same-day double close as interchangeable tools, using transactional funding for MLS deals or large spreads such as a $50K buy against a $120K sale, and insisting that the deal picks the exit [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 01:05:23]. Alex Reese prefers to take title outright, warning that assignments are time-intensive and get more fragile the longer they run [iC5tSNnegIw @ 01:14:34]. On listed land, Thomas calls lowballing on-market and FSBO sellers a low return on time, while Reese fires high volumes of informal text offers at overpriced listings and put an $85K listing under contract at $20K on land worth about $45K [iC5tSNnegIw @ 01:29:07]. Clayton Hepler dismisses the builder infill lane Thomas started in, calling roughly $2,500 per deal the worst way to run the business [HE45qWS8txg @ 00:07:26]. Valuation splits too: Thomas comps by median price per acre inside acreage bands, while Reese says price per acre is irrelevant for residential land, where location, neighborhood home values, zoning, topography, and soil set the number. Even the market screen differs, with Hepler wanting under 90 days on market and Thomas ignoring days on market because agents post lazy land listings.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The dirt itself kills more deals than any negotiation. Ron Apke names soil as the main fallout point: with no city sewer or water, a property needs well and septic, and about 5% of deals die when the land fails the percolation test [Z_ZynszdCFo @ 00:05:02]. Thomas says soils have "killed more of my deals than anything," after paying about $600 per test, and now pushes that verification onto the buyer during the inspection period [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 01:37:27]. Landon Bleau ran an 18% fallout rate in 2024 while skipping perc tests, surveys, and title commitments, a shortcut that only held while properties were going under contract within 48 hours [Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:23:09]. Zoning text is the quieter trap. Alex Reese's worst deal was seven non-conforming lots in Bladen County bought for about $36K, all-in about $40K, where a contiguity clause in the zoning ordinance allowed only 3 homes; the land sold for about $47K and netted roughly $300 [iC5tSNnegIw @ 00:55:20]. Wetlands, floodways, slope, and access that only looks real round out the list, and the operators still standing treat every cheap parcel as guilty until the soil, the ordinance, and the road frontage clear.

Capital and hold time form the second failure cluster. Landon Bleau self-funded purchases expecting four-week resales and watched them take four months, locking up cash until moving to 4 lenders with $800K to $1M in liquidity [Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:53:04]. Bleau also admits to doubling mail and texting while adding cold calling and PPC in a single month, having "optimized for gross profit, which was really stupid," and reports a $25K haircut when a $100K listing sold at $75K. Alex Reese warns that roughly $20K of monthly overhead in payroll and mail can lose $15K to $20K in slow months, and tells newcomers to expect break-even only after about a year [iC5tSNnegIw @ 00:09:45]. Seth Williams's Alabama deal, bought at $4,587 and sold at $20,000, still dragged for 15 months with panic price cuts along the way [pBstDNy9IuM @ 00:10:47]. Thomas self-funded a Nevada desert parcel about 45 minutes from Las Vegas instead of using a transactional lender, cleared about $8K, and judged the hassle not worth it [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 04:00:56]. The economics check is blunt: a paper margin means nothing when capital is frozen and overhead keeps billing every month.

Process failures quietly bleed the rest. Thomas ranks failing to follow up as the number one mistake, noting that someone who says no in April can turn around and sell in June, and warns that 72-hour expiring contracts backfire because owners paying around $300 a year in taxes feel no urgency [ZfyoS572Kbk @ 03:09:08]. Ron Apke's biggest margin regret was missing highest-and-best use: subdividing could have produced 4x instead of a double, though chasing every $10,000 margin stalls investors who should still favor quick projects [Z_ZynszdCFo @ 00:07:02]. Seller financing carries a hidden default bill; Seth Williams puts the odds at 40% or 50% that loosely approved buyers default, calls it a huge hassle, and dropped no-pulse approvals in favor of underwriting and large down payments [4xzZ7rKlL4E @ 00:27:38]. Hiring can be the most expensive mistake of all: Landon Bleau says a poorly trained US-based acquisition manager cost $200K to $300K, and year-one skip tracing alone ran about $60K [Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:58:07]. Closing carries its own trap, with seller-impersonation scams forcing extra verification on web leads. Thomas also reports that nine out of every 10 deals hit some issue at closing, which makes an investor-friendly closer that has handled same-day double closes a requirement rather than a luxury.

callout.title: Four checks before money goes hard
callout.body: Each gate below comes straight from a loss or near-miss an operator reported. Clear all four before earnest money goes non-refundable or capital leaves the account.
items: Soil and septic verified on any parcel without city sewer; Thomas paid about $600 per test and now has the buyer verify inside the inspection period [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 01:37:27].
Legal, deeded access confirmed, because sometimes it looks like you have access, but you don't [DealMachine Podcast — HE45qWS8txg @ 00:12:30].
Funding lined up before scaling purchases, since self-funded deals expected to sell in 4 weeks took 4 months [REtipster — Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:53:04].
Earnest money never goes hard on an unsold deal; amend to extend closing and inspection by 30 to 45 days and sign the amendment first [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 04:16:16].

chapters.pull_quote: "The deal picks the exit." — Thomas | Land Flipping (ZfyoS572Kbk @ 04:56:20).
action_checklist: Screen counties for at least 200 land sales per year with fewer active listings than sold, and bundle nearby counties until each campaign reaches at least 1,000 texts [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 00:52:56].
Scrub the 40% to 50% of bad parcels from every list before marketing: wetlands, flood plain, slope, and flag lots [DealMachine Podcast — HE45qWS8txg @ 00:09:22].
Cut opening texts to roughly 100 characters, which lifted Landon Bleau's reply rate from 13% to 15% up to nearly 20% [REtipster — Uaqe67xWZN0 @ 00:43:33].
Comp by price per acre inside acreage bands of 2-5, 5-10, 10-20, 20-40, 40-80 and 80+ acres, then discount about 10% before backing into the offer [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 02:39:30].
Write contracts with $100 to $500 earnest money held by title or an attorney, fully refundable for any reason inside the inspection period [Thomas | Land Flipping — ZfyoS572Kbk @ 03:03:27].
Follow up with every non-closing lead on a 1, 3 or 6 month cadence instead of treating offers as lottery tickets [REtipster — bFiThXyiz7c @ 00:13:20].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I run direct mail campaigns to landowners, and should I send blind offers or neutral letters?
chapters.title: Direct Mail Campaigns for Vacant Land
chapters.subtitle: Blind offers vs. neutral letters, direct mail ROI and deal numbers, pricing offers inside mailers, response rates and angry replies, a 1,000-letter test, direct mail vs. other channels, and RocketPrint & Mail investor case studies
chapters.executive_summary: Land flippers running mail at scale converge on one engine: priced offers sent to scrubbed county lists, mailed consistently at roughly 58 to 69 cents a piece. Apke Brothers model one deal per 2,500 mailers and $1,500 of marketing per deal against roughly $18,500 net, while Sumner Healey reports members earning $30K to $50K per deal at 8x to 23x return on ad spend. The street mechanics center on filter stacking for landlocked, flood, wetland, and HOA parcels, hand-comped acreage anchors, acreage-band pricing, and hard mailing deadlines. The live disagreements are offer depth, from 20-30% of value up to 40-70%, blind versus neutral versus range letters, and whether automated pricing tools like Prycd gut yields. Consistency through slow early drops is the recurring survival rule.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Breaking down the unit economics of their model, Apke Brothers rank direct mail above texting, cold calling, and emailing on both scalability and ROI [U4C3AVYK9M4 @ 00:02:53]. Among operators running land at volume, mail is the acquisition backbone rather than a side channel. Dan Weige of Land N Deed, a former fire department worker from Murrieta, California who copied mentor Clint Turner, names mail the number-one lead source, calls consistency 'the key,' and has hired an employee [pIgr8VsT8qA @ 00:01:38]. The second pillar of agreement is that the letter carries a number. Land Academy draws the line bluntly: a mailer without a price is 'a letter of interest,' not an offer, because 'Your offer to a potential seller needs to include an offer price' [qBNi7kpsYC4 @ 00:00:18]. Apke Brothers run exactly that play at roughly 30,000 pieces a month, with mail producing about 95% of their acquisitions; every letter quotes a cash figure, such as $18,000 for 5 acres in North Carolina closing in 2 to 3 weeks, and targeting is cut by county, region, or zip [NqZ26rAeL40 @ 00:03:26]. Priced letters mailed in steady volume form the shared baseline that every other tactic on the land side is built on.

Volume and consistency outrank polish in every operator's account. Sumner Healey tells blind-offer mailers that 'high volume' beats a perfect mailer [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:03:53], and Mike Alder, who sends thousands of offer letters a week to a PO box, says not to be discouraged by the 'no' responses because more offers produce more yeses [sLTyh9dkCbY @ 00:02:02]. Michael Mesela of Enchanted Farms LLC in Key West, who started on land in June 2022 after more than 20 years flipping houses, credits consistency and a priced offer as the two drivers of results and warns that early response was low but the right move was to keep going [xY-aEaO4M98 @ 00:01:49]. Camille Barbosa of Bare Hands Land Ventures in Marietta, Georgia shows the slow build in real numbers: about 5,000 letters in year one across 8 mailings, roughly every other month, produced about 50 leads, 6 closed deals, and more than $90,000 of gross profit [hJL_lnI6O1g @ 00:00:50]. Barbosa now mails 30,000 and sums up the lesson as 'stop overthinking it.' The shared instruction is to commit to a mailing schedule and judge the channel across months of drops rather than on a single mailing.

The entry ticket is also agreed. Apke Brothers call direct mail 'probably the most expensive of any of the outreach methods' and set the bar at six months of sending 2,000 pieces a month; without that runway, 'I don't think it's for you' [cFfiZJm0txo @ 00:08:16]. The second prerequisite is a clean list. Sumner Healey says 30 to 40% of DataTree records are garbage that must be scrubbed before mailing [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:04:05], and Land Academy's rule is to drop records with incomplete addresses outright rather than burn time researching them [qBNi7kpsYC4 @ 00:03:44]. Ryland of Land Insights stacks filters to cut landlocked parcels, bad slope, HOA lots, and wetland or flood parcels, capping wetland and flood exposure at 50%, and prices each cut in postage saved, because a parcel that can never become a deal costs the same stamp as one that can [Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:11:16]. The third shared habit is measuring the channel per deal rather than per response. Every operator who publishes numbers frames them as mailers per deal, marketing dollars per deal, and profit per deal, since response rates swing from drop to drop while the per-deal math is what decides whether the next batch goes out.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The unit economics are published in unusual detail. Apke Brothers model mail at about 60 cents a piece and one deal per 2,500 mailers, which puts marketing at $1,500 per deal; with 2022 average gross profit just over $20,000, that leaves roughly $18,500 net, so a $500,000 year takes 27 deals, 67,500 mailers, or 5,625 pieces a month [U4C3AVYK9M4 @ 00:01:03]. Apke Brothers' back-end data on a $20,000 offer shows resale typically in the low-to-mid $40s, sometimes $50,000, rarely below $35,000 to $38,000, and on average a little over double [iSZpxOj5Cus @ 00:04:26]. Sumner Healey's numbers run richer: members see one deal per 2,500 to 3,500 letters at $30,000 to $50,000 per deal, and one member, Anthony, sent 14,000 letters and netted over $200,000, about 23x return on ad spend, while new members land around 8x to 10x and seasoned members 10x to 20x [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:04:49]. Dan Weige runs a smaller engine: 4,000 mailers a month return 25 to 30 responses and 2 to 3 acquisitions at about $10,000 each [pIgr8VsT8qA @ 00:00:55]. Weige's best quarter produced 6 properties and $100,000 to $150,000 in revenue, a return Weige calls 'tenfold.'

Pricing is where the operators say deals are won or lost. Apke Brothers warn against letting Prycd auto-price a list: one user mailed 50,000 pieces and got 2 deals, and Prycd users typically see about one deal per 10,000 mailers against the Apkes' one per 2,200 to 2,500 [JRIbKp3FaEs @ 00:04:01]. Their fix is manual: split a county only when data supports it, lean on a few great comps and drop outliers, then price by acreage band, 2 to 4, 4 to 6, 6 to 8, 8 to 12, 12 to 15, and 15 to 20 acres, with price per acre falling as size rises, the 'Costco effect' [JRIbKp3FaEs @ 00:11:13]. Their companion rule is that 3 to 4 good comps beat 15 decent ones [iSZpxOj5Cus @ 00:07:37]. Ryland of Land Insights automates only the interpolation: comp the 5, 10, 20, 40, and 80-acre points by hand, for example 5 acres at $30,000, 10 at $50,000, 20 at $90,000, and 40 at $120,000, set the offer at 55%, and let Claude fill in every parcel between those anchors [Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:22:08]. The Gini reading decides whether to price by county when low or by zip when high, and the template merge variable must match 'offer price' exactly.

Format and cadence are just as specific. Ryland's copy rules assume a 10-second read: lead with a pain point such as tax delinquency, write 'you' instead of 'we,' highlight one thing, promise closing in 'as little as 20 days' rather than 10, add a testimonial and an FAQ, and repeat one call to action; the same Land Insights session adds a closed-face envelope in blue handwriting font as a 3-cent upgrade and reserves robotic-pen letters for hot lists only [Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:57:16]. Apke Brothers quote $0.69 all-in on the platform they demo, with no minimum, the same price for 1 piece or 10,000, and data free when mailing [cFfiZJm0txo @ 00:30:07]. For a first month they prescribe two drops of 1,200 to 2,000 pieces, up to 2,500, sent two weeks apart for 3,000 to 4,000 total; a 4,500 to 5,000 first drop is too risky, and without systems the cap is 5,000 a month [72e1idlc19Q @ 00:08:06]. The response clock is predictable: days 1 to 3 after the mail lands bring hate calls, days 3 to 7 bring real interest, about four purchase agreements go out, one likely closes, and the operator owns a property in 4 to 5 weeks [72e1idlc19Q @ 00:14:19].

callout.title: Squeezing More Deals From the Same Postage
callout.body: Small operational edges the practitioners use to pull extra contracts out of lists and letters they have already paid for.
items: Remail lists that flopped: one mailer produced zero deals, and the same data remailed 3 months later made $100K [Sumner Healey — R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:06:24].
Keep working stale leads, including 'red sellers'; deals still close from leads up to 2.5 years old [Sumner Healey — R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:08:35].
Get a merged proof of 10 to 20 letters from the print house and confirm the template variable matches 'offer price' before the full drop [Land Insights — Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:29:27].
Enclose a one-page purchase agreement with the blind offer; sellers have texted back a photo of the signed agreement [Land Investing Pros — gMTr4Kngzx8 @ 00:05:52].

sop_steps.title: Build and Scrub the County List
sop_steps.action: Pull the county, strip landlocked, bad-slope, HOA, and heavy wetland or flood parcels, drop low Seller IQ records, and dedupe owners.
sop_steps.detail: Dedupe owners, skip skip tracing for mail-only campaigns, and comp manually rather than trusting the data feed [Land Insights — Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:14:36].

sop_steps.title: Price by Hand Using Acreage Anchors
sop_steps.action: Choose a few great comps, discard outliers, and set per-acre prices by acreage band before any automation touches the list.
sop_steps.detail: Use a few great comps and drop the outliers, then apply acreage bands where price per acre falls as size rises [Apke Brothers — JRIbKp3FaEs @ 00:09:32].

sop_steps.title: Set a Hard Deadline and Drop
sop_steps.action: Commit to a fixed send date and split the first month into two drops two weeks apart.
sop_steps.detail: Set a hard deadline such as 5,000 mailers out by Friday so pricing work cannot stall the campaign [Apke Brothers — JRIbKp3FaEs @ 00:12:53].

sop_steps.title: Work Responses and Line Up Title
sop_steps.action: Field hate calls in days 1 to 3, send purchase agreements to real interest, and close through a fast title company.
sop_steps.detail: Call 3 to 5 title companies, up to 5 to 7, and favor a 2 to 3 week turnaround with e-sign and statewide coverage [Apke Brothers — 72e1idlc19Q @ 00:00:45]; expect blind offers to renegotiate 10 to 30% [Sumner Healey — R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:02:46].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in land mail is whether the letter carries a number. Land Academy draws a hard line: without a price it is 'a letter of interest,' not an offer, and neutral mail triggers '7 million phone calls' from owners with inflated asks [qBNi7kpsYC4 @ 00:00:18]. At Land Insights, Ryland backs blind offers for beginners, but Deb from RocketPrint pushes back: blind mail gets fewer, warmer calls, neutral gets more calls from owners wanting 'five times what it's worth,' and both end up 'producing about the same ROI' [Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:47:18]. Ryland's resolution is operational, reserving neutral mail for high-operating teams with staff to work the phones [Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:47:48]. Land Investing Pros credits neutral letters with easier contact, an edge in saturated Florida and Texas markets, and a fit for low budgets, with the catch that the owner sets a high first price and you must learn to negotiate [ipLt_cz8tEY @ 00:04:42] [ipLt_cz8tEY @ 00:07:28]. Hayden Crabtree shows neutral mail can still land a whale: 1,000 handwritten neutral letters to commercial owners produced 21 calls, a 2.1% response, five interested owners, four offers and one accepted deal [Hh6ptGrGpDQ @ 00:02:17]. Neutral buys volume of conversations; blind buys filtered ones.

Offer depth is the second fault line, and the spread runs from 20% to 80% of value. Land Investing Pros targets sellers at '20 to 30% of the market value,' then lifts blind offers on higher-value properties to '40 to 60%, maybe eighty,' because a 20% margin worth $20,000 to $50,000 is 'worth it' [gMTr4Kngzx8 @ 00:03:11] [gMTr4Kngzx8 @ 00:05:22]. Sumner Healey tells operators to 'stop' offering 10 to 30% and instead hit mid-market land at $25,000 to $250,000 with 40 to 60% offers, sometimes 70%, the percentage rising with price [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:02:05]. Land Insights mocks the '25% of full market value' model, with Ryland conceding very low offers 'used to work,' and runs its AI pricing example at 55% [Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:01:45] [Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:22:08]. The Apke Brothers split it by familiarity: 60 to 65% of value where you know the ground, but aim to double your money in remote or unknown markets because of risk [iSZpxOj5Cus @ 00:11:21]. They add that more aggressive pricing brings more deals at lower margins, so the job is finding the sweet spot between deal count and spread per deal [iSZpxOj5Cus @ 00:07:09].

Range offers and letter formats split the camps again. Ryland flatly says 'I hate the range offers' for mail, and Sumner Healey tells solo operators to skip neutral and range offers entirely [Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:00:54] [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:00:36]. The Apke Brothers keep range offers on the menu, such as $12,000 to $17,000 for five acres, for operators who are good at sales [cFfiZJm0txo @ 00:18:17]. On format, Land Insights runs a closed-face envelope in a blue handwriting font as a 3-cent upgrade, while the Apke Brothers criticize printer-made handwriting and pay roughly $2 to $2.70 for real pen on a robotic arm, about 2.5x the cost, reserving it for big deals [Tj5JsRK_YdQ @ 00:57:16] [cFfiZJm0txo @ 00:21:38]. On channel, the Apke Brothers concede that operators who cannot mail 3,000 to 5,000 pieces a month can cold call for two straight months, though they doubt it actually saves money, and they flag texting for legal and opt-in risk plus older sellers who do not text [NqZ26rAeL40 @ 00:13:51] [NqZ26rAeL40 @ 00:14:30]. Sumner Healey's tiebreaker on all of it: high volume beats perfect mailers [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:03:53].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest failures trace back to bad pricing. The Apke Brothers warn against letting Prycd auto-price a county: one user sent 50,000 mailers for two deals, and Prycd users see about one deal per 10,000 mailers against their own one per 2,200 to 2,500 [JRIbKp3FaEs @ 00:04:01] [JRIbKp3FaEs @ 00:05:29]. Their fix is manual: price 80 to 90% of mail at 40 to 50%, use a few great comps, drop outliers, and price by acreage bands because price per acre falls as size rises [JRIbKp3FaEs @ 00:06:22]. A separate Apke episode adds the anchoring trap, where one expensive pocket of a county leaves bad land overpriced and superior land underpriced, and says 3 to 4 good comps beat 15 decent ones [iSZpxOj5Cus @ 00:05:00] [iSZpxOj5Cus @ 00:07:37]. Land Investing Pros flags blanket blind offers on blocks with mixed values, such as $150,000 to $160,000 on one side and $50,000 across the street, and demands a market analysis first [ipLt_cz8tEY @ 00:10:26]. Even with clean pricing, the Apke Brothers report months of zero deals per 5,000 mailers and others with five, and refuse deals under $10,000 profit [U4C3AVYK9M4 @ 00:02:24].

Launch sizing burns new operators in both directions. The Apke Brothers say 450 pieces is too few, a 4,500 to 5,000 first drop is too risky, and admit they sent 10,000 their own first month and got few deals [72e1idlc19Q @ 00:06:27] [72e1idlc19Q @ 00:10:23]. Their reset is two drops of 1,200 to 2,000 pieces two weeks apart, capped at 5,000 a month until systems exist [72e1idlc19Q @ 00:08:06]. Land Academy is blunter about cheap tests: running 3,000 postcards 'will be the end of your real estate career' [qBNi7kpsYC4 @ 00:09:54]. Quitting early is the other trap. Sumner Healey describes a mailer that produced zero deals, then the same data remailed three months later made $100,000, and estimates only about half of new campaigns work [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:06:24] [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:07:32]. Michael Mesela of Enchanted Farms saw low early response, kept mailing, and now sends 2,000 letters a week for about $1,200, pulling 10 to 20 responses and about five deals at $20,000 profit each [xY-aEaO4M98 @ 00:01:49] [xY-aEaO4M98 @ 00:01:06]. Consistency, not the first drop, decides the outcome.

Inbound hostility and dirty data are the daily grind. The Apke Brothers expect hate calls for the first three days after mail hits, real interest in days 3 to 7, about four purchase agreements, and likely one purchase [72e1idlc19Q @ 00:14:19]. Mike Alder, who mails thousands of offers a week to a PO box, got replies such as 'add a zero to your 500 offer' and a $2,000 counter with no contact information that could never be answered, while one probate lead and one 'yes' from Ohio came through [sLTyh9dkCbY @ 00:01:01] [sLTyh9dkCbY @ 00:01:20]. Sumner Healey says 30 to 40% of DataTree records are garbage that must be scrubbed before mailing, and that deals still come from leads up to 2.5 years old [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:04:05] [R4icAmTE4WI @ 00:08:35]. The economics check from the Apke Brothers is brutal: direct mail is the most expensive outreach method, operators without six months of 2,000 pieces a month should not start, typical spend runs $3,000 to $4,000 of marketing per deal, and one $150,000 deal covers roughly 250,000 mailers [cFfiZJm0txo @ 00:08:16] [cFfiZJm0txo @ 00:33:07] [cFfiZJm0txo @ 00:11:31].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I use cold calling and texting to get land under contract without getting sued?
chapters.title: Cold Calling, Texting, and Multichannel Deal Acquisition
chapters.subtitle: Live cold calling sessions on vacant land, tax-delinquent, and code-violation lists, texting systems that produce contracts, DNC and TCPA legal rules and lawsuit risk, getting landowners to say yes, the 4-channel marketing and 4-part acquisition systems, and why old direct-response tactics are failing
chapters.executive_summary: Land operators agree that outbound volume plus fast offers drives contracts: Michael Bull says calling, texting and mail all profit and reach different sellers on one list, while Dylan Applegate's students hit 6 contracts in 7 days by pushing 20 offers a day. The street math varies widely. The Apke Brothers clock one deal per 5,000 texts for a skilled texter versus one per 20,000 for beginners; Bull says 10,000 to 40,000 texts per contract; Clay Hepler logs 30,000 to 250,000. Ajay Sharma prices callers at $4 to $8 an hour, and Maximilian Dier says stacked government lists convert roughly 10x better. The split is sharp: Land Academy and Bull favor mail, Applegate and the Apke Brothers start with SMS, and TCPA demand letters, honey-pot sellers and million-dollar settlements haunt every texting playbook.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every serious operator here treats deal acquisition as a volume game built on outbound reach, and none of them claims a single channel is the only one that pays. Michael Bull, who once ran three separate channel teams across 300-plus transactions, says cold calling, texting and direct mail are all profitable and hit mutually exclusive seller types, so the same 10,000-record list can be worked three ways [PMSn1EaZ42Y @ 00:00:53]. Maximilian Dier frames wholesaling as a pyramid: mass outreach at the base, follow-up in the middle, the close at the top, with paid upgrades like callers, pay-per-lead, Google ads and mailers layered on once cash exists [uQ2jDRUrtoY @ 00:00:36]. Jeff and DeAndre of the Land Flipping Empire run text-first because sellers respond faster to SMS than to cold calls, pushing about 1,000 texts a day through the Flip Force CRM [4KWC7a6vLcY @ 00:40:39]. Clay Hepler, with 200-plus deals across 25-plus states at a $37K average profit, adds the discipline layer: pick one channel, one data type, and commit to it for a year before adding another, and only stack new channels after crossing $1M a year [c8ekY72VGy0 @ 00:06:04]. The shared baseline is relentless, repeatable outreach rather than clever one-off hustle.

The second point of agreement is that leads are worthless until an offer goes out, and that qualification, not raw lead count, is what scales. Dylan Applegate's diagnosis of struggling students is blunt: everyone has the same tools, but the people who fall behind let leads stall in the qualify stage instead of pushing every single one to offer given, with phone offers preferred and text as the fallback [MaWsUKnc8CI @ 00:06:33]. Clay Hepler compresses the same idea into two lines: scale qualified leads, not gross leads, because qualified leads equal offers [c8ekY72VGy0 @ 00:11:05]. The Apke Brothers list the skills that separate a texter who closes from one who burns two to three months with nothing: qualifying and disqualifying both the person and the land, copywriting, A/B testing, follow-up, and a tight definition of what counts as a lead [Ls2lelB6ImM @ 00:10:28]. Ajay Sharma builds that filter into payroll, putting a roughly $6-an-hour lead manager in place whose entire job is to confirm the owner would sell, extract an asking price, and book the appointment [Jb9R7WTh63s @ 00:14:01]. Across channels, the operators converge on speed and volume of offers as the real needle mover.

Baseline prerequisites are cheap in hardware and expensive in discipline. DeAndre says a phone, a laptop and Wi-Fi are the only three things needed to start, and the assignability clause lets the pair sell contracts with no license and no capital of their own [4KWC7a6vLcY @ 00:21:51]. Where the operators get demanding is the front end: data and market selection. Ajay Sharma's four-part acquisition system starts with data and market selection before lead generation, lead management and closing [Jb9R7WTh63s @ 00:03:15]. Dylan Applegate screens counties for a 100% one-year sell-through rate, at least 15 actives and 15 solds in six months, a pending sell-through of 20% or more, a rising trend across every window, and a median pending price of at least $125K, then pulls rural 2-plus-acre parcels owned 36-plus months with government, church, school, landlocked, heavy-wetland and heavy-flood parcels scrubbed out, and adds that only about 13 to 14 counties fit everything at once [Hyk7GilIJ8g @ 00:04:17]. Clay Hepler runs a parallel screen, targeting 10 to 15% monthly sell-through and 60 to 75% over six months, and reads a weak six-month number as a slowing market [c8ekY72VGy0 @ 00:01:54].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On the texting side, the Apke Brothers lay out a full monthly stack: Launch Control at $500, Land Portal Unlimited Pro at $500 for 20,000 data points, and roughly $400 of skip tracing at 4 cents a record, landing at about $1,400 a month for 10,000 new contacts, or $1,400 to $1,800 for 20,000 [Ls2lelB6ImM @ 00:12:06]. They flag REI Reply at $50 to $90 a month as cheaper but less legally compliant, and their student Roy texts from 9 to 11 every day, closing about one deal per 5,000 texts against roughly one per 20,000 for beginners, at an average margin near $12K. Maximilian Dier runs a far cheaper send cost through GoHighLevel via XLeads at a penny a text, so 20,000 texts cost $200, and calls SMS the highest return on ad spend at 10 to 30 times [xPy40xTlt64 @ 00:23:27]. Ajay Sharma's staffing benchmark is one VA handling about 2,000 texts a day, roughly 50,000 a month, using SmarterContact or Launch Control, and insists owners should not be sending texts themselves [Jb9R7WTh63s @ 00:06:51]. Michael Bull's team model for a text shop adds a sender, a valuations manager, an acquisition manager and a transaction coordinator [PMSn1EaZ42Y @ 00:05:47].

Cold-calling mechanics hinge on dialer throughput and honest yield math. Maximilian Dier runs the Enzo dialer across up to 14 lines at once, scaling from 1 to 14 based on how many people answer, and logged 680 calls in 1 hour 7 minutes against roughly 100 calls in 30 minutes on a regular dialer [hIbsCLgyqbg @ 00:54:33]. Dier's KPI is one hot lead per 1,000 contacts on average, and $300 buys XLeads plus Enzo with about 25,000 skip-traced numbers a month. Nick, the cold-calling agency guest of the Apke Brothers, publishes the package math: 5,000 records skip trace to about 4,000 mobile numbers at an 80% match, worked in 8,000 dials across two passes with no double-dialing, yielding one lead per 150 to 350 dials [lWYFLEd7PA0 @ 00:35:06]. Layer SMS on top at one lead per 80 to 150 texts and the package delivers 40 to 100 leads for $3,600 with an American caller, at roughly one deal per 20 leads, or 5 to 10 contracts and 2 to 5 closings [lWYFLEd7PA0 @ 00:38:10]. Ajay Sharma prices ReadyMode callers at $4 to $8 an hour and expects about 40 leads a month from one full-time caller, roughly 1.7 to 1.8 a day [Jb9R7WTh63s @ 00:09:24].

The scripts are built to disarm. The Apke Brothers' session with cold-calling agency owner Nick lays out an opener that is a deliberately flustered 'sorry to bother,' asks whether the owner has ever maybe considered selling, counts a maybe-plus as a lead, and bans the word investor because investor already means lowball offer [lWYFLEd7PA0 @ 00:24:44]. The same session's rules: never ask the seller's price, since an early offer is like kissing at the start of a first date, start low and go up, and run 11 questions ordered easy to hard. Maximilian Dier's live call on a 2-acre Port Charlotte lot shows the lowball in action: two comps at $9,000 and $9,500, then a hard line that Dier couldn't go a dollar over $7,000 while covering closing costs, a roughly $500 survey and no agent fees, framed as a way to lowball without offending people [hIbsCLgyqbg @ 00:22:12]. When renegotiating after contract, Dier brings ammunition such as a repair estimate jumping from $40K to $60K, blames a $15,000 gap with the lender, asks what do we do, then stays silent, landing about a 50% success rate [uQ2jDRUrtoY @ 01:08:14]. Dylan Applegate's rule closes the loop: if the seller cannot be reached by phone within 24 to 48 hours, text the offer anyway [Hyk7GilIJ8g @ 00:13:10].

callout.title: Street-Tested Edges From the Dialer and SMS Floor
callout.body: Small moves the operators use to squeeze more contracts out of the same list and the same spend.
items: Stack lists before you touch them: code violations combined with pre-foreclosure or tax delinquency get the sniper treatment of hand-dials, texts and a 20-second video, while single-list records get the power dialer and text blast [Maximilian Dier — xPy40xTlt64 @ 00:04:41].

When a seller claims a higher bid, ask to see the contract or offer to match legitimate recent offers; about 50% of the hosts' deals were not the highest offer, as with 117K on 90 days versus 85K now [Apke Brothers — lWYFLEd7PA0 @ 00:19:10].

Watch deliverability: under 13% signals carrier flags, so verify numbers with Number Verifier and triple-dial for 48 hours before dropping to double-dial in two-week blocks [Ajay Sharma — Jb9R7WTh63s @ 00:16:29].
Text the sellers but call the buyers, qualifying each buyer by zip code, city, county and subdivision inside the Flip Force CRM [DGB Media — 4KWC7a6vLcY @ 00:39:07].

sop_steps.title: Pull a Filtered List in a Proven Market
sop_steps.action: Screen the county on sell-through, then pull a scrubbed rural list.
sop_steps.detail: Pull rural 2-plus-acre parcels owned 36-plus months, off the MLS, with no more than 25% wetlands or flood zone, and scrub government, county, church, school and landlocked owners; pull broad rather than only tax-delinquent owners [Dylan Applegate — Hyk7GilIJ8g @ 00:06:48].

sop_steps.title: Skip Trace and Launch Outreach Volume
sop_steps.action: Skip trace the list and start at a fixed monthly send volume.
sop_steps.detail: Start with 10,000 texts a month, scaling toward the 4,000 to 6,000 monthly texts the hosts tie to a $100K year once copy and qualification are dialed in [Apke Brothers — Ls2lelB6ImM @ 00:09:48].

sop_steps.title: Qualify Every Positive Response
sop_steps.action: Run each responder through the qualification questions fast.
sop_steps.detail: Ask about utilities, other owners, how long they have owned it and the reason for selling; try for the asking price first, but send an offer even if they will not give one [Dylan Applegate — Hyk7GilIJ8g @ 00:11:08].

sop_steps.title: Push Offers Out Daily
sop_steps.action: Set a hard daily offer quota and let the CRM handle follow-up.
sop_steps.detail: Jacob set a goal of 20 offers a day, did not wait for perfect comps or phone contact, let the CRM automate follow-up and re-engagement, and landed 6 contracts in 7 days [Dylan Applegate — MaWsUKnc8CI @ 00:02:04].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split is which channel to lead with. Michael Bull ran three separate channel teams before settling on one: “Now, we just do direct mail because I love the simplicity of it” [PMSn1EaZ42Y @ 00:08:28]. Bull prices 1,000 letters at about $650 and pitches mail as a 10-hour-a-week, one-operator lifestyle business running mid-six to low-seven figures. The Apke Brothers reverse the order, “if I were to start over I'd start with texting first,” because texting pulls 10%+ response against 1–1.5% on mail and works as a clear on-off button [Ls2lelB6ImM @ 00:16:11]. They still concede blind-offer mail is easier for beginners, while texting is the higher-skill, transferable channel. Jeff and DeAndre of Land Flipping Empire run fully text-first, pushing about 1,000 texts a day through the Flip Force CRM because “a lot of people respond faster to text,” and they closed a Georgia acre contracted at 20K and sold at 40K in 30 days by text alone [4KWC7a6vLcY @ 00:40:39]. Land Academy rejects both calling and texting, dismissing texting as a “worse version of emailing” that recipients report as spam, and keeps only plain-envelope mail with the exact dollar offer in the first sentence at roughly 1% response [NqKIWNpO1Ic @ 00:12:48].

Texting volume thresholds don't reconcile. Michael Bull says a text operation needs at least 50–80K messages a month, ideally 100K, to carry the fixed cost of a sender, valuations manager, acquisition manager and transaction coordinator, and at about 10K texts per contract for a skilled team, “if you're going to send a 100,000 texts a month, it's only three contracts a month” [PMSn1EaZ42Y @ 00:06:15]. The Apke Brothers say 4–6K texts a month gets a $100K year, and their student Roy closes about one deal per 5,000 texts against roughly one per 20,000 for beginners [Ls2lelB6ImM @ 00:14:06]. Clay Hepler's benchmark is wider still at 30K–250K texts per deal, set beside one deal per 5–8K mail pieces and one deal every six weeks per cold caller [c8ekY72VGy0 @ 00:08:17]. Ajay Sharma describes top texters firing 100–300K messages a month off whole-state pulls with minimal filtering, with one VA handling about 50K a month [Jb9R7WTh63s @ 00:06:51]. Deal size splits the same way: the Apke Brothers say they are “very very Pro bigger deals and less volume,” point to a $400K subdivide closed by brother Mike, and call Roy's roughly $12K average a small margin that could reach $15–20K.

Legal exposure is the sharpest fault line. Zach of Flip With Rick reads Jantz v. Home Run Offer as a green light for unlicensed wholesalers, “Neither definition encompasses a scenario in which the caller offers to buy something from the recipient of the call,” and adds, “I've never been attacked once” [U4t9j_wTBLk @ 00:08:03]. Josh Stevens of McMurray & Shuster, interviewed by REIPrintMail's Jeff Charlton, counters with Anderson v. Catalina Structured Funding, Eagle v. GVG Capital and Pepper v. VGG Capital, where courts treated as-is buying as a service paid for through the purchase-price discount, motions to dismiss were denied, and the cases settled [L4oZCP8R6RQ @ 00:07:26]. Josh says there are “really good arguments” those rulings are wrong, but fighting one is very expensive. Nick, the cold-calling agency guest of the Apke Brothers, takes a third line: “Laws and enforcement are two different things,” with callers using only the client's first name from the agency's own number, producing one one-star review and zero lawsuits in nine years, while the hosts book a $5,000 litigator demand as an operating expense [lWYFLEd7PA0 @ 00:06:06]. Ryan Dossey says about half a dozen of roughly 240 community members got tagged and points to B2B prospecting of LLC owners through registered agents as the clean lane [hzDGK6PCjPg @ 00:06:37].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The litigation trap is real and documented. Ryan Dossey lays out the honey pot: a fake seller feigns motivation, may even allow photos or an inspection, and “what they're waiting for is for you to send them the purchase and sale agreement,” the document that identifies your company [hzDGK6PCjPg @ 00:02:41]. From there the pipeline runs through a ChatGPT demand letter, an OpenCorporates lookup, certified mail and small claims, where four texts at $1,500 each makes $6,000 under an $8,000 ceiling, and ignoring the summons ends in a default judgment against company assets, rentals or the owner personally. REIPrintMail's Jeff Charlton reports a customer who settled for $1M plus hundreds of thousands in legal fees, and Josh Stevens prices defense at $300–1,000 an hour, calling $500K in fees ruinous for a shop clearing $200–300K a year [L4oZCP8R6RQ @ 00:08:18]. Michael Bull says courts treated paying closing costs or a quick close as services, that “99.9%” of operators skip DNC scrubbing, litigator scrubbing and safe harbor, and concludes, “to me, that risk wasn't worth it” [PMSn1EaZ42Y @ 00:07:54]. Land Academy adds that class actions over these channels are spreading, and its hosts treat mail as the one channel that works [NqKIWNpO1Ic @ 00:14:04].

The economics checks are blunt. Maximilian Dier says, “If you have thousand bucks a month, you shouldn't be cold calling,” adds that a VA at about $800 a month produces only one to two good leads a day, puts 20 good leads at one close worth roughly $5K, and walked away from a Conway seller demanding $250K per lot on a back-end split [uQ2jDRUrtoY @ 00:33:47]. Land Academy pegs an eight-hour calling day at maybe one warm lead every two weeks, or roughly two deals a year, and one host quit cold calling doctors' offices to sell gloves in under two weeks [NqKIWNpO1Ic @ 00:07:15]. The Apke Brothers warn that without qualifying and disqualifying people and land, copy, A/B testing, follow-up and a clear lead definition, a new texter should expect two to three months with no deals while the roughly $1,400 monthly stack keeps billing [Ls2lelB6ImM @ 00:14:49]. Ajay Sharma's dashboards catch the slow leaks: deliverability under 13% means carriers are flagging numbers, burnt lists and an 8-pushed, 5-connected, 0-booked gap mark where the pipeline stalls, and a $100K take-home needs $200–250K gross profit, which means underwriting $30–40K of deals a month [Jb9R7WTh63s @ 00:16:29].

Time and trust are the other bottlenecks. One of the Land Flipping Empire founders admits, “it took me 5 months to get my first deal which it took too long,” and Jeff spent four to five months on houses with no results before moving to land [4KWC7a6vLcY @ 00:47:32]. Dylan Applegate cold called government lists for about two months with zero success before an SMS system on a housing list produced an $11,000 first deal [Hyk7GilIJ8g @ 00:01:48]. Dylan's diagnosis of students who fall behind is that everyone has the same tools, but leads stall in the qualify stage instead of reaching “offer given”: “This is not a game of perfection” [MaWsUKnc8CI @ 00:06:33]. Anthony Weiler names the trust crisis that sinks lowball-only blasting: sellers get the same envelopes several times a month, promised one-to-three-week closes stretch to 30 days or 90 on a double close, and offers below 40–50% of perceived value stop working once sellers see a lot “bought for 30,000, listed for 90,000” [4vZN9zHC26c @ 00:02:29]. Weiler's fix is solving easement, clearing or minor-subdivision problems so the offer can go higher, then farming sellers with direct-mail drips, QR-code interest checks and retargeting.

callout.title: Clear These Four Checks Before a Single Text or Dial Goes Out
callout.body: Each check maps to a loss, lawsuit or dead month that practitioners took firsthand.
items: Treat a seller who feigns motivation and pushes hard for the purchase and sale agreement as a possible honey pot, because that document is what identifies you in the demand letter [Ryan Dossey — hzDGK6PCjPg @ 00:02:41].

Scrub the national and state DNC registries before first contact and at least every 30 days, scrub litigator lists such as LexisNexis, Blacklist Alliance and Contact Center Compliance, and honor removals within 10 business days [REIPrintMail — L4oZCP8R6RQ @ 00:30:55].
Open every cold text with who you are, who you are contacting for and the marketing purpose, since casual or cryptic openers become screenshot evidence [REIPrintMail — L4oZCP8R6RQ @ 00:14:59].
Check budget against channel math before dialing: about $1,000 a month should not go to cold calling, and a VA yields only one to two good leads a day [Maximilian Dier — uQ2jDRUrtoY @ 00:33:47].

chapters.pull_quote: “If you have thousand bucks a month, you shouldn't be cold calling.” — Maximilian Dier (uQ2jDRUrtoY @ 00:33:47).
action_checklist: Run the 1-1-1-1 framework of one channel, one data type, one year and one million, spending 2–4 hours a day on marketing and adding channels only after $1M a year [Clay Hepler — c8ekY72VGy0 @ 00:06:04].

Stack code violations with pre-foreclosure or tax delinquency, then hand-dial, text and send a 20-second video to stacked records while power-dialing single lists [Maximilian Dier — xPy40xTlt64 @ 00:04:41].
Start texting at 10K texts a month and build qualifying, copy, A/B testing, follow-up and a clear lead definition before scaling [Apke Brothers — Ls2lelB6ImM @ 00:09:48].
Set a goal of 20 offers a day and text the offer when the seller cannot be reached by phone within 24–48 hours [Dylan Applegate — Hyk7GilIJ8g @ 00:13:10].
Never say “investor” on a call, never ask the seller's price, and start low before working up [Apke Brothers — lWYFLEd7PA0 @ 00:24:44].

Scrub national, state and litigator lists, skip ATDS and pre-recorded voices, make opening disclosures, and contact only between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. at the called party's location [REIPrintMail — L4oZCP8R6RQ @ 00:26:37].

chapters.question_prompt: Where do I get landowner data, and how do I build and filter the right list before I market?
chapters.title: Data Tools and List Building
chapters.subtitle: DataTree, TitlePro, and RealQuest Pro compared, parcel tagging, PRYCD process flow, list upload, and out-of-county owner maps, PropStream for land, county GIS and parcel viewers, public-record data basics, SiteFact reports, and pulling tax-delinquent and off-market lists
chapters.executive_summary: Land and wholesale operators converge on one rule: build the list by stacking cheap public-record filters until only unlisted, long-held, absentee owners remain, then price and verify every parcel before a dollar goes to mail. DataTree, PropStream, RealQuest, TitlePro, PRYCD and free county GIS all draw on the same county tax-roll backbone keyed to the APN. The street mechanics are numeric. Setting improvement value to zero isolates raw land. DataTree records run 10 cents each, and PRYCD priced 300 records for $24. PropStream cut 82,328 Lehigh Acres lots to 1,250, and vacant-land mail pulls 2-5% response at $0.79 a piece. Operators split on equity filters (none to 99%), hold periods (2 to 10-plus years), RealQuest versus DataTree, texting versus mail, and whether niche lists are too small to work.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every paid list tool in this chapter is a front end on the same raw material: the county tax roll. DataTree by First American lays out the backbone. Each of 3,144 counties produces a tax roll, and the APN works like a Social Security number for the parcel. It carries land use, zoning, acreage, frontage and depth, utilities, ownership, vesting, five types of value, and tax fields down to the delinquent year [EmWzMGDpkTY @ 00:01:13]. Stephen Jack Butala and Jill DeWit of Land Academy, licensed on DataTree, TitlePro and RealQuest Pro, say all three serve the same purpose and now all deliver decades of deeds and mortgages [CbpqiGq5E5Y @ 00:09:33]. That is why the free layer matters too. Luke Harris of The Farm Finders, featured by Country Land Sellers, searches county GIS by tax account number for tax history, balance and boundary coordinates. To find any county's map, Harris Googles the county, state and GIS, then tries portal, tax lot finder or zoning map [6qNh515jvww @ 00:06:16]. Joséphine Saffert works the same way on Metro Nashville's parcel viewer. Saffert searches by address or owner, then reads frontage, overlays, floodplain and contours before a deal moves [_kxaCpUojPw @ 00:00:42]. The consensus is that paid tools buy speed, bulk export and mapping, not a different underlying truth about the parcel or its owner.

The second point of agreement is the target owner. Across land and house lists, operators strip out anything listed, anything corporate and anyone who bought recently, then lean into distance and tenure. Great Lands LLC's PropStream walk-through insists on unlisted property. It then filters for individual owners who have held at least 10 years, people who have owned land a long time and are tired of it, followed by out-of-state absentee owners [Mdkx15sX_XM @ 00:05:19]. Max Edson of PRYCD builds a whole county-level map on the same theory. Out-of-county owner records are divided by total county parcels, because distant owners sell more readily, and the map is filtered to counties at 40% or higher [mhHvzO1O8To @ 00:00:52]. On the house side, Lauren Hardy of The Well Entrepreneur drops owner-occupants because they ride it out. Hardy keeps individuals and trusts only, the mom and pops, and cuts LLCs [p_LcZVcrC3U @ 00:04:31]. Maximilian Dier's core Dallas pull is single-family, absentee, individual owner, seven-plus years owned, 30% equity and built 2010 or earlier. Dier's reasoning is that absentee owners are inherited, out-of-state or tired landlords [KmEcpx-t8YM @ 00:00:41]. The filters differ in degree, but the profile is the same: an owner who is far away, has held for years, and is not already working with an agent or listing the parcel.

The third consensus is that list building is a numbers game backed by hard verification. Matt of MS Partners LLC reports hundreds of deals from direct mail alone. Matt puts residential, commercial and multifamily response at 0.5-1% and vacant land at 2-5%, so 2,000 letters at 1% yields 20 owners. The secret is consistency: do not quit after 200 letters [hemWETr8VGg @ 00:01:14]. Maximilian Dier runs the same math on phones. Usually 1,000 calls produce one lead and 30 leads produce one deal, so the play is to pull 10,000 records, call each three times, and treat skip-trace quality as critical [KmEcpx-t8YM @ 00:01:55]. Volume only pays if the parcel survives scrutiny. Don Healy, speaking with Seth on the REtipster podcast, frames land as a war of due diligence. Whatever the end buyer will find that could trip the deal, the investor wants to know first [IS6mrT0hkGw @ 00:09:56]. Healy's two always-check items are zoning for intended use and soils plus slope. On zoning, Healy points to EFU land carrying an 80-acre minimum lot size [IS6mrT0hkGw @ 00:34:49]. Healy adds that a confirmed no is almost as valuable as a yes, because it kills a bad offer before money moves and before a buyer discovers the problem [IS6mrT0hkGw @ 00:33:41].

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The Apke Brothers' DataTree demo runs Boulder County, Colorado. A lot acreage filter of 5 to 5.5 returns 714 results, including houses. Setting assessed improvement value to zero strips that to 309 raw-land parcels [tZnXE47jWp4 @ 00:02:39]. Under 1,000 results, the set displays on the map with parcel, terrain, owner-name and APN layers. MLS recently-sold and for-sale neighbors also show, including one listed at $1.4 million [tZnXE47jWp4 @ 00:03:18]. Records cost 10 cents each with membership. Removing duplicate owners lowers the charge, though the deduped count is not shown before you pay [tZnXE47jWp4 @ 00:07:14]. Land Academy credits DataTree with mapping and book-and-page documents on top of the core record pull [CbpqiGq5E5Y @ 00:10:39]. For narrow, hand-picked targets, Seth of REtipster skips Advanced Search and uses parcel tagging. The sequence is More Map, the pencil icon, Freehand, mark each parcel, then Apply, Less Map and Export [oJpqcR4iFy8 @ 00:01:48]. Seth's example was 5-plus-acre self-storage sites in Millington, Michigan. Seth is willing to offer high there because the plan is to entitle or rezone. A small town produces 20 to 40 properties, which then get skip traced for texting or calling [oJpqcR4iFy8 @ 00:03:29]. The same tagging works for lakes, mountainsides or specific roads [oJpqcR4iFy8 @ 00:04:47].

PRYCD turns the pull into a priced offer file. Max Edson's process starts on the research page, which holds 1M-plus comps from Zillow, LandWatch, Lands of America and LandFlip. Counties are ranked by sold-to-for-sale ratio and parcels-on-market. In Colorado, filtering to population under 20 per square mile and parcels-on-market under .05 left six counties [7jGQIvwqBwc @ 00:05:19]. On the search page, Costilla County's 39,785 records get a 20-100 acre range, with the top typed as 100.01 to avoid rounding to 99.99. Residential codes require improvement value of zero. Corporate and do-not-mail owners are excluded, and flood codes and active or pending listings are dropped. The result is 1,930 records [7jGQIvwqBwc @ 00:12:32]. The offer slider defaults to 25% and can be overridden manually, and 300 records cost $24. The raw file carries 240-plus columns, and scrub filters remove on average 0.5% churches and 4.4% government owners. Five files then arrive, and the scrub file is the one that gets mailed [7jGQIvwqBwc @ 00:20:36]. Outside lists plug in too. Edson uploaded 1,359 records, smart-tagged county, state and acreage, and changed the default 30% discount to 25%. The output added five columns feeding a blind-offer letter, plus a Google Earth KML of owners and comps [3kN1hBRUqVU @ 00:02:51].

PropStream is the house tool that land operators bend to fit. Great Lands LLC ran a Lehigh Acres, Florida funnel in steps. Residential vacant land returned 82,328 records, and not on market left about 80,000. Individual owners holding 10-plus years left about 44,000, and out-of-state absentee owners about 20,000. Assessed value at or under $5,000 cut it to 17,000, 99% equity to 16,000, and last sale at or under $5,000 to 1,250 [Mdkx15sX_XM @ 00:10:07]. Comps get narrowed to a quarter mile with houses removed. The offer rule is double your money: a lot bought for $3,000 in 2004 gets a $1,500 offer, $2,000 max, and deed documents cost $5 [Mdkx15sX_XM @ 00:12:48]. Lauren Hardy cut Albuquerque's 12,000 tax-delinquent records to a 565-record final list. Hardy's plan is 10,000 records a month for $99, then export to BatchLeads [p_LcZVcrC3U @ 00:06:30]. Zach Ginn, with 1,000-plus wholesale deals, gets the tax-delinquent list free from the county clerk, appraiser or assessor. Ginn files a FOIA request if refused and asks for Excel to dodge page fees. TruePeopleSearch is the free skip-trace option [3VKazhO11yk @ 00:04:37]. For delivery, Matt pays Land of Enchantment Direct Mail $0.79 per piece, including letter, envelope and postage [hemWETr8VGg @ 00:01:50].
