callout.title: Small settings that change list quality and cost
callout.body: These are the keystroke-level moves practitioners use to keep records clean and spend down before the first letter drops.
items: Type 100.01 rather than 100 as the top of an acreage range so the filter does not round to 99.99 and drop parcels [PRYCD — 7jGQIvwqBwc @ 00:07:50].
Dedupe owners on DataTree before buying to lower the per-record charge, knowing the deduped count is not shown in advance [Apke Brothers — tZnXE47jWp4 @ 00:07:14].
When a county clerk resists, say you are a private tax-paying citizen doing private independent research, and request the file in Excel [Zach Ginn — 3VKazhO11yk @ 00:04:24].
Skip PropStream's improvement-value and estimated-value filters on land pulls, because Great Lands found them poorly populated or broken [Great Lands LLC — Mdkx15sX_XM @ 00:08:52].

sop_steps.title: Pick the county
sop_steps.action: Screen counties by absentee ratio and market velocity before pulling a single record.
sop_steps.detail: Use the out-of-county owner ratio map and keep counties at 40% or higher [PRYCD — mhHvzO1O8To @ 00:00:52]. Then filter the research page to population under 20 per square mile and parcels-on-market under .05, which left six Colorado counties [PRYCD — 7jGQIvwqBwc @ 00:05:19].

sop_steps.title: Pull raw land owners
sop_steps.action: Stack acreage, zero improvement value, unlisted status, tenure and absentee filters.
sop_steps.detail: Set acreage, then set improvement value to zero to isolate raw land, as Boulder County went from 714 to 309 [Apke Brothers — tZnXE47jWp4 @ 00:02:39]. Then require unlisted, individual owners holding 10+ years and out-of-state, as in Lehigh Acres going from 82,328 to 1,250 [Great Lands LLC — Mdkx15sX_XM @ 00:10:07].

sop_steps.title: Price the list
sop_steps.action: Upload the export, map county, state and acreage, and set the discount.
sop_steps.detail: Upload any DataTree, RealQuest Pro or assessor list and change the default 30% discount to 25%. This appends market price, market price per acre, offer price, offer price per acre and source columns for a blind-offer letter [PRYCD — 3kN1hBRUqVU @ 00:01:50].

sop_steps.title: Verify and mail
sop_steps.action: Check GIS access and tax balance, then mail consistently at a known per-piece cost.
sop_steps.detail: Confirm tax balance, boundaries and real road access on county GIS aerials and Street View [Country Land Sellers — 6qNh515jvww @ 00:03:48]. Then mail at $0.79 per piece and keep mailing past the first 200 letters [MS Partners LLC — hemWETr8VGg @ 00:01:14].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Land Academy's Jill DeWit and Stephen Jack Butala hold licenses for DataTree, TitlePro, and RealQuest, and they still split on which one belongs in a land operator's stack. Jack rarely touches RealQuest and calls DataTree the 21st century answer to pulling land and house data and then visually seeing it. Jill calls RealQuest best for land because its export format stays consistent, while DataTree columns shift county by county and break a multi-county mailer merge [CbpqiGq5E5Y @ 00:11:10]. The Apke Brothers lean into DataTree's map side: once a raw-land search drops below 1,000 results, the whole list plots on the map with parcel, terrain, owner-name, and APN layers stacked on top [tZnXE47jWp4 @ 00:03:18]. Great Lands LLC runs land through PropStream instead, conceding the platform is specialized in houses but arguing that the land data and built-in comps carry the workflow [Mdkx15sX_XM @ 00:01:45]. PRYCD's Max Edson sidesteps the platform fight entirely: pull a list from DataTree, RealQuest Pro, or a county assessor file, then upload it so PRYCD appends market price, offer price, and a campaign map regardless of where the records came from [3kN1hBRUqVU @ 00:00:14]. The real split is format consistency versus visual mapping versus pricing layered on top of any source.

Filter depth is where the list builders openly contradict each other. Maximilian Dier stacks absentee, individual owner, seven-plus years owned, and equity, calling 30% the magic number and reasoning that people sell every 7 to 10 years [KmEcpx-t8YM @ 00:04:58]. Great Lands LLC goes far harder on land in Lehigh Acres: individual owners holding at least 10 years to reach people tired of the lot, then 99% equity, then last sale at or under $5,000, shrinking 82,328 residential vacant parcels down to 1,250 [Mdkx15sX_XM @ 00:10:07]. Lauren Hardy refuses the equity filter outright because it is often wrong, sets ownership at four years, keeps individuals and trusts only to reach the mom and pops, and warns that stacking vacant on top of tax delinquent collapses Albuquerque to 269 records [p_LcZVcrC3U @ 00:02:04]. Ryan Dossey runs the loosest version for agents: equity of only 10 to 15% versus the 35 to 100% investors use, ownership of just two years, and a trust-owned filter that landed 3,361 West Jordan homes before trimming to roughly 300 actually mailed [1VVAkFWqVKE @ 00:02:42]. Hardy's tiebreaker is blunt: when in doubt, a bigger list beats a smaller list, because over-stacking makes the list tiny.

The outreach channel and list size arguments run in parallel. Zach Ginn works tax-delinquent lists by call, text, and mail but gives texting a slight edge over cold calling, and the script never mentions the taxes, leading instead with the me-and-my-partner-are-buying-in-the-area line [3VKazhO11yk @ 00:06:41]. Matt at MS Partners LLC built hundreds of deals on direct mail alone, quoting 0.5 to 1% response on residential, commercial, and multifamily versus 2 to 5% on vacant land, and pointing to the physical piece that some owners hold onto and call about a year later [hemWETr8VGg @ 00:00:34]. Dier pushes pure volume from the other direction: niche lists like 11 zombie properties or 608 tax delinquent records are too small to feed a dialer, so pull 10,000 records and call each one three times [KmEcpx-t8YM @ 00:01:39]. REtipster's Seth runs the opposite play, skipping Advanced Search and freehand-tagging 20 to 40 parcels in a small Michigan town for 5-plus acre self-storage sites, willing to offer high because the exit is entitlement or rezoning [oJpqcR4iFy8 @ 00:02:47]. Volume callers need thousands of dials; hand-taggers need conviction on a handful of parcels, then a skip trace to text or call each owner directly.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common self-inflicted loss is trusting a data field that was never populated correctly. Great Lands LLC tested PropStream's improvement-value and estimated-value filters live and found them poorly populated or flatly broken, so the raw-land screen had to lean on assessed value of $5,000 or less and last sale price instead [Mdkx15sX_XM @ 00:08:52]. Lauren Hardy calls the data tricky: MLS and pre-foreclosure filters come from data-mining firms, East Coast records are error-prone, and equity gets skipped because it is so often wrong, even though Hardy later calls the remaining data super accurate [p_LcZVcrC3U @ 00:03:36]. Country Land Sellers flags timing rot on the county side: GIS ownership lags roughly a month, the Recorder is the most current source, and the Assessor updates only afterward, so an owner name on the map may already be stale when the letter prints [6qNh515jvww @ 00:04:53]. Don Healy sees the same problem at scale, with CoreLogic and Regrid data packages dated enough that recent partitions do not match the ground, and jurisdiction PDFs sometimes contradicting the GIS layers they are supposed to back up [IS6mrT0hkGw @ 00:27:32]. Every field that drives a filter or a price needs a second source behind it before money goes out the door.

The expensive failures arrive after the contract, when a lot that looked clean turns out to be hobbled. Don Healy warns that a county saying buildable may mean buildable only under a conditional use, that utilities available can mean a 300-foot mainline extension, and that resource zones once imposed 100-foot setbacks on three sides, leaving a lot darn near unbuildable; Seth no longer calls listings buildable at all [IS6mrT0hkGw @ 00:15:38]. Healy's landslide case carried a clean seller disclosure, yet the assessor code read unbuildable and a title note pointed to a slide, forcing helical piles and a geotech review before anything could go up [IS6mrT0hkGw @ 00:17:57]. Luke Harris used the aerial basemap and Street View to catch a parcel that had no real road access, the kind of flaw that never shows on a spreadsheet export [6qNh515jvww @ 00:03:48]. Joséphine Saffert reads floodplain layers and contour lines on a Nashville lot, tracking roughly a 10-foot drop from 524 to 502 and circling the low drainage point before ever touring in person [_kxaCpUojPw @ 00:04:03]. Healy's pricing rule follows directly: an 18-month, $40,000 approval process has to come out of the offer, and a listing that says buyer's due diligence is a red flag.

The unit economics punish anyone who quits early or misreads the bill. Dier's cold-calling math runs 1,000 calls to one lead and 30 leads to one deal, which is why Dier pulls 10,000 records, calls each three times, and runs Enzo Dialer on 14 lines at about 2,000 calls a day [KmEcpx-t8YM @ 00:01:55]. Matt prices mail at $0.79 per piece through Land of Enchantment Direct Mail, with letter, envelope, and postage included, and says the secret is consistency because it is a numbers game: operators who quit after 200 letters never see the response math play out [hemWETr8VGg @ 00:01:14]. The Apke Brothers flag a billing trap inside DataTree: records cost 10 cents each with membership, and removing duplicate owners lowers the charge, but the deduplicated count is not shown before purchase, so the true bill stays hidden until checkout [tZnXE47jWp4 @ 00:07:14]. PRYCD's Max Edson reminds operators that the analysis rank reflects pricing confidence, not the best place to mail, that the scrub file strips church and government owners at averages of 0.5% and 4.4%, and that 300 priced records cost $24 before a single stamp is bought [7jGQIvwqBwc @ 00:13:45].

callout.title: Pre-Spend Data and Buildability Gate
callout.body: Clear these four checks before paying for records, mailing a list, or signing a purchase contract on raw land.
items: Confirm the raw-land screen actually works on your platform: residential land-use codes need improvement value set to 0, and PropStream's improvement-value field may be poorly populated [PRYCD — 7jGQIvwqBwc @ 00:09:40].
Verify zoning for the intended use plus soils and slope on every parcel, since EFU land carries an 80-acre minimum lot size [REtipster — IS6mrT0hkGw @ 00:34:49].
Pull ownership from the Recorder rather than the Assessor or GIS layer, which update later and can be stale [Country Land Sellers — 6qNh515jvww @ 00:04:53].
Budget for volume before launching: 1,000 calls per lead and 30 leads per deal, with each record dialed three times [Maximilian Dier — KmEcpx-t8YM @ 00:01:55].

chapters.pull_quote: "But a confirmed no is almost as valuable as a yes." — Don Healy on REtipster (IS6mrT0hkGw @ 00:33:41).
action_checklist: Shortlist counties on the PRYCD research page by filtering population under 20 per square mile, then parcels-on-market under .05 [PRYCD — 7jGQIvwqBwc @ 00:04:32].
Isolate raw land in DataTree by setting assessed improvement value to 0, then keep the result under 1,000 so it plots on the map [Apke Brothers — tZnXE47jWp4 @ 00:02:39].
Exclude corporate and do-not-mail owners, filter flood codes, and drop active and pending listings before pricing the list [PRYCD — 7jGQIvwqBwc @ 00:10:09].

Request the tax-delinquent list free from the county as a private citizen doing independent research, file a FOIA if refused, and ask for Excel to avoid page fees [Zach Ginn — 3VKazhO11yk @ 00:04:37].
Upload the list to PRYCD, map county, state, and acreage, and set the offer discount, for example from the 30% default to 25% [PRYCD — 3kN1hBRUqVU @ 00:01:50].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I figure out what a piece of vacant land is really worth before I make an offer?
chapters.title: Comping and Pricing Vacant Land
chapters.subtitle: Zillow, Redfin, and LandWatch comps, acreage price-per-acre adjustments, scraping LandWatch listings, pricing in non-disclosure states, why Zillow misleads on land values, avoiding overpaying, picking counties with Zillow data, and comping a subdivide
chapters.executive_summary: Land operators converge on one rule: value vacant land off sold, land-only comps in a tight size band and a six-to-twelve-month window, then adjust for wetlands, septic, and frontage. Seth of REtipster turns Redfin or LandWatch exports into a price-per-acre average, and Price Boss and PRYCD automate the pull. Offer math is blunt: Cool Wholesaling pegs Fairmont retail at $5,000 to $6,000 an acre and caps an 8-acre buy at $35,000; Brent Bowers aims under 50 cents on the dollar. Acrewell's Alex Reese says asking prices run two to four times market value. In non-disclosure states, Sumner Advanced haircuts last list price by days on market, while the Apke Brothers leaned on a realtor's opinion to justify a seven-parcel subdivide. They split on tooling: Bowers calls PRYCD his easy button, while Seth says Zillow often omits acreage.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who runs land numbers starts in the same place: strip the search down to vacant land and lean on what actually closed. Brent Bowers clicks sold-only, deselects every home type, re-selects lots and land, and keeps the window to six months, stretching to nine only when nothing shows, because 'what someone is willing to pay for it is what the value actually is' [JNufnuENoDM @ 00:01:05]. Seth of REtipster makes the identical cut on Redfin, calling sold data 'almost always the better way to go' since it is not some seller's or realtor's opinion, and warning that reaching back two or three years makes the numbers less relevant [rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:01:58]. The Cool Wholesaling crew filters Fairmont, North Carolina by sold and home type land, and reports that Jasper's team comps on Zillow almost exclusively and doesn't even have PropStream [3x8J7AdyCEw @ 00:00:01]. Damian of WE ARE LAND SPECIALISTS opens every Zillow pull with the price filter switched off and a twelve-month sold window, then widens to 24 months, or cross-checks county GIS last-sale data, when dirt barely trades in the pocket [JRa_lwdSNjo @ 00:10:48]. The shared logic: the older or more distant the sale, the less it tells you about today's buyer.

The second universal rule is apples to apples on size, because price per acre collapses as parcels get bigger. Valuing an 8-acre lot in Fairmont, the Cool Wholesaling crew set aside 37 acres at roughly 3,000 to 4,000 an acre and 50 acres for 139,000, saying the per-acre price 'gets smaller as you go up in size,' so those big tracts 'don't really apply' [3x8J7AdyCEw @ 00:01:22]. Seth of REtipster calls it a statistical constant: look at thousands of vacant lots in one area and the smaller ones command more per acre, so a five-acre subject comped off a 2.37-acre sale deserves a discount on the per-acre figure [9cX2NuhnYro @ 00:09:39]. Brent Bowers brackets hard, giving a 10-acre subject only 9-to-11-acre comps, and wants them within a couple of miles, calling five miles out a stretch [JNufnuENoDM @ 00:03:14]. Setting matters as much as acreage. Pricing a rural lot between Antioch and Shannon near Red Springs, North Carolina, the Cool Wholesaling team refused city comps, threw out subdivision lots as a builder charging premium, dropped a 6,500 sale that looked landlocked behind the main road, and landed on roughly 13,000 as max retail for a rural parcel in a not-high-end area [t8XDRE0ZjFc @ 00:02:57].

The third point of agreement: raw per-acre math is only the skeleton, and physical traits plus a local land agent finish the valuation. Once Upon a Brick warns that 'not every two acres is the same': flat versus sloped, wetland or not, road access, a pond, a skinny strip versus a rectangle with road frontage, and how close electric and water run all move the price [Tmf12E9Dg7A @ 00:06:15]. Alex Reese of Acrewell turns that into a six-step check called ASSESS (access, soil, slope, environmental, street view, satellite view) and shows a 3.3-acre lot with 2.8 acres outside mapped wetlands behaving like a bigger property than a 4.58-acre lot with only 1.1 acres outside [TbH_4hSsYHU @ 00:22:24]. Outliers get cut without apology: Seth deletes any sale that does not line up with the rest, guessing it carried some issue or was a deal between friends or family members [rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:06:17]. And almost everyone ends at the phone. Seth calls two or three agents who list multiple vacant lots, asks what price moves a five-acre parcel in 30 days, three months, or six months, and expects different numbers from different agents, the same reason one comp is never enough [9cX2NuhnYro @ 00:16:31].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The cleanest bulk method comes from Seth at REtipster, who credits Carl James and Todd Millin from the REtipster community. Filter Redfin to land, set a lot-size band, switch to sold, and hit the download button to pull every comp into a spreadsheet [rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:03:07]. Delete everything except sale price and lot size, then add two columns: acres, calculated as lot square feet divided by 43,560, and dollars per acre, calculated as price divided by acres; drag both formulas down and finish with =AVERAGE over the column [rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:04:15]. Where Redfin hides the download button, as in Costilla County, Colorado, Seth runs the free Chrome extension Instant Data Scraper, points its locate-next button at Redfin's page arrow so it crawls past the first 40 of 296 results, exports a CSV, and uses find-and-replace to strip the word acres out of the size column, which in one pass made 310 replacements [rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:08:23]. Where Redfin does not operate at all, like Tallapoosa County, Alabama, the same scraper runs on LandWatch. Price Boss automates the LandWatch version: advanced search by state and county, price 0 to 50,000, property type land, sort by most recent so paid-to-the-top ads do not skew the pull, paste each page into the yellow bar, and hit compute [FOpRZxfMs4I @ 00:01:32].

Once the per-acre number is set, operators move straight to offer math. The Cool Wholesaling crew read Fairmont comps of 5 acres at 30,000 and 9 acres at 50,000 as retail of 5,000 to 6,000 an acre, took the conservative 5,000 because big parcels sell slower than single building lots, priced the 8-acre subject at 40,000 retail, and set the buy target at 30,000, 35,000 max, without even pulling up the parcel [3x8J7AdyCEw @ 00:03:12]. Seth reverse-engineers a single lot: 17,900 divided by 2.37 acres is $7,552 an acre, then he knocks it to 7,000, 6,500, or 6,000 for a larger five-acre subject [9cX2NuhnYro @ 00:09:00]. Brent Bowers caps comp research at 15 to 20 minutes per new area because land runs on averages and the offer is ideally under 50 cents on the dollar, leaving room for error [JNufnuENoDM @ 00:10:39]. Alex Reese adjusts comps line by line: against a $20,000 sale in the same Middleburg, Florida subdivision, an installed septic adds about $10,000, a well about $15,000, and site prep at least $5,000, putting the listed lot near $50,000, which is exactly what he would offer against a $75,000 ask [TbH_4hSsYHU @ 00:07:34].

Non-disclosure states force operators to price off list data, and the street method is a days-on-market haircut. Sumner Advanced reads the last list price where a sold comp went under contract, never as the sale price: same-day contingent likely closed at list, a 117-day listing gets maybe 10 to 15 or 20 percent off, a 317-day listing 30 to 35 percent, and the six-month-to-a-year band can run toward 50 percent, while active listings older than a year are left out of the math [8pB5HoHJ4Bk @ 00:04:05]. The Apke Brothers ran exactly this play in Tate County, Mississippi: a 9.4-acre sale with a long listing history was guessed near $35,000, a 12-acre listed at 125,000 that went pending after five months was pegged near $100,000, and when comps still could not justify the price, a trusted local realtor's 50,000-to-70,000 opinion closed the gap [bIqgihxHoo8 @ 00:05:17]. When only for-sale listings exist, Seth discounts them 20 to 30 percent [rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:02:42]. Jeff checks LandWatch descriptions for seller-finance terms, where one ad showed 1,997 cash versus 297 down and 97 a month for 48 months, and multiplies the monthly payment by the months to get the terms price before treating it as a comp [mM0tCRujCDM @ 00:01:35].

callout.title: Shortcuts the Operators Actually Use
callout.body: Small moves that sharpen a land number fast, taken straight from how these operators run their own deals.
items: Ask for the '30-day blowout price,' not the pie-in-the-sky number: Brent Bowers called a land realtor about a parcel he had at $285, heard about $10,000 within 45 days, then took the realtor's own $5,000 offer and closed four days later [Brent Bowers — JNufnuENoDM @ 00:07:30].

Sort LandWatch by most recent before scraping so the pull is not stacked with only cheap ads, only expensive ads, or ads someone paid to push to the top; then use the green 'subdivision' highlight or the city to fill the subdivision column [LandSpeed Price Boss — FOpRZxfMs4I @ 00:01:32].

Read demand off the listing page: most Cedar Springs lots sitting under 100 days and one lot pulling 498 views in 57 days signals decent land demand, while 10 or 20 views and no saves after months signals a dead market [REtipster — 9cX2NuhnYro @ 00:13:12].

In non-disclosure counties, check land.com sold listings: sellers self-report the sold price there, and more times than not they report it accurately; LandFlip only shows actives [Sumner Advanced — 8pB5HoHJ4Bk @ 00:05:17].

sop_steps.title: Lock the Search Box
sop_steps.action: Filter Zillow or Redfin to sold, lots and land only, a bracketed acreage band, and a six-month window.
sop_steps.detail: Bowers deselects every home type, reselects lots and land, matches HOA status to the subject, brackets a 10-acre parcel at 9 to 11 acres, and widens to nine months only when nothing appears [Brent Bowers — JNufnuENoDM @ 00:01:39].

sop_steps.title: Build the Per-Acre Sheet
sop_steps.action: Export or scrape price and lot size, convert to acres, compute dollars per acre, and average it.
sop_steps.detail: Divide square feet by 43,560 for acres, divide sale price by acres, delete outliers that do not line up, and run =AVERAGE down the dollars-per-acre column [REtipster — rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:05:19].

sop_steps.title: Haircut List Data and Adjust for Improvements
sop_steps.action: Discount list-price comps by days on market, then add or subtract for septic, well, site prep, and wetlands.
sop_steps.detail: Take up to 15 percent off inside 90 days, around 20 to 30 percent at three to six months, 35 percent or more past six months, and skip actives older than a year [Sumner Advanced — 8pB5HoHJ4Bk @ 00:04:05]; credit installed septic, well, and site prep the way Alex Reese added about $30,000 over a raw comp [Acrewell Land Company — TbH_4hSsYHU @ 00:08:06].

sop_steps.title: Verify by Phone, Then Set the Offer
sop_steps.action: Get a quick-sale number from a land-specialist agent and back the offer out of conservative retail.
sop_steps.detail: Find the land specialist on LandWatch and ask what the parcel sells for in 30 days [Brent Bowers — JNufnuENoDM @ 00:08:59], then work backward from conservative retail, as with 8 acres at $5,000 an acre for $40,000 retail and a $30,000 to $35,000 max buy [Cool Wholesaling+ Land Deals-Real Estate Investing — 3x8J7AdyCEw @ 00:03:12].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is over which free portal deserves to be the primary comp engine. Cool Wholesaling+ Land Deals argues Zillow now works really well for comping and says Jasper's team runs almost exclusively on it without even paying for PropStream [3x8J7AdyCEw @ 00:00:01]. REtipster's Seth backs Zillow for scouting a new county because it serves the most markets and has the best mapping and filtering functionality [E9KBudZB1Do @ 00:00:30], but for hard per-acre math the order flips: Zillow is a poor fit because it does not consistently put acreages in its listings, so the Redfin spreadsheet download comes first, with LandWatch as the backup [rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:13:46]. LandSpeed Price Boss skips the house portals entirely, running a LandWatch advanced search by county with a 0 to 50,000 price band and land-only property type, sorting by most recent so the results are not skewed toward the cheapest ads, the priciest ads or the sellers who paid to float to the top of the page [FOpRZxfMs4I @ 00:01:32]. The real choice is about data shape. Zillow suits map-based eyeballing in thick markets where sold pins are plentiful. Redfin exports or scraped LandWatch pages suit operators who want a clean column of prices divided by a column of acres and averaged across dozens of rows.

Practitioners also disagree on how far back and how wide to cast the net. DannyG Real Estate starts at six months sold, as tight as possible, and only expands if nothing turns up, because starting narrow finds the best possible comp [UqPvFZ6TGGo @ 00:00:46]. Brent Bowers also anchors on six months because a lot can change in that window, stretching to nine months only when land comps are scarce, and insists on a tight apples-to-apples size band of 9 to 11 acres for a 10-acre subject [JNufnuENoDM @ 00:03:14]. WE ARE LAND SPECIALISTS runs the opposite default: kill the price filter, pull the last 12 months of lots and land, and if the pocket is thin, push Zillow or the county GIS sales layer out to 24 months [JRa_lwdSNjo @ 00:10:48]. Once Upon a Brick sets a far looser size band, telling a buyer comping a 2-acre parcel to search 1 to 10 acres and then average about five similar sales rather than trusting any single one [Tmf12E9Dg7A @ 00:02:01]. The tension is volume versus relevance. Narrow windows protect against stale prices in markets that are moving, but when the sold pins run dry, the tight operators end up expanding anyway, while the wide-net operators accept noisier per-acre numbers and lean on averaging to smooth the spread.

The sharpest numeric disagreement is how hard to haircut asking prices. REtipster applies a 20 to 30 percent discount when forced to use for-sale listings in thin markets [rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:02:42]. Sumner Advanced builds a sliding scale off days on market in non-disclosure states: a listing that went contingent within about 90 days gets 0 to 15 percent, three to six months roughly 20 to 30 percent, six months to a year 35 percent or as much as 50 percent, and anything active longer than a year gets thrown out of the discount math entirely [8pB5HoHJ4Bk @ 00:04:05]. Acrewell Land Company goes much further, calling asking prices made-up numbers that can run two, three or 400 percent of market value, with sellers accepting offers 50 to 80 percent below ask, often without even countering [TbH_4hSsYHU @ 00:03:07]. Brent Bowers frames it as a national rule of thumb that people ask a little more than they actually get, yet the example given has a 10,000 ask on five acres hopefully landing around 5,000 [JNufnuENoDM @ 00:04:31]. Which scale an operator adopts directly sets the retail anchor, and every offer built downstream inherits that error in either direction.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Acrewell Land Company's Alex Reese documents how badly list prices mislead. A 0.62-acre lot in Citrus Springs, Florida came to market at 75,000 and was cut to 42,000 within three months, a 44 percent drop, while sitting at 119 days on Zillow with 26 views, 18 saves and no buyer [TbH_4hSsYHU @ 00:01:13]. A Middleburg lot at 5309 Chickory Circle went from an 85,000 ask to a 20,000 sale after two and a half years and three separate listings, never drawing a buyer until the price fell below 28,000 [TbH_4hSsYHU @ 00:05:46]. The cause was physical: roughly 40 percent wetlands and flood zone, with the remaining ground in Kinault peat, a very poorly drained soil that may force an alternative septic system at much higher cost [TbH_4hSsYHU @ 00:06:46]. For Land and Country hits the same wall on a 47.53-acre Lebanon, Tennessee listing, where the stream corridor is mapped as floodway that cannot be built in at all, shrinking the usable building envelope toward the road frontage and handing the buyer leverage to push for a better price [7FfLOUMhyyA @ 00:04:11]. The trap is comping a lot by acreage and address alone. Two parcels in the same subdivision at the same size can sit tens of thousands apart once wet ground, drainage and buildable area are measured.

Non-disclosure states are where comp math breaks first. Sumner Advanced warns that the MLS in a state like Texas shows the last list price where a sold property went under contract, not what it closed at, so reading a 149 last list price as a 149 sale is the core mistake [8pB5HoHJ4Bk @ 00:00:52]. Apke Brothers ran straight into this on a 70-acre Tate County, Mississippi subdivide under contract at 135,000 plus a 5,000 survey: a nearby 9.4-acre parcel listed in late 2023 probably closed around 35,000, which did not make them feel good when they needed 40,000 to 50,000 per 10-acre lot to double their money [bIqgihxHoo8 @ 00:04:41]. With too few comps to justify the price, they called realtors and got a 50,000 to 70,000 opinion; eight months in, four parcels averaged 62,000 for about 240,000 back on roughly 140,000, with three left listed at 50,000 to 65,000 to move fast [bIqgihxHoo8 @ 00:06:27]. Sumner frames the cost of thin data as time: a non-disclosure county might take two mail campaigns to get pricing right versus one in a disclosure state, with offer feedback filling the gap [8pB5HoHJ4Bk @ 00:06:22]. The economics check: when the only sold signal is a guessed close below your per-parcel break-even, the deal rides on realtor opinion until real sales land.

The rest of the firsthand mistakes are process errors. Brent Bowers locked up a lot for 285 dollars with no idea how to comp it, got a 45-day estimate of about 10,000 from a local realtor, then took that same realtor's 5,000 offer and closed four days later, a fast win that still left roughly half of the realtor's own retail estimate on the table [JNufnuENoDM @ 00:07:44]. REtipster admits to scraping LandWatch without first restricting the search to sold comps, which mixed asking prices into the output, and repeatedly deletes outliers that would otherwise throw off the per-acre average [rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:13:34]. Cool Wholesaling+ Land Deals comped an 8-acre Fairmont, North Carolina lot at 5,000 to 6,000 per acre, roughly 40,000 to 48,000 retail, and found the wholesale price at or above retail once ponds, drainage and a zoning change back to residential were factored in, forcing a 30,000 to 35,000 max [3x8J7AdyCEw @ 00:02:26]. WE ARE LAND SPECIALISTS throws out a pocket comp because it was a waterfront lot with a boat slip, a premium the subject cannot share [JRa_lwdSNjo @ 00:04:48]. Each error points the same way: unscreened comps inflate retail, and inflated retail erases the spread.

callout.title: Pre-Offer Comp Gate
callout.body: Every item below comes from a deal where an operator either lost margin or nearly mispriced a parcel. Clear all four before a number goes into an offer letter or a purchase contract.
items: Pull wetlands, flood zone and soil layers before trusting any acreage comp; a lot about 40 percent wet with very poorly drained Kinault peat sold at 20,000 after an 85,000 ask [Acrewell Land Company — TbH_4hSsYHU @ 00:06:46].
In non-disclosure states, discount last list prices by days on market and drop any listing that has been active longer than a year from the discount math [Sumner Advanced — 8pB5HoHJ4Bk @ 00:03:49].
On any subdivide, call the county on minimum lot rules first; Tate County would only allow mobile homes on parcels of 10 acres or more [Apke Brothers — bIqgihxHoo8 @ 00:01:48].
Delete outliers that do not line up with the rest of the sold list before averaging per-acre values, since one odd sale throws everything else off [REtipster — rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:06:17].

chapters.pull_quote: "Every successful land buyer has one thing in common, which is that they ignore asking price. They make their offer based on market value." Attributed to Acrewell Land Company (TbH_4hSsYHU @ 00:24:06).
action_checklist: Filter Zillow to sold only, deselect every home type, reselect lots and land, and match the HOA setting to the subject parcel [Brent Bowers — JNufnuENoDM @ 00:01:39].
Download Redfin sold land comps, divide lot square feet by 43,560 for acres, divide price by acres, then run AVERAGE on the dollars-per-acre column [REtipster — rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:04:15].
Where Redfin shows no download button, install Instant Data Scraper, locate the next button and crawl every results page into a CSV [REtipster — rYCHQ59jzhY @ 00:07:27].
Copy filtered LandWatch result pages into Price Boss, hit compute, and tag each comp with its subdivision or city before analysis [LandSpeed Price Boss — FOpRZxfMs4I @ 00:03:34].
Call the land specialist listed on LandWatch for the area and ask for the 30-day blowout price, not the one-year number [Brent Bowers — JNufnuENoDM @ 00:09:15].

chapters.question_prompt: What due diligence must I run to confirm a parcel can support a septic system and a home?
chapters.title: Due Diligence: Perc Tests, Septic, and Site Checks
chapters.subtitle: Perc test walkthroughs and Title 5 measurements, what a failed perc test means and alternative septic options, health department soil review, slope and water-table concerns, Florida wetlands and deal-killing checks, and 15-point due diligence checklists
chapters.executive_summary: Land operators and septic pros agree that on any parcel without sewer, the soil decides whether a house can go there, so the perc or site evaluation has to run inside the due diligence window, never after closing. Apke Brothers screen overlays for slope, access, wetlands and flood in five to ten minutes, buy at 40 to 45% of market value, and cap standard diligence at 48 hours. The tests are timed water drops or soil-morphology reads, and the money spread is wide: $150 to $1,500 for a county perc, roughly $5,000 to $20,000 for conventional systems, and $15,000 to $60,000 for mounds, treatment units and drip. Practitioners split on risk: REtipster's Seth has skipped perc on sub-$1,000 lots and has never been burnt, while Mason Dixon Acres skipped it and hit car-sized rock.

key_metrics.label: Standard land due diligence window
key_metrics.value: 48 hours max
key_metrics.context: Apke Brothers say standard post-contract diligence on cash land buys at about 40% of market value should take 48 hours max, because slow diligence lets sellers back out.

key_metrics.label: County perc test cost range
key_metrics.context: Seth at REtipster reports the county health department typically charges $150 to $1,500, depending on what the county charges and how many people and machines are involved.

key_metrics.label: Florida conventional septic install
key_metrics.context: Florida Land Facts says conventional systems run $3,600 to $12,500 nationally but Florida installs usually land at $10,000 to $15,000, often more than an $8,000 lot.

key_metrics.label: Survey boundary mismatch rate
key_metrics.value: 25 to 30% of the time
key_metrics.context: Neil Clements reports surveys come back with boundaries different from GIS and mapping programs roughly 25 to 30% of the time, which is why the team orders a survey on every purchase.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who touched septic lands on the same baseline: if the parcel has no sewer line, buildability lives or dies in the dirt. Seth at REtipster frames the perc test as the issue that can make or break a land deal, because a lot that cannot drain wastewater cannot carry a house, and a lot that cannot carry a house loses its highest and best use [yp6qPMTkjgE @ 00:01:51]. Builder Roy Hunter, on site with Virginia agent Ben Quann, puts it bluntly: the purpose of the test is to make sure the property is buildable, and the way you prove buildable is whether a septic system fits [uvqvdLjMBL0 @ 00:01:47]. Acrewell Land Company adds that roughly 25% of US households rely on septic, and once you leave town your ability to build depends on it [AYim3zSksEs @ 00:01:03]. Groundwork, a civil engineer in water utilities, explains why the soil matters more than the hardware: the buried tank only separates solids from liquid, while the soil in the drain field does the real cleaning every day for the 15 to 40 years the system is supposed to last [dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:01:03]. The operator takeaway is consistent across all four: on rural paper, the soil report is the real valuation document.

The second point of agreement is sequencing: test while you can still walk. Florida Land Facts, a Sebring-area operator, says never close first and test later; run the soil evaluation inside the due diligence period and start early, because in a busy building season scheduling the evaluator and getting results back can take weeks [zWTn3NY8wqc @ 00:02:14]. Groundwork spells out why the clock matters: if the lot fails after closing, the seller pays nothing and the unbuildable lot is yours, while the three outs, paying for a different system, moving the field, or renegotiating and walking, are all cheaper before you close [dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:01:20]. The installer behind Wells, Septic & More closes the same loop from the contractor side, telling buyers to make sure a property perks before purchasing a home or land so they know a proper system can go in [F-UdA3MqSzw @ 00:10:22]. Mason Dixon Acres is the live counterexample: the couple skipped the test because the price was good and the timber had value, then pulled a rock the footprint of a small car out of the second pit and admitted that without septic the property is essentially rendered useless [8h9gMkksdD8 @ 00:02:22]. The test is cheap; the surprise is not.

Practitioners also agree that a failed perc is a cost problem before it is a death sentence. Jack Bosch calls the belief that a failed test means you cannot build one of the most misunderstood factors in real estate, because sand-filter, hydraulic, and self-contained toilet systems can still let you build at a higher price [nVJMPjUWdZw @ 00:07:25]. Liberty Acres says the same in one line: a failure usually means the soil cannot take a conventional drain field, not that the land can never hold a home, and the state and local health department decide which alternatives are allowed [Mio31c7ePlc @ 00:00:00]. The flip side of that consensus is that nobody trusts the neighbors. Acrewell warns that soil characteristics can change within 10 feet in any direction, so septic on both adjoining houses does not mean the vacant lot in the middle qualifies [AYim3zSksEs @ 00:06:00]. Seth at REtipster uses adjoining houses only as a vague signal when speed matters, stressing that neighbors pulling it off does not mean you will [yp6qPMTkjgE @ 00:04:51]. Net consensus: price the alternative system, check local approvals, and treat the house next door as a clue rather than proof.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Apke Brothers run a four-stage acquisition screen after the purchase agreement is signed. Stage one is a computer check in The Land Portal: toggle contour lines, flood zones, wetlands, and water features, mark problems on paper, and confirm road access and slope, which they call the two biggest items; the pink contour lines sit 20 feet apart, the 3D button exposes valleys where water collects, and a KML export drops the parcel into Google Earth street view [j3-xqUjgb7k @ 00:06:08]. A rookie takes an hour, a veteran five to ten minutes. Stage two is the price check: they average buying at 40 to 45% of market value, like to double their money, grade every deal A to F on price, property, and location, and renegotiate with the seller when land and price do not line up [j3-xqUjgb7k @ 00:07:40]. Stage three moves to the county for deed, zoning, setbacks, and any perc record at the health department. Stage four is boots on the ground, roughly $200 for a drone photographer, done while the file sits in title so they can still back out and list immediately [j3-xqUjgb7k @ 00:23:39]. Neil Clements adds a survey on every single purchase, calling a skipped $1,000 survey ludicrous [w08yc3MEaGE @ 00:10:38].

The test itself is a timed drop. MassDEP walks through the Title 5 version: measure the shelf so the test sits in the most restrictive layer, dig the hole at least 12 inches wide and 18 inches deep, hold water at the 12-inch mark for 15 minutes to swell the soil, then time the drop from 9 inches to 6 inches and divide by three to get minutes per inch [Q3kV6OiudSU @ 00:00:34]. Groundwork cites Alabama extension guidance of at least six holes 24 to 42 inches deep, soaked at least four hours, read every 5 to 30 minutes, with 60 minutes per inch or slower failing a standard field and the water table or bedrock needing to sit at least 4 feet below the trenches [dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:01:40]. In the field, Mason Dixon Acres ran a probe stage first, two 7-foot holes about 70 feet apart for the sewage enforcement officer to read the limiting zone, before six post holes get the actual water [8h9gMkksdD8 @ 00:00:20]. Roy Hunter's crew no longer pours water at all; they read soil morphology, color, texture, and consistency, looking for 36 inches of good soil under trenches at least 18 inches deep [uvqvdLjMBL0 @ 00:02:33].

The money side is where operators get blindsided. Seth at REtipster pays the county anywhere from $150 to $1,500 for a perc test, and on lots bought free and clear for well under $1,000 has skipped it entirely when the deal had to close that week, reporting they have never been burnt [yp6qPMTkjgE @ 00:02:04]. Groundwork's cost guide runs $150 to $500 for the soil evaluation, $1,000 to $5,000 for a designer, about $5,000 for a conventional system, $15,000 to $25,000 for a mound, and $15,000 to $30,000 or more for an aerobic treatment unit, warning that two identical-looking lots can differ by $10,000 or more [dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:05:35]. Ben Quann calls $20,000 the going rate for a conventional system in Virginia, estimates about $30,000 for the treatment-unit design on their buyer's lot, and puts drip systems at $45,000 to $60,000 [uvqvdLjMBL0 @ 00:06:08]. Jack Bosch frames the decision as a ratio: a roughly $10,000 normal system versus $30,000 to $50,000 for an alternative kills a $5,000 lot carrying a $30,000 mobile home, yet barely registers on a $250,000 lot under a million-dollar custom home [nVJMPjUWdZw @ 00:09:46].

callout.title: Squeezing more signal out of every pit, drone flight, and soil map
callout.body: These are the small operational moves practitioners use to catch soil and site problems early and turn diligence spend into marketing and pricing leverage.
items: Give your drone pilot or realtor exact orders, such as walking the first couple hundred feet back to check how wet it gets, and reuse the shots as listing photos [Apke Brothers — j3-xqUjgb7k @ 00:21:01]

Copy the health department reviewer's habit: John Dixon skips the consultant's existing pits and digs where nobody has studied yet to catch bedrock, ledge, or a perched water table [Soils Inc. & VA Septic — vTDxU1jKGSI @ 00:02:40]
On a big parcel, one failed hole is not the verdict: Seth had a 12-acre tract fail in several spots and pass in one corner [REtipster — yp6qPMTkjgE @ 00:05:17]

Commission a soil scientist's mapped evaluation before you list, because sellers who have it in hand get way more leverage and pricing power with buyers [Acrewell Land Company — AYim3zSksEs @ 00:07:50]

sop_steps.title: Run the desktop overlay screen
sop_steps.action: Pull contours, flood zones, wetlands, water features, and road access on the parcel before spending money.
sop_steps.detail: Apke Brothers flag every wetland, slope, and access issue on paper, cross-check with the 3D view and a KML export to Google Earth, and expect a veteran to finish in five to ten minutes [Apke Brothers — j3-xqUjgb7k @ 00:12:45].

sop_steps.title: Call the health department before the offer
sop_steps.action: Ask whether the lot was ever tested, approved, or turned down, whether a permit exists, and how old any soil report is.
sop_steps.detail: Groundwork calls the county health department before making an offer [Groundwork — dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:07:05] and warns that in Wayne County a soil report is valid for two years, so a seller's old report can be stale [Groundwork — dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:04:29].

sop_steps.title: Lock the contingency and the calendar
sop_steps.action: Make the purchase contingent on a passing soil evaluation with enough time for wet-season testing.
sop_steps.detail: Groundwork writes the soil contingency with room for wet weather testing [Groundwork — dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:06:49], and Bill Bower notes wet-season lots must test from mid-February to mid-April or wait for the next season [The Jen Holden Group of Compass — 3ppoErpmGfs @ 00:02:43].

sop_steps.title: Read the written result and reprice
sop_steps.action: Get the failure condition in writing, retest other spots, and fold the required system cost into the offer.
sop_steps.detail: Liberty Acres asks which condition failed, whether another spot can be tested, and gets a written estimate for the system and upkeep [Liberty Acres — Mio31c7ePlc @ 00:01:08]; Florida Land Facts says that septic bill belongs in your offer price [Florida Land Facts — zWTn3NY8wqc @ 00:03:18].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether a land flipper pays for a perc test before closing at all. Seth of REtipster buys many vacant lots for well under $1,000 free and clear, and when a deal has to close that week, Seth says it may be worth rolling the dice rather than paying more for the test than for the property itself, adding that the approach has never burned the business to date [yp6qPMTkjgE @ 00:03:14]. Mason Dixon Acres ran the same logic as owner-builders: they got such a good price and saw enough money in logs that they skipped the perc test, then hit rock big enough that the inspector ruled the site unsuitable for any septic system, a result they say essentially renders the property useless [8h9gMkksdD8 @ 00:02:22]. Florida Land Facts takes the hard line the other way, telling buyers never to close first and test later, and to start the soil evaluation early because a busy building season can push evaluator scheduling and results out by weeks [zWTn3NY8wqc @ 00:02:14]. Groundwork frames it as sequence: if a lot fails, paying for a different system, moving the field, or renegotiating are all cheaper before closing, so the rule is test first, buy second [dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:06:32]. The practical divide comes down to the price paid versus how much of the resale value depends on a house going in.

Practitioners also clash on how fast diligence can move. The Apke Brothers run a four-step process on cash land buys and argue standard diligence should take 48 hours max, because sellers back out when a deal bought near 40% of market value sits too long [j3-xqUjgb7k @ 00:29:06]. Bill Bower, speaking with The Jen Holden Group of Compass, describes a calendar no investor can compress: in parts of Anne Arundel County, wet season perc lots must be tested from roughly mid-February to mid-April, and missing that window means waiting until the next season to design the system [3ppoErpmGfs @ 00:03:01]. Even the test itself is disputed. Roy Hunter, appearing on Living in Virginia With Ben Quann, says the dig-a-hole-and-time-the-water method was dropped probably 20 to 25 years ago, replaced by soil morphology that reads color, texture, and consistency, even though everybody still calls it a perc test [uvqvdLjMBL0 @ 00:02:21]. MassDEP still walks through a timed water test: hold the water at the 12-inch mark for 15 minutes, then time the drop from 9 inches to 6 inches and divide by three for minutes per inch [Q3kV6OiudSU @ 00:01:52]. An operator promising a seller a fast close has to know which regime the county runs, and which season it demands, before quoting any timeline.

What a failed perc actually means divides the field. Jack Bosch calls it one of the most misunderstood factors in real estate, insisting land that fails can still carry a house through sand filter, hydraulic, or self-contained toilet systems, just at a much higher price [nVJMPjUWdZw @ 00:07:25]. Wells, Septic & More reports a harsher local reality: most of the time in that area, a lot that does not perc will not be allowed to develop at all, and existing homes with failed systems get pushed onto holding tanks [F-UdA3MqSzw @ 00:02:56]. The neighbor shortcut splits operators too. When rushing a cheap deal, Seth of REtipster checks adjoining parcels for houses as a vague signal that the septic question has been solved nearby, while warning that neighbors passing does not mean the lot will [yp6qPMTkjgE @ 00:04:37]. Acrewell Land Company goes further, saying soil characteristics can change 10 feet in any direction, so septic systems on both sides prove nothing about the vacant lot in the middle. Acrewell's alternative is paying a soil scientist for a mapped evaluation across the whole property, which costs more than the county route but samples far more ground and gives the seller more pricing power and confidence with buyers [AYim3zSksEs @ 00:06:00].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap is learning the soil after the money is gone. Mason Dixon Acres closed without a perc, then the first probe pit hit rock about three feet down for a 36-inch limiting zone, good enough only for a sand mound they describe as roughly twice the cost of conventional and up to five feet tall out of the ground [8h9gMkksdD8 @ 00:00:53]. The second pit, 70 feet away on the contour, produced a boulder roughly the footprint of a small car, the site was ruled out for any septic system, and the team ended up dragging a big excavator into dense woods to dig five more pits, filling one in immediately when it hit rock again [8h9gMkksdD8 @ 00:04:58]. Seth of REtipster saw the same pattern on a 12-acre parcel that failed the perc in several spots before one corner passed, which is why one bad hole should never end the search on a larger tract [yp6qPMTkjgE @ 00:05:17]. On the reviewer side, John Dixon, filmed at a health department review by Soils Inc. & VA Septic, deliberately digs where no consultant dug and explores deeper than the minimum to catch bedrock, ledge, or a perched water table that varies across the site [vTDxU1jKGSI @ 00:02:40].

Septic math routinely swallows the land price. Florida Land Facts points to Highlands County lots near Sebring trading around $8,000 an acre, then prices Florida conventional installs at $10,000 to $15,000 and engineered mounds at $15,000 to $25,000, meaning the septic can cost two or three times the dirt [zWTn3NY8wqc @ 00:02:56]. Jack Bosch runs the same check on an end buyer's budget: a $5,000 lot carrying a $30,000 mobile home cannot absorb a $30,000 to $50,000 alternative system, while a $250,000 custom-home lot under a million-dollar house can [nVJMPjUWdZw @ 00:09:46]. On Living in Virginia With Ben Quann, the team estimates about $30,000 for an alternative treatment unit against roughly $20,000 for conventional, with drip systems running $45,000 to $60,000, and warns a budget gets blown by having a lot perced for the wrong thing [uvqvdLjMBL0 @ 00:06:08]. Wells, Septic & More shows the worst branch: a holding tank, usually around 3,000 gallons giving roughly 10 days of water, at a couple hundred to nearly $1,000 a month in pumping, which drags resale value down [F-UdA3MqSzw @ 00:04:02]. Every one of those numbers belongs in the offer price before signing.

The quieter traps sit in paperwork and calendars. Neil Clements of REtipster orders a survey on every deal because roughly 25 to 30% of the time the boundaries come back different from what the GIS program showed, and a survey can expose an easement that makes the whole parcel unbuildable [w08yc3MEaGE @ 00:10:54]. Neil also leaned on title insurance on a $200,000 purchase where a wrong legal description meant buying the neighboring property, forcing a PI and 20 signatures gathered across five or six states to clear it [w08yc3MEaGE @ 00:12:08]. Bill Bower tells The Jen Holden Group of Compass about clients who never walked their whole site and had no idea a steep slope and floodplain sat out back until the tight survey contours exposed them [3ppoErpmGfs @ 00:04:35]. Groundwork flags the stale-paper trap: in Indiana's Wayne County a soil report is valid two years and the permit one, so an old report from the seller may be stale by the time you buy, and a dry August test can show a number March will not honor [dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:04:29]. The closing reminder from Neil is blunt: before the wire goes out you can always say no, because once you own it, there are no takebacks.

callout.title: Four Soil and Septic Kill Switches Before Money Goes Hard
callout.body: Kill, reprice, or retest the deal if any of these checks comes back wrong before closing.
items: Do not close until the soil evaluation is back while you can still walk away, and start it early because evaluator scheduling can eat weeks [Florida Land Facts — zWTn3NY8wqc @ 00:02:14].

Price the system the soil actually demands against the end buyer's build budget; a $30,000 to $50,000 alternative system kills a $5,000 lot meant for a $30,000 mobile home [Jack Bosch — nVJMPjUWdZw @ 00:09:46].
If one spot fails, test other areas before declaring the parcel dead; a 12-acre tract failed several spots and still passed in one corner [REtipster — yp6qPMTkjgE @ 00:05:17].
Ask the county how old any seller-supplied soil report is and whether it is still accepted, since reports and permits expire [Groundwork — dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:04:29].

action_checklist: Run the computer check first on wetlands, flood zone, slope, and road access overlays, a five-to-ten-minute pass once practiced [Apke Brothers — j3-xqUjgb7k @ 00:06:58].
Make the purchase contingent on a passing soil evaluation with enough time for wet weather testing if the county requires it [Groundwork — dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:06:49].
Call the county health department before making an offer and ask whether the lot was ever tested, approved, or turned down, and whether a permit exists [Groundwork — dSAQlt9llvM @ 00:07:05].

After any failure, get the written result, ask which condition failed, ask whether another spot can be tested, and request the list of approved alternative systems [Liberty Acres — Mio31c7ePlc @ 00:01:08].

Pull the FEMA flood map for the parcel yourself rather than trusting the seller, and budget an elevation certificate if the lot sits near a zone boundary [Florida Land Facts — zWTn3NY8wqc @ 00:03:18].

Send a drone pilot or realtor with specific questions about wet or sloped areas while the deal sits in title, so you can still back out and have listing photos ready [Apke Brothers — j3-xqUjgb7k @ 00:23:52].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I spot and solve landlocked parcels, and how do flood zones affect a land deal?
chapters.title: Access, Easements, and Flood Zones
chapters.subtitle: What landlocked means, easements by necessity and case law, Texas and Florida access options, knocking on neighbors' doors for access, appraising access easements, turning landlocked land into profit, easements vs. encroachments, reading FEMA flood maps, and changing flood determinations with a LOMA
chapters.executive_summary: Land operators agree that a parcel is only truly landlocked when it lacks both legal and physical access, that lenders and title insurers will not touch it until access is recorded, and that a negotiated express easement beats litigation on cost and speed. Jack Bosch cuts landlocked value at least in half, offers around $4,000 on a $40,000-access parcel, and either flips as-is at $12,000 to $15,000 or pays a neighbor about $500 for an easement to capture the $20,000 spread. The Apke Brothers will pay 70 to 80 percent of retail for the road-fronting tract. On flood, PushLeads prices elevation certificates at $400 to $800 and LOMAs at $1,500 to $5,000. They split on whether access is automatic: LandGate and Holmes say neighbors cannot deny it, while Lashmet says Texas grants no automatic right.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Jack Bosch, who reports over 4,000 deals with co-founder Michelle Bosch, opens every landlocked question in the Bosch Facebook group by challenging the definition: a parcel is only truly landlocked when it has neither legal nor actual road access [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:01:59]. If county records show a recorded easement running to the parcel, Bosch treats it as accessible, because the easement holder can bring in a backhoe and grade a road across it and the burdened neighbor cannot stop it [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:02:45]. Chris Thomas of Land Flipping 101 sets the physical test even tighter: to have access without an easement, at least one boundary of the parcel must coincide exactly, without gap or deviation, with the edge of the roadway, known as the right-of-way line; if those lines miss, the buyer needs an easement giving the legal right to cross whatever sits between the parcel and the public road [gwLVELHJjbc @ 00:06:58]. Tiffany Lashmet, an agricultural law specialist with Texas A&M, kills the most common myth on the rural circuit: land absolutely can be landlocked in Texas, and nobody is automatically obligated to hand you access [D_ZiLS1CYJg @ 00:00:22]. The operator takeaway is that a missing road is a research question to run down in the records, not a verdict that kills the deal.

Every practitioner who touches the money side agrees that no-access land is a cash-only, deep-discount asset. Attorney David Holmes, interviewed by Alabama broker David Miller, says a parcel can only be loaned on if the lender has some way to reach it in a foreclosure, and that no lender will lend money on land that cannot be accessed [orMrWlpfWj4 @ 00:02:13]. Holmes adds that a driveway used for twenty years without paperwork may ripen into a prescriptive easement, but financial institutions want something in writing; the land can still be bought and sold, you just buy it with cash and figure out the easement afterward, and Miller knows people who have done exactly that [orMrWlpfWj4 @ 00:03:28]. Lashmet stacks a second wall on top: you cannot get title insurance on a property with no legal access, and without title insurance you cannot borrow to buy it or pledge it as collateral [D_ZiLS1CYJg @ 00:01:17]. That is why the Apke Brothers, answering a Discord member named Sean who had a landlocked parcel under contract and neighbors unlikely to cooperate, say the first job is making sure you are buying it like a landlocked property and never paying more than you should for it [5p6zCt25Tyw @ 00:00:27].

On the fix, lawyers and flippers alike land in the same place: negotiate before you litigate. Lashmet calls an express easement from a neighbor the best, cheapest, cleanest option, one that saves everybody time, legal fees, court costs and headaches, and notes Texas offers about five legal methods to pursue access in court, each with its own elements to prove [D_ZiLS1CYJg @ 00:02:49]. Legal Counsel P.A. in Florida ranks a negotiated agreement as the best, least expensive and most expeditious route, while an easement by necessity usually means suing the neighbor and asking a judge for a judicial determination, a long and expensive process [4mnTabZRS60 @ 00:00:37]. Flood exposure is the second baseline check every land operator runs. Jeremy of PushLeads stresses that the zone letter dictates mandatory insurance on federally backed mortgages, elevation minimums and what you owe a buyer at sale, and pegs FEMA's own figure for zone AE at a 26% chance of flooding over a 30-year mortgage [fXtOfFlKqmc @ 00:00:36]. Felicia of Compass Land USA frames the entire flood-zone fight the same way: everything is based around elevation, and a parcel only comes out of a high-risk area when documentation shows the mapped zone is wrong [bPbMFP-bGyU @ 00:01:00].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Bosch's repricing rule is mechanical. Take a 10-acre rural parcel worth $40,000 with road access; once it proves truly landlocked it might only be worth $15,000 to $20,000, so Bosch personally cuts value at least in half and makes the offer from there [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:05:47]. At a typical 20 to 25 percent offer, that is about $4,000 for the parcel, and Bosch says the Facebook group sees students posting deals at 10, 15 and 20 cents on the dollar nearly every week. From a $4,000 basis, the fast exit is a quick resale at $12,000 to $15,000 for an $8,000 to $10,000 profit [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:06:58]. If four separate owners stand between the parcel and the road, Bosch skips the easement hunt entirely: put it under contract at $3,500 to $4,000, sell at $12,000, and let the next buyer deal with it, disclosing that there is currently no legal or physical access while pitching that installing access could double the value toward $40,000 [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:07:47]. The Apke Brothers read proximity the same way, calling a 60-acre Oklahoma tract with a pond in the middle a great situation to be in precisely because it sits so close to the road [5p6zCt25Tyw @ 00:00:42].

When only one parcel separates the land from the street, Bosch pulls the neighbor's information from public record, sends a letter or calls, and pitches a strip along the side of the neighbor's property that would not affect anything they do; the leverage, which Bosch says you keep to yourself, is that a judge would grant the easiest access anyway [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:08:30]. A reasonable neighbor might ask $500, and that payment captures the spread between a $20,000 landlocked value and a $40,000 accessible value [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:09:36]. Bosch then sells at $35,000 on seller financing, takes a $5,000 to $7,000 down payment that alone exceeds the purchase price, collects $500 to $600 a month, and estimates the interest pushes the take roughly $50,000 past what the deal would otherwise produce. The Apke Brothers run a heavier version: buy the 10 acres fronting the road outright, paying 70 to 80 percent of retail, and still double the money because the landlocked tract was bought so cheap [5p6zCt25Tyw @ 00:01:08]. Chris Thomas closes the paper loop through a title company, which drafts a separate easement agreement, often a simple one-page document notarized with witnesses, usually backed by a survey, and recorded like a deed [gwLVELHJjbc @ 00:10:27].

Flood screening starts free. Chad, executive director of the National Association of State Floodplain Managers, walks through searching for the FEMA flood map viewer, typing an address into the search bar, and reading the colors: the highest-hazard part of the flood zone, a reddish-tan moderate hazard area beyond it, and the floodway, the especially risky strip marked with blue hatching; county maps can add local detail [ptM7-3KSnO4 @ 00:01:15]. Jeremy at PushLeads then orders an elevation certificate from a licensed surveyor at $400 to $800, calling it the single most powerful lever on premium because every foot above base flood elevation earns a discount [fXtOfFlKqmc @ 00:04:04]. If that survey shows the parcel sits above BFE but was mismapped, a letter of map amendment runs $1,500 to $5,000 in engineering and survey costs and can cut premiums by $1,000 or more a year, paying back within months; a preliminary map carries a 90-day appeal window, after which the new zone is final [fXtOfFlKqmc @ 00:04:43]. Felicia at Compass Land USA quotes a LOMA at around 500 to submit with responses taking upwards of 60 days, insists the map be revised before building starts, and flags imported fill dirt as a LOMR-F opportunity once the permit is pulled [bPbMFP-bGyU @ 00:03:48].

callout.title: Leverage Moves Practitioners Use on Access and Flood Deals
callout.body: Small tactical edges the practitioners use to shift cost, time, and negotiating power in their favor.
items: When a neighbor overprices an easement, have the appraiser value the neighbor's diminution in value rather than your lot's gain; the appraiser says roughly $20,000 in legal fees likely wins the suit when the route is the only option, so your negotiating room is the cost of litigation [dhall3000 — GpQWztIpKSo @ 00:05:17].

Dodge survey costs: tell the seller the title company needs a survey to close and ask how they want to pay, get the surveyor paid from closing proceeds, or have seller and buyer each pay half so both think they are splitting it with you [Land Flipping 101 — gwLVELHJjbc @ 00:12:02].
Revise the flood map before you start building, and pull the permit before bringing in fill dirt if you plan a fill-based map revision [Compass Land USA — bPbMFP-bGyU @ 00:02:22].

If a driveway has been used for years without paperwork, use that history as leverage: the crossed owner is already used to the access, which makes getting it in writing easier [David Miller — orMrWlpfWj4 @ 00:03:10].

sop_steps.title: Prove the Access Status
sop_steps.action: Pull county records, order a title search, and check whether any boundary matches the right-of-way line.
sop_steps.detail: Thomas runs a title search on all properties and conditions every purchase on road access, while Bosch treats any recorded easement in county records as legal access that ends the landlocked label [Land Flipping 101 — gwLVELHJjbc @ 00:06:37] [Land Profit Generator with Jack & Michelle Bosch — tfERI-RnheU @ 00:02:31].

sop_steps.title: Reprice Before You Offer
sop_steps.action: Cut the accessible value at least in half, then offer roughly 20 to 25 percent of the reduced figure.
sop_steps.detail: Bosch drops a $40,000 parcel to $15,000-$20,000 when truly landlocked and offers around $4,000; the Apke Brothers warn never to pay more than a landlocked price [Land Profit Generator with Jack & Michelle Bosch — tfERI-RnheU @ 00:05:47] [Apke Brothers — 5p6zCt25Tyw @ 00:00:27].

sop_steps.title: Screen Flood Zone and Elevation
sop_steps.action: Search the parcel in the FEMA flood map viewer, read the zone colors, and order an elevation certificate if it lands in a high-risk zone.
sop_steps.detail: Enter the address in the viewer search bar to read hazard colors, then get a $400-$800 elevation certificate that controls premium and supports a LOMA [LAVERNE MCGEE TV — ptM7-3KSnO4 @ 00:00:57] [PushLeads — fXtOfFlKqmc @ 00:04:04].

sop_steps.title: Choose the Exit and Record It
sop_steps.action: Flip as-is with disclosure when multiple neighbors block the road, or buy the easement and record it when one neighbor stands in the way.
sop_steps.detail: Bosch flips hard-to-unlock parcels and captures the upside on easy ones, while Legal Counsel P.A. has an attorney memorialize any agreed easement and record it in the county public records [Land Profit Generator with Jack & Michelle Bosch — tfERI-RnheU @ 00:10:43] [Legal Counsel P.A. — 4mnTabZRS60 @ 00:01:06].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether access is a birthright or a fight. LandApp by LandGate tells owners flatly that neighboring owners cannot deny access because federal and state laws protect it [2lVnO8IebI0 @ 00:01:54], and attorney David Holmes, on David Miller's channel, says anyone holding landlocked property has an absolute right to reach the nearest accessible public right-of-way, either by negotiated easement or, if all else fails, a condemnation action [orMrWlpfWj4 @ 00:00:50]. The landlocked owner on dhall3000 hears the same from their appraiser: in Washington you can't be landlocked, so the suit is highly likely to win, though it might burn $20,000 in legal fees [GpQWztIpKSo @ 00:04:16]. Tiffany Lashmet of Texas Agriculture Law calls that belief a misconception to clear up once and for all: property absolutely can be landlocked in Texas, there is no automatic right to access, and each of roughly five legal methods carries elements you must prove before a court hands you a judgment [D_ZiLS1CYJg @ 00:00:22]. The operator takeaway is jurisdictional: the same parcel can be a winnable lawsuit in one state and a dead asset in another, so the price you pay has to reflect which rulebook governs the dirt you are buying.

On deal structure, the land flippers run three different plays. Jack Bosch cuts the value of a truly landlocked parcel at least in half before offering, so a $40,000 ten-acre tract becomes a $15,000 to $20,000 asset, and the offer lands around 20 to 25 percent of that, roughly $4,000 [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:05:31]. From there Bosch forks the deal: if four properties sit between the parcel and the road, put it under contract at $3,500 to $4,000 and sell it for $12,000, letting the next buyer chase the easements; if only one neighbor stands in the way, call or mail that owner and pay something like $500 for the easement [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:07:31]. The Apke Brothers skip the easement entirely on a 60-acre Oklahoma lake parcel sitting close to the road: go to the owner of the 10 acres between it and the road and buy that frontage outright, paying 70 to 80 percent of retail because the landlocked piece was bought at such a discount that the combined deal can still double [5p6zCt25Tyw @ 00:00:55]. The appraiser on dhall3000 adds a third lens, reporting that a before-and-after valuation of the benefited lot and a diminution analysis of the neighbor's lot produce widely divergent numbers, and either can be used to negotiate [GpQWztIpKSo @ 00:02:17].

Practitioners also split on how much an unwritten path is worth. Bosch treats a long-used physical road with no recorded easement as a fixable asset: after roughly 10 years of use in some states and 15 in others, it ripens into an easement by prescription that can be entered into the county records, so the parcel is not truly landlocked [tfERI-RnheU @ 00:04:19]. Holmes puts the clock at 20 years or so and warns that a prescriptive easement is not written and documented, so financial institutions won't recognize it; its real value is as leverage to get the crossing owner to sign something in writing [orMrWlpfWj4 @ 00:02:51]. On the flood side, the cost of fighting a bad map diverges sharply between channels. Compass Land USA prices a LOMA at around $500 to submit with upwards of 60 days for a response, and stresses revising the map before you start building if you want to avoid paying for flood insurance [bPbMFP-bGyU @ 00:03:48]. Jeremy of PushLeads quotes $1,500 to $5,000 in engineering and survey costs, but says a successful LOMA can cut premiums by $1,000 or more per year and pay back the investment within months [fXtOfFlKqmc @ 00:04:43].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap is relying on access nobody wrote down. In Barry v Hasseldine, the plot's original access ran over a disused airfield on a stranger's land by permission; in 1950 the stranger fenced it off, and Barry had to sue to force a way of necessity over the seller's retained land, with the court holding that a mere permissive way can be terminated at any time [wij1Dm2XEX8 @ 00:00:18]. NBC 10 WJAR documented the street version: the Stone and King families pay thousands in taxes on roughly 8 and 64 acres in North Smithfield, but about 10 years ago the neighbors to the north put massive boulders and a metal gate across two paper roads that appear on town documents back to 1843, so the families now paddle across a pond to reach their land legally [gnZroureXsw @ 00:00:56]. When the Stones finally got back in, 2.7 acres of trees were missing, now part of a Superior Court lawsuit against the businesses [gnZroureXsw @ 00:03:17]. Chris Thomas of Land Flipping 101 frames the same risk in deal terms: if there is no legal language in the deed covering a road that crosses another person's property, the new owner can close that road off [gwLVELHJjbc @ 00:02:19].

The second trap is assuming an exit buyer can borrow. Lashmet says you can't get title insurance on a property with no legal access, and without it most lenders will not allow a mortgage or let you use the land as collateral, which shrinks the buyer pool for the flip [D_ZiLS1CYJg @ 00:01:17]. Holmes agrees that no lender will loan on land it cannot reach in a foreclosure, so landlocked tracts get bought with cash and the easement gets figured out afterward; a buyer who skips a legal-access condition in the purchase contract is the one who pays to acquire the access later [orMrWlpfWj4 @ 00:01:54]. Thomas responds by conditioning every purchase on road access, ordering a title search on every deal because not all easements are searchable in public records, and insisting on utility line and pipe rights alongside the road easement because without them the land loses a lot of its value [gwLVELHJjbc @ 00:06:37]. Survey cost is treated as a negotiation rather than an expense: Thomas pushes it onto the seller, onto the closing proceeds, or splits it so seller and buyer each think they are halving it with Thomas while the survey gets paid for 100 percent by them [gwLVELHJjbc @ 00:12:02].

Flood labels carry their own reversals. Jeremy of PushLeads warns that more than 20% of National Flood Insurance Program claims come from zones with no federal mandate, where one inch of water averages a $25,000 loss, and that renovations exceeding 50% of pre-improvement market value can trigger full structure elevation costing $30,000 to $100,000 or more [fXtOfFlKqmc @ 00:04:24]. Miss the 90-day appeal window on a preliminary map and the new zone is final, with FEMA updating maps every 5 to 10 years [fXtOfFlKqmc @ 00:05:02]. Compass Land USA adds that a LOMA does not change the flood risk itself, the property may still flood after removal, and fill dirt brought in for building needs a permit before it arrives [bPbMFP-bGyU @ 00:02:22]. On the ground, Amber Shah's door-knocking run in St. Augustine shows how messy the cheap neighbor easement can get: the only route crosses a fenced backyard at an absentee owner's non-primary residence, drops toward an off-road area where improvements may be barred, and runs into St. John's River District land, with no way to be sure what anybody is willing to do [O6tZ8o1scfY @ 00:03:22].

callout.title: Kill-or-Proceed Checks Before Signing on Access or Flood Risk
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, lawsuit, or dead end practitioners hit firsthand. Clear all four before committing earnest money or pricing the exit.
items: Do not price a deal as landlocked until county records confirm there is neither a recorded easement nor a long-used physical road; Bosch only treats a parcel with neither legal nor actual road access as truly landlocked [Land Profit Generator with Jack & Michelle Bosch — tfERI-RnheU @ 00:01:59].
Never count permissive access as legal access; a mere permissive way can be terminated at any time, as the airfield fence in Barry v Hasseldine proved [Law Case Summaries — wij1Dm2XEX8 @ 00:01:14].
Assume the exit buyer cannot get title insurance or a mortgage on a parcel with no legal access, and price the flip for cash buyers only [Texas Agriculture Law — D_ZiLS1CYJg @ 00:01:17].

Check the flood zone before any build or renovation, because work exceeding 50% of pre-improvement market value can trigger $30,000 to $100,000 or more in elevation costs [PushLeads — fXtOfFlKqmc @ 00:04:24].

chapters.pull_quote: "First figure out exactly: are they truly landlocked? If it's too hard to get the easement, just flip them. If it's easy to get the easement, get it and capture that upside." — Jack Bosch, Land Profit Generator with Jack & Michelle Bosch (tfERI-RnheU @ 00:10:43).
action_checklist: Open the FEMA flood map viewer, enter the parcel address in the top-left search bar, read the zone colors and floodway hatching, then call the county for any local flood maps [LAVERNE MCGEE TV — ptM7-3KSnO4 @ 00:00:57].
For any A or V zone parcel, order an elevation certificate from a licensed surveyor at $400 to $800 to control premiums and support a LOMA challenge [PushLeads — fXtOfFlKqmc @ 00:04:04].
Run a title search on every deal and condition the purchase on legal road access plus utility line and pipe rights [Land Flipping 101 — gwLVELHJjbc @ 00:06:37].

If only one neighbor sits between the parcel and the road, pull their public-record contact info, send a letter or call, and offer a small payment such as $500 for the easement [Land Profit Generator with Jack & Michelle Bosch — tfERI-RnheU @ 00:08:30].

Have a title company or real estate attorney draw up the easement as a one-page document, notarized with witnesses, and record it in the county public records [Land Flipping 101 — gwLVELHJjbc @ 00:10:07].
If the neighbor refuses, commission an appraisal of the neighbor's diminution in value and negotiate knowing your ceiling is the cost of litigation [dhall3000 — GpQWztIpKSo @ 00:05:17].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I subdivide a parcel to multiply profit on a land deal?
chapters.title: Subdividing Land for Profit
chapters.subtitle: Step-by-step subdivides in Land Portal, minor vs. major subdivides, types of subdivisions, rural acreage splits, the 80-acre Minnesota and $192K case studies, $500K from a minor subdivide, surveying projects, and Australian plan-of-subdivision processes
chapters.executive_summary: Land operators converge on one engine: buy acreage at the bulk per-acre price and resell smaller pieces at the higher small-lot per-acre price, with road frontage, minimum lot size, utilities and access deciding how many lots a parcel can yield. Rural paper splits and exempt plats run cheap and fast: Jack Bosch cites a roughly $400 application and six weeks in Arizona, Clay Hepler netted $235K on 80 Minnesota acres in under six months, and Jon Jasniak turned 79 Texas acres into $818K of seller-financed notes. Urban and suburban operators like Jerome Maldonado and David Reitz split half-acre to two-acre infill lots for builders. Disagreements center on deal size, seller financing versus cash exits, infill versus rural recreational land, and how much engineering, hearings and timeline risk to absorb.
