sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The engine every operator describes is price-per-acre arbitrage. Jack Bosch frames it as a $30 cake sold as twelve $5 slices for $60, then puts numbers on it: a 40-acre parcel worth $40,000 cut into ten 4-acre lots at $10,000 to $15,000 each lands around $150,000, roughly a 4x, and seller financing can push it toward $300,000 [JXUkA5K7RSc @ 00:02:11]. The Apke Brothers make the spread the market filter itself: 25 acres at $125,000 is $5,000 an acre, while five 5-acre lots at $50,000 each total $250,000, and any county where small and large acreage price the same gets skipped [8LneZstpCGY @ 00:01:56]. Neil Clements on REtipster uses the same logic to justify paying sellers 90 to 100 percent of market value instead of the usual 50 to 60 percent, because 50 acres bought at $10,000 an acre and resold as five 10-acre lots at $20,000 an acre exits at $1 million [TzjxQStPaW4 @ 00:02:36]. Paul Jang's Oklahoma deal shows the small-scale version: 10 acres bought for $32,000, cut into five lots worth a combined $95,000 to $120,000, roughly 3x, with bigger tracts carrying thinner margins but fatter dollar totals, such as 100 acres at $100,000 split into ten $30,000 lots for $300,000 [e8Ouv9k5iag @ 00:04:56].

Before any line gets drawn on a map, the gating variables are the same across the board: road frontage, legal access, minimum lot size and utilities. Clay Hepler calls failing to check road access the single biggest mistake and screens for 10 to 100 acres with public road frontage, power nearby and no flood or slope problems [o_c7zC-iYqE @ 00:03:26]. Dr. Dirt calls road frontage 'super super important' for minor subdivides and runs the math live: 1,300 feet of frontage divided by four is 325 feet per lot, but a 350-foot county minimum yields only 3.7, so the parcel supports three lots [7wJsf4BbLHY @ 00:57:06]. Simply Invested, staking a just-under-one-acre lot beside a standard tract subdivision, puts it bluntly: more road frontage makes lots easier to cut up and market, while narrow frontage yields one lot, maybe two, as 'awkward long rectangle Lots' [bYgyURXYuP0 @ 00:04:26]. Sumner Healey adds that utilities can dictate the minimum lot size outright, screens out topography with 20 to 30 degree slopes, generally rejects flood or wetlands coverage above roughly 30 to 50 percent, and refuses any deal that requires building a road [pWQCNBiSpUY @ 00:04:23]. The shared conclusion is that frontage and access, not raw acreage, set the lot count.

Every operator also agrees the county or city planning office is the first call, not the last. Jack Bosch tells subdividers to check zoning minimums, sketch the setback building envelope, then talk to the city or county because some processes take a year [JXUkA5K7RSc @ 00:04:39]. Clay Hepler's script is three questions for the county planner: minimum lot size, deed split versus survey plat, and approval timeline [o_c7zC-iYqE @ 00:02:56]. The consensus tiering runs from cheapest to heaviest. BiggerPockets describes the simple path as a legal description, a recorded deed and a certificate of title, versus the complex path of preliminary plat, engineering review, construction and final plat, with timelines ranging from weeks to years [y_3SP6N-l4c @ 00:04:55]. Dr. Dirt pegs a minor subdivide at plat-and-record, about three months of process and nine months total, against a major subdivide with road, sewer and electric that can run about 30 months, the territory of entitlement specialists who do two deals a year, gross around $1 million annually and may front $500,000 [7wJsf4BbLHY @ 00:45:36]. That gap is why nearly every operator here hunts minor splits, paper splits and statewide exemptions first, and treats major plats with new roads as a separate, capital-heavy business.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The cheapest street-level split is the Arizona five split. Jack Bosch lays out the rules: pieces over one acre, road access to each, a new legal description for each, and no survey or corner markers required, which is why it is 'simply also called a paper split' [JXUkA5K7RSc @ 00:06:06]. The run is a title company charging a few hundred dollars for descriptions, an application fee around $400 and about six weeks to approval, typically carving one 20-acre piece plus four 5-acre pieces sold at $15,000 each on $3,000 down and $300 a month for eight years [JXUkA5K7RSc @ 00:09:17]. In Texas the lever is the statewide exemption for resulting lots of 10 acres or more; Neil Clements says only a surveyor is needed and the exempt plat can produce 1.5 to 2x [TzjxQStPaW4 @ 00:03:40]. Jon Jasniak ran that exemption on 79 acres near Stanton in Martin County, cutting six 10-acre lots and one 19-acre lot after sending the surveyor a Google Earth sketch. The purchase was $70,000 down on a $210,000 note with a two-year balloon, the 10-acre lots went out at $1,250 down and $1,250 a month for 120 months, everything sold within three days, and $818,000 of notes became roughly $538,000 after debt and the down payment [N5LpbcKdDVE @ 00:04:19].

Suburban infill runs on different math because the buyer is a builder. Jerome Maldonado splits one-acre lots into half-acre lots in $500,000 to $800,000 custom-home areas, skipping the $200,000 to $400,000 median-price builders, and budgets a pencil sketch, a survey of a few hundred dollars and a city development meeting of a couple hundred dollars, with council meeting every 30 days for about 60 days total [ffCHGUtstfA @ 00:07:25]. Maldonado's builder math: two half-acre lots at $100,000 each net about $99,000 after roughly $1,000 in costs [ffCHGUtstfA @ 00:12:20]. On a 2.1-acre lot listed at $150,000, Maldonado negotiated down to about $110,000 because of a waterway, spent about $15,000 on dirt work for a $125,000 basis, and keeps the split plan hidden from the seller behind a delayed close [fNHhVpzVhdo @ 00:04:56]. David Reitz entitles while under contract: a 1.2-acre parcel in Depew at a $45,000 contract price, $2,500 for engineer concept drawings, a $60,000 to $80,000 shared driveway, and four $50,000 to $60,000 lots, a roughly $200,000 asset on $120,000 to $150,000 all-in, with the engineer, architect, permits and fees charged to an AMEX card [WHUzvXvl_18 @ 00:03:49].

Sourcing is systematized. The Apke Brothers run Landportal's LP Intelligence across Georgia counties, flagging Gilmore at $9,000 an acre for 25 to 50 acres versus $20,000 an acre for 3 to 7 acres, then filtering Carroll County for road frontage over 800 feet, FEMA flood zone and wetlands each under 50 percent, AI buildability over 50 percent, and 25 to 60 acres outside city limits, which returned 50 results to skip trace and hit by mail, text and cold call [8LneZstpCGY @ 00:05:35]. Dr. Dirt works Zillow instead: owner-posted lots and land, pending listings included because contracts fall through, one acre or more, over 12 months on market, saves near 10 percent of views, and a price cut five days in as a motivation tell, with Land Insights and Land Portal used on free tiers [7wJsf4BbLHY @ 00:02:36]. For rules, Sumner Healey Googles the county subdivision regulations, reads page count as a complexity signal, as with Wilson County's 97 pages, and searches 'exemptions' to find the over-10-acre unlimited-cuts rule [pWQCNBiSpUY @ 00:15:43]. Dr. Dirt also feeds the APN into Claude or ChatGPT to pull county minor-subdivide rules before calling planners [7wJsf4BbLHY @ 00:49:34].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over what size dirt to chase. Jerome Maldonado runs small infill: carve 1-acre lots into half-acre lots in $500K to $800K custom-home areas, because appraisals follow the house's square footage, not the lot, and two half-acre lots at $100K each net about $99K after roughly $1K in costs [ffCHGUtstfA @ 00:12:20]. Dr. Dirt goes the opposite way. He focuses on rural recreational land of 5-plus acres and avoids infill entirely, where he says buying at $5K and selling at $10K nets only $1K to $2K [7wJsf4BbLHY @ 01:08:29]. David Reitz sits in between. He targets half an acre to 2 acres because bigger projects drag in HOAs and attorney fees, refuses townhomes for the same reason, and uses a shared maintenance agreement instead of an HOA [WHUzvXvl_18 @ 00:05:13]. Paul Jang frames the trade-off in pure scale terms: bigger lots carry thinner margins but fatter dollar amounts. His example is 100 acres bought for $100K and cut into ten $30K lots for $300K, against his 10-acre Oklahoma deal that ran roughly 3x [e8Ouv9k5iag @ 00:04:56]. Infill rewards builder relationships and high home values, while rural acreage rewards frontage, volume, and buyer financing.

Practitioners also disagree on how much engineering a split really needs. Jack Bosch teaches the Arizona five split as a pure paper split. The pieces must be over 1 acre, each needs road access and a new legal description, and no survey or corner markers are required. A title company charges a few hundred dollars, the application fee runs roughly $400, and approval takes about six weeks [JXUkA5K7RSc @ 00:06:56]. Jon Jasniak went nearly as light in Texas, sending his surveyor a Google Earth sketch on a 79-acre platting-exempt deal [N5LpbcKdDVE @ 00:03:29]. On the other side, BiggerPockets says getting through for under $2K is rare and that impact fees alone can reach tens of thousands per lot [y_3SP6N-l4c @ 00:05:45]. Kent Cliffe puts a basic Australian house-lot subdivision at $25K to $30K in WA, $30K to $40K in other states, and up to $60K in some areas [Ie0jq4Go9is @ 00:00:46]. Bosch himself says that outside five-split states the work becomes surveys, corner stakes, maps, and hearings over three to nine months. Jurisdiction decides it: an exempt rural split runs on paper, while anything that triggers a plat, new utilities, or a council hearing becomes an engineering project with a real budget.

Acquisition posture and exit structure split the field too. REtipster's Neil Clements argues a value-add subdivider can pay 90 to 100 percent of market value instead of the usual 50 to 60 percent, because the split itself creates the margin [TzjxQStPaW4 @ 00:01:17]. Jerome Maldonado plays harder at the table. He negotiated a 2.1-acre lot listed at $150K down to about $110K by pointing to a waterway, and he teaches hiding the split plan from the seller and using a delayed close [fNHhVpzVhdo @ 00:04:56]. On the exit, Jack Bosch says seller financing can double a $150K cash split to $300K [JXUkA5K7RSc @ 00:02:59]. Jon Jasniak sold his 10-acre lots at $1,250 down and $1,250 a month for 120 months, then sold the notes to investors before his own 2-year balloon came due [N5LpbcKdDVE @ 00:04:19]. Maldonado instead sells finished dirt to builders such as D.R. Horton, or builds himself for $250K to $300K profit per house. David Reitz keeps three exits open: sell paper lots, build one, or build all. Cash buyers and builders mean a fast, clean payday. Terms buyers mean a bigger total and a note book to manage or sell.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated trap is access. Clay Hepler names not checking road access as the biggest subdivision mistake [o_c7zC-iYqE @ 00:03:26], and Dr. Dirt warns that without physical access, value drops sharply [7wJsf4BbLHY @ 00:50:27]. Frontage math quietly cuts lot counts. Dr. Dirt walks through 1,300 feet of frontage divided by four, which looks like 325 feet per lot. But the county minimum is 350 feet, which yields only 3.7 lots, so the deal is really three [7wJsf4BbLHY @ 00:54:54]. Simply Invested hits the same ceiling in the field. He notes that a narrow-frontage parcel would probably be one lot, maybe two, and then you are stuck with awkward long rectangle lots [bYgyURXYuP0 @ 00:04:26]. Dr. Dirt adds that just because a layout works on a map does not mean it is going to sell, and he calls flagpole lots love-it-or-hate-it with buyers. Sumner Healey refuses to build roads at all. He screens out 20 to 30 degree slopes and parcels with more than 30 to 50 percent flood or wetlands before ever drawing lines. Divide the frontage by the county minimum and round down before putting a number on any lot.

Hidden infrastructure costs are where margins evaporate. Kent Cliffe hit a 4.5-metre-deep sewer with a 2.5-metre water table that required dewatering, turning a roughly $3.5K connection into about $17K. Separately, a structural truncation of about 6 square metres cost him around $40K [Ie0jq4Go9is @ 00:05:32]. David Reitz's Depew layout needed a shared driveway priced at $60K to $80K plus utility feed lines. That pushed a $50K land deal to $120K to $150K all-in for four lots worth roughly $200K [WHUzvXvl_18 @ 00:02:15]. Dr. Dirt flags power as a deal-breaker: if bringing electricity runs around $200K, lot prices must rise or the cost gets split across every lot [7wJsf4BbLHY @ 00:49:01]. Jerome Maldonado tells operators to check utilities and infrastructure first, naming asphalt, curbs, and gutters, and says sewage became a huge issue on his 110-acre project [ZvmmZBcu3kc @ 00:02:42]. Smaller line items stack up too. Sumner Healey laid out vertical cuts specifically to avoid brush hogging. Kent Cliffe calls stormwater soakwells, concrete, and retaining big lumpy costs. Price utilities, access construction, and site clearing before making the offer.

Time and approvals are the final failure layer. REtipster warns that a major plat brings new roads, a civil engineer, and six-figure plan costs, and the risks include a buyer walking away or plans being rejected [TzjxQStPaW4 @ 00:09:40]. Dr. Dirt calls public hearings a real risk on rezoning. He tells operators to keep multiple exits or make the purchase contract contingent on rezoning [7wJsf4BbLHY @ 00:35:22]. He also notes that ag land is assessed lower, so rezoning brings a tax hike. Jerome Maldonado says a missing item in the application package costs a 30-day delay. That package is the address or legal description, the survey, the proposed lot line, and the covenants [fNHhVpzVhdo @ 00:04:14]. Peter Kelly says rookies focus on the build and fail to give the subdivision process the respect it requires, and any slip pushes back settlement and payday. If there is a mortgage, the bank holds the original title and must release it [3jBR5FOYoag @ 00:04:33]. Sumner Healey received one survey quote of $12K and six months. David Reitz deals with a variance board that meets only every two to three months. Build the approval calendar before signing the contract.

chapters.question_prompt: What approvals, restrictions, and encumbrances limit what can legally be done with a parcel?
chapters.title: Approvals, Restrictions, and Encumbrances
chapters.subtitle: Minor partitions, subdivision approval steps and costs, road frontage requirements, backyard subdivision mistakes, raw land traps on access and utility costs, wetland reserve easements, coastal storm flowage zones, deed restrictions and how to remove them, HOA CC&Rs, and mineral, timber, and grazing rights
chapters.executive_summary: Land flippers who survive approvals treat the recorded file and the county rulebook as the real product. Restriction specialists agree that deed restrictions and CC&Rs run with the land, that 'no HOA' still leaves recorded covenants able to bar livestock, RVs, or garages, and that only the original grantor or their heirs can lift a deed restriction. Subdivision operators agree every parcel needs real road frontage and a recorded plat before lots sell. The street numbers are hard: perc tests near $1,300, septic $5,000 to $30,000, utilities $9,000 to $34,500 or $40,000 to $80,000 with site work, Nashville plats at $1,375, and county roads demanding 20 feet of surface and 40 to 50 feet of right-of-way. Disagreement centers on scale: Cody Bjugan says partition paydays are not comparable to his 250-lot projects yet still backs them for beginners.

key_metrics.label: Average Perc Test Cost
key_metrics.value: About $1,300 (typical $750-$1,900; full range $250 to over $3,500)
key_metrics.context: Raw-land buyers should make offers contingent on the perc test and use a licensed local tester; results stay valid 2-5 years.

key_metrics.label: County Approved Road Upgrade Spec
key_metrics.value: About 20 ft surface, 6-8 in base rock, 40-50 ft right-of-way, max 15% grade (more likely 12%)
key_metrics.context: What a driveway must be upgraded to so split parcels have frontage on a county approved road; described as very costly.

key_metrics.label: Nashville Final Plat Fee
key_metrics.value: $1,375 final plat; $3,000 major concept plan
key_metrics.context: Compared with Huntsville at $50 plus $1 per lot and Toledo at $150 per split; the government fee is often the smallest line.

key_metrics.label: Backyard Split Access Width
key_metrics.value: About 4 m clear width, not 3 m
key_metrics.context: Minimum practical access to a rear lot, with 1 parking space for 2-bed and 2 for 3+ bed homes on both titles.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across the restriction-focused operators, the baseline is blunt: whatever is recorded against the dirt travels with the dirt, and the buyer inherits it whether or not anyone mentioned it at the showing. Just Call Maggie frames deed restrictions as private controls written into the deed by the seller, enforced privately by the previous owner, a developer, or an HOA rather than by government, and binding every future owner; her example is a 'No commercial businesses' clause that blocks a cafe or shop permanently unless it is legally lifted [sazxc_VdXOw @ 00:01:05]. The Real Estate Lawyer lands in the same spot, describing deed restrictions such as 'no livestock' as legal limits that run with the land [gP3fDaUu5Iw @ 00:00:15]. Danielle Dojcak attacks a common assumption in land deals: agents and buyers hear 'no HOA' and conclude there are no rules, yet recorded covenants can still bar chickens, livestock, horses, detached garages, or boat and RV parking [ieOUjD1jQXA @ 00:00:24]. Tyler Bobo sees the same pattern in the Alaska valley, where buyers move to escape rules but most subdivisions still carry CC&Rs that travel with the property and stay enforceable even when vague and ignored [zzxrwQSJnC4 @ 00:00:49].

On the approval side, the subdivision operators agree that the county, not the seller, decides what a parcel can become. Tim Howell treats any new parcel, or even moving a line between two parcels, as a subdivision, and says each resulting parcel needs frontage on an actual road rather than an easement, though some counties accept a joint permanent easement [rtRAjfGZ_nY @ 00:00:14]. Liberty Acres runs the same front-end screen: check zoning, minimum lot size, frontage, and setbacks, then ask planning staff whether the split is minor or major and get the checklist; a minor split runs along an existing road, while a major one needs a new street, utilities, or engineering [qSoWEXftiCQ @ 00:00:20]. Cody Bjugan draws the line by count, saying a minor partition is about three parcels and that in a lot of jurisdictions four or more lots counts as a subdivision, and he concedes partitions are easier and quicker to push through [1B8q3q_Xt-s @ 00:00:00]. Liberty Acres also flags the legal hook that kills shortcut flips: most states bar lot sales until the plat is recorded, and selling the whole parcel instead shifts the risk to the buyer [qSoWEXftiCQ @ 00:01:22].

The third point of agreement is timing: dig up every restriction and access instrument before money goes hard, not after the buyer has fallen in love. US Realty Training warns that buyers fall for a house without knowing its restrictions and tells agents to research before the buyer plans substantial changes, naming two lookups, a title search and the county clerk's deed abstract that lists all restrictions [B_XnC97BYF8 @ 00:03:38]. Dana Sparks of Real Estate Made Crystal Clear pins the window precisely: pull the CC&Rs during due diligence so the buyer can still terminate and protect earnest money [okIP6dYiTD4 @ 00:04:03]. Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision applies the same logic to raw land, where sellers usually are not required to disclose problems, and insists that physical access is not legal access; verbal access means nothing because lenders and title companies need a recorded easement [VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:04:05]. Danielle Dojcak turns it into a field rule for anyone representing land: when a buyer says 'I want land,' ask why, then hunt for recorded deed restrictions that conflict with that use, alongside zoning, easements, permits, and health-department requirements, and stop, verify, and ask before making representations [ieOUjD1jQXA @ 00:00:36].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Liberty Acres lays out the approval run in five moves: check zoning, minimum lot size, frontage, and setbacks; get the minor-or-major call and checklist from planning staff; have a licensed surveyor draw the plat; do the septic soil work before the vote; then collect utility sign-offs, file, attend the hearing, and record the plat [qSoWEXftiCQ @ 00:00:00]. The thresholds and fees swing by jurisdiction: Washington allows four or fewer lots as a short subdivision, Toledo allows up to five as a lot split, Huntsville charges $50 plus $1 per lot, Toledo charges $150 per split, and Nashville charges $1,375 for a final plat and $3,000 for a major concept plan, with Toledo clearing in several weeks against roughly 120 days in Huntsville [qSoWEXftiCQ @ 00:01:00]. The channel's point is that the government application fee is often the smallest line in a stack that also carries surveyor, septic, engineering, road, bonds, and recording. Tim Howell shows where that stack explodes: upgrading a driveway to a county approved road means about 20 feet of surface, six to eight inches of base rock, a 40 to 50 foot right-of-way, and a grade no steeper than 15 percent, more likely 12, which he calls very costly [rtRAjfGZ_nY @ 00:01:20].

Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision prices the hidden approval stack on raw land, opening with the warning that an $8,000 acre can turn into $60,000 more [VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:00:00]. A perc test averages about $1,300, typically $750 to $1,900 and anywhere from $250 to over $3,500, with survey at $370 to $770 and design and permitting at $500 to $1,200; septic then runs $5,000 to $25,000 for a standard system, $15,000 to $30,000 for a mound, $12,000 to $25,000 aerobic, and $15,000 to $25,000 for a sand filter [VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:02:13]. The channel tells buyers to make the offer contingent on the perc test, use a licensed local tester, and remember results stay valid two to five years. Utilities total $9,000 to $34,500, or $40,000 to $80,000 and up with full site work: power at $5 to $25 per foot with some utilities charging $50 to $100, poles at $1,200 to $5,600 each, and wells at $25 to $65 per foot complete, typically 100 to 300 feet deep, with contractor bids varying 30 to 60 percent [VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:06:13]. Peter Kelly Property adds the backyard-split version: about four metres of clear access width, not three, plus compliant parking for both homes [KmCwZ5I6BYU @ 00:03:49].

On recorded restrictions and mineral claims, the mechanics are records work. Dana Sparks hunts CC&Rs through the seller, the Georgia HOA directory, county deed books, the gsccca.org real estate index using 'view image' with printing costing extra, and the Secretary of State corporations search to pin down the HOA's legal name [okIP6dYiTD4 @ 00:07:16]. The Real Estate Lawyer warns that removing a deed restriction means tracing the original grantor's heirs or successor entities; in one case two children fanned out to ten grandchildren, and a single holdout makes removal challenging if not impossible [gP3fDaUu5Iw @ 00:01:53]. When an HOA claims minerals, HOA LAND WARS runs the chain parcel by parcel: a county parcel map showed the lease acreage exceeded HOA-owned parcels, five document requests went out for the lease, board resolution, legal description, recorded authority instrument, and the payee-determining company, and the recorder search turned up a reservation, assignment, and partial release, none naming the HOA [CnlqGcAGqOo @ 00:06:26]. In the HOA Insanity case, the owner spent two weeks tracing title back to the 1890s, found no severance in the chain, and defended a $50,000 signing bonus and 18 percent royalty offer against the HOA's common-assets claim [KuFkYy1kf7s @ 00:02:28].

callout.title: Field Moves From The Recorder's Office And The County Counter
callout.body: These are the small moves the operators use to read a parcel's real constraints before they commit capital or make a promise to a buyer.
items: Drive the neighborhood and compare actual compliance to the CC&Rs: if there are no horses, don't get horses, and if farms are everywhere, enforcement is less likely [Tyler Bobo Investor, Alaska Realtor — zzxrwQSJnC4 @ 00:01:33].

Run the Secretary of State corporations search to find the HOA's exact name, then pull the recorded covenants from the gsccca.org index with 'view image'; the broker may pay for printing [Real Estate Made Crystal Clear — okIP6dYiTD4 @ 00:08:27].

On coastal parcels, check the date of the coastal study rather than the map date, because detailed FEMA analysis exists only at transects that are interpolated between [MassDEP — lRc-2cEUn7U @ 00:08:36].
Ask your local planner, small-site designer, and experienced builder 'If this was your money, would you do it?' and be willing to walk away [Peter Kelly Property — KmCwZ5I6BYU @ 00:11:48].

sop_steps.title: Screen the split at the planning counter
sop_steps.action: Check zoning, minimum lot size, frontage, and setbacks, then get the minor-or-major call and checklist.
sop_steps.detail: Ask planning staff whether the split runs along an existing road as a minor split or needs a new street, utilities, or engineering as a major one, and get the surveyor drawing the plat [Liberty Acres — qSoWEXftiCQ @ 00:00:20].

sop_steps.title: Lock legal access and road frontage
sop_steps.action: Confirm a recorded easement and frontage on an actual road built to county standards.
sop_steps.detail: Physical access is not legal access, so demand the recorded easement and watch for multi-owner roads, seasonal roads, and maintenance agreements; each split parcel needs county-road frontage [Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision — VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:04:05] [Tim Howell — rtRAjfGZ_nY @ 00:00:43].

sop_steps.title: Price the dirt-to-buildable stack
sop_steps.action: Make the offer contingent on the perc test and load septic, power, well, and driveway costs.
sop_steps.detail: Add a 10 to 20 percent buffer to the utility and site budget and keep every contingency in place until each check is done [Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision — VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:10:09].

sop_steps.title: Pull every recorded restriction and mineral link
sop_steps.action: Run the title search and deed abstract, and chain any mineral claim parcel by parcel.
sop_steps.detail: Use the title search and the county clerk's deed abstract to list all restrictions, and when an HOA claims minerals, chart deeds, reservations, assignments, and releases until a conveyance to the HOA is proven or missing [US Realty Training — B_XnC97BYF8 @ 00:03:38] [HOA LAND WARS — CnlqGcAGqOo @ 00:22:46].

sections.title: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split among land operators is how big to cut. Cody Bjugan judges every deal on 'return on effort,' runs projects of 100 to 500 lots averaging around 250, and calls it 'highly unlikely' he would ever do another minor partition because 'paydays aren't even comparable'; matching one 240-lot project would take 80 partitions [1B8q3q_Xt-s @ 00:01:06]. Yet he refuses to trash the small play: 'I don't want to poo poo on minor partitions,' he says, ranking them above a lot of real estate strategies and pushing beginners to start there, then level up [1B8q3q_Xt-s @ 00:01:56]. Liberty Acres draws the line on infrastructure instead of lot count: a minor split runs along an existing road, while a major one needs a new street, utilities or engineering, and the thresholds move by jurisdiction, with Washington capping short subdivisions at 4 lots and Toledo allowing up to 5 as a lot split [qSoWEXftiCQ @ 00:00:20]. Peter Kelly Property works the opposite end of the scale, a single backyard split, and argues the hurdle rate depends on motive: a pure investor needs margin after costs, interest, tax and a risk buffer, while an owner-occupier living in one home can accept a slimmer return [KmCwZ5I6BYU @ 00:01:24].

Practitioners split on how hard a recorded restriction actually bites. Tyler Bobo, working Alaska valley deals, says most subdivisions still carry CC&Rs that are often vague and unenforced yet still enforceable, so his playbook is to drive the neighborhood and compare real compliance against the paper: if nobody keeps horses, don't get horses, but if farms are everywhere, enforcement is less likely [zzxrwQSJnC4 @ 00:01:33]. Just Call Maggie takes the hard line, teaching that deed restrictions run with the land, bind every future owner, and that a 'No commercial businesses' clause blocks a cafe or shop permanently unless it is legally lifted [sazxc_VdXOw @ 00:02:11]. The Real Estate Lawyer says lifting one is far narrower than buyers assume: only the original grantor can remove a deed restriction, not a later seller, and if the grantor is gone you trace heirs or successor entities, as in one case where 2 children branched into 10 grandchildren and a single holdout makes removal 'challenging if not impossible' [gP3fDaUu5Iw @ 00:01:53]. Danielle Dojcak attacks the comfort zone from the other side, warning that 'no HOA' does not mean no rules because recorded covenants can still ban chickens, horses, detached garages or boat and RV parking [ieOUjD1jQXA @ 00:00:24].

On mineral fights, two owner war stories show different playbooks against an HOA claiming the rights. In the HOA Insanity case, a $50,000 signing bonus and 18% royalty offer triggered a two-week courthouse title trace back to the 1890s that found no severance; the owner then ignored $50 to $100 fines to build a harassment record, pursued fees, and leaned on the principle that a covenant 'cannot supersede a recorded deed' [KuFkYy1kf7s @ 00:11:46]. The HOA LAND WARS narrator went quieter and more surgical: five document requests (lease, board resolution, legal description, recorded authority instrument, and payee-determining company), then a parcel-by-parcel chain chart sent with an attorney letter to the energy company's land department, which got private lots stripped out of the lease without a courtroom win [CnlqGcAGqOo @ 00:18:31]. The consolidation pitch also splits the room: the HOA Insanity board pitched a '$20M' pool with a 10% management fee the owner tagged as a '$2 million' payday, countering that owners can negotiate collectively through their own transparent trust with minimal fees [KuFkYy1kf7s @ 00:18:22]. James Tanner frames the separate-estate logic: owners can lease mineral rights without leasing the land, and with wind turbines owners collect rent while still grazing cattle [potSOIxnw0E @ 00:10:54].

sections.title: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The biggest economic trap is buying cheap dirt and then paying for everything underneath and around it. Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision warns an $8,000 acre can turn into $60,000 more, and that sellers usually are not required to disclose problems on land; the perc test averages about $1,300, while septic runs $5,000 to $25,000 standard and $15,000 to $30,000 for a mound [VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:03:09]. The same channel prices utilities at $9,000 to $34,500, or $40,000 to $80,000 and up with full site work, notes bids vary by 30 to 60 percent, and insists on a 10 to 20 percent buffer [VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:06:13]. Tim Howell shows how frontage kills splits: upgrading a driveway to a county approved road means about 20 feet of surface, 6 to 8 inches of base rock, a 40 to 50 foot right-of-way and a grade no steeper than 15 percent, more likely 12, which he calls 'very costly,' and counties won't let you create a non-conforming lot [rtRAjfGZ_nY @ 00:01:20]. Liberty Acres adds that 'the government application fee is often the smallest line' once surveyor, septic, engineering, road, bonds and recording stack up [qSoWEXftiCQ @ 00:01:22].

Site geometry and mapping errors are the quiet killers. Peter Kelly Property says the position of the existing house matters more than total land size even at 600 to 700 square meters, and his access rule is blunt: 'If you cannot get cars to the back safely and comfortably, you do not have a project,' with about 4 meters of clear width needed, not 3, and the front house often losing compliant parking [KmCwZ5I6BYU @ 00:03:49]. He also flags that services bring easements, protected trees and existing pits, that building behind an existing house means hand work and slower progress, and that feasibility must be stress-tested for delays and a softer market because 'a quick permit is not the goal' [KmCwZ5I6BYU @ 00:10:58]. On coastal parcels, MassDEP's presenters warn about the 'invisible A zone': a transition narrower than 0.2 inches on the map, roughly 80 feet on the ground, is simply not mapped, and because detailed analysis happens only at transects that get interpolated between, operators should check the date of the coastal study rather than the map date [lRc-2cEUn7U @ 00:08:36]. Claiming a less restrictive zone needs a Letter of Map Change, while photo evidence of higher flooding can make an area more restrictive without one [lRc-2cEUn7U @ 00:16:14].

Encumbrance traps hit after the contract is signed if the paperwork pull comes late. Dana Sparks of Real Estate Made Crystal Clear says to get the CC&Rs during due diligence so the buyer can terminate and protect earnest money, warning that assessments 'tend to increase' and covenants can be amended; she pulls them from the seller, county deed books, the gsccca.org index or a Secretary of State search for the HOA's name [okIP6dYiTD4 @ 00:04:03]. The amendment risk is real: in the HOA Insanity case, the mineral clause was slipped in 7 years earlier through a 30-day 'silence equals acceptance' notice with only 12 of 30 owners attending, the TRO was denied, and $3,000-plus in fines became a lien while the HOA's cease-and-desist delayed drilling for months [KuFkYy1kf7s @ 00:19:15]. The Real Estate Lawyer warns the seller side too: adding restrictions without disclosing them before contract risks breach under the North Carolina standard offer to purchase [gP3fDaUu5Iw @ 00:03:30]. Conservation encumbrances cap income as well: on the MissStateExtension Panther Tract, a Wetland Reserve Easement means crops can't be pulled, the trees are too young for pulpwood, and hunting leases are the 'number one income generator' [UkiDG5GpG_Y @ 00:02:46].

callout.title: Do Not Close Until These Four Checks Clear
callout.body: Every item below comes from a cost overrun, a dead split, or a covenant fight practitioners ran into firsthand. Keep contingencies alive until each one is answered on paper.
items: Make the offer contingent on a perc test run by a licensed local tester, knowing results stay valid 2 to 5 years and a mound system can run $15,000 to $30,000 [Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision — VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:03:30].
Confirm a recorded easement or frontage on an actual county approved road, because verbal access means nothing to lenders and title companies [Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision — VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:04:05].
Run a title search and pull the county clerk's deed abstract listing every restriction before the buyer plans substantial changes [US Realty Training — B_XnC97BYF8 @ 00:03:38].

Follow the mineral chain through deeds, reservations, assignments and releases, since HOA ownership of common property does not automatically mean ownership of minerals under lots [HOA LAND WARS — CnlqGcAGqOo @ 00:05:01].

chapters.pull_quote: 'Physical access is not legal access.' Attributed to Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision (VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:04:05).
action_checklist: Check zoning, minimum lot size, frontage and setbacks, then ask planning staff whether the split is minor or major and get their checklist [Liberty Acres — qSoWEXftiCQ @ 00:00:00].
Write the perc test in as an offer contingency and keep every contingency in place until each due diligence check is done [Barndo And Tiny Homes Vision — VIdzLB23cAw @ 00:03:30].
Verify each new parcel fronts an actual county approved road, or budget a 50 ft flag-lot strip where the county allows it [Tim Howell — rtRAjfGZ_nY @ 00:00:14].
Ask the buyer 'Why?' when they say they want land, then dig for recorded deed restrictions that conflict with that use [Danielle Dojcak — ieOUjD1jQXA @ 00:00:36].

Pull the CC&Rs during due diligence from the seller, county deed books, the gsccca.org index or a Secretary of State search for the HOA's name [Real Estate Made Crystal Clear — okIP6dYiTD4 @ 00:07:16].
Before signing or contesting a mineral lease, trace title at the courthouse to confirm whether surface and minerals were ever severed [HOA Insanity — KuFkYy1kf7s @ 00:02:28].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I take a land deal from offer to closing, including double closes and title?
chapters.title: Offers, Double Closing, and Title
chapters.subtitle: Making offers to landowners, double closing vs. assignment vs. novation, pitching double closes to sellers, why double closes fail and workarounds in restricted states, transactional funding, the regulatory squeeze on land investors, and owner's vs. lender's title insurance
chapters.executive_summary: Land operators converge on a volume-driven offer engine and a narrow lane for double closing. Joe McCall's baseline is five seller conversations a day, with mailed offers re-sent every 30 days. Sumner Healey and Clay Hepler pitch two offers on every lead: a fast cash number and a higher 90-to-120-day number. They reserve double closes for questionable property, questionable markets, or compressed margins. Michael Bull cash-closes anything at 50% of market value or under. The street numbers are a $15,000 minimum spread and $500 to $1,000 in non-refundable buyer earnest money. Doubled closing costs of $5K-6K shrink a $10K spread to about $4K. Land Academy calls the double-close pattern 'tainted and bad and slimy' and buys outright instead. Seth Williams and Hepler report state restrictions tightening. Title practitioners push owner's policies on cash and vacant purchases.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Offers run on volume and paper. Joe McCall's rule on Flipping Mastery TV is blunt: talk to five sellers a day, or three sellers plus two Realtors. Five offers a day nearly guarantees a deal inside a month [YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:02:26]. Every seller gets a written offer by physical mail, and the same offer goes back out every 30 days, because 'an email gets lost text message gets blocked' [YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:27:07]. The double-closing operators add a second lever to that cadence: never send just one number. Sumner Healey always makes two offers, a quick cash number and a longer, higher one, after first finding the seller's real problem [GsUpcKZrJAQ @ 00:00:49]. Clay Hepler's 'I have two offers' script frames the choice as $30K in 30 days as-is or $50K-plus in 90 to 120 days. Hepler credits the script with adding two deals and about $20K a month for Marcus, who had been walking away from 40% of leads because sellers wanted 45 when Marcus needed 30 [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:05:27]. The Apke Brothers run the same fork from the flip side. They offer 50% for a straight flip. If the seller wants more, they pivot to a double close with an attorney-in-fact and 120 days to sell [LDjHRRkWVYE @ 00:09:28].

Across camps, the rule for when to double close is the same: never on the obvious winners. Healey cash-closes any 'obvious no-brainer deal.' The double close is reserved for question marks on access, topography, flood zones, or wetlands, or for an unfamiliar market. Healey notes that a property that sold in 90 days two years ago no longer moves that fast [GsUpcKZrJAQ @ 00:02:40]. Hepler's use cases line up almost word for word: questionable property, questionable market, or compressed margins [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:04:50]. Hepler's no-go list adds slam-dunk deals, uncomfortable sellers, self-listing, and $3K-5K margins, with the instruction to 'save this for deals where you're going to make 10, 15, 20K at least' [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:15:28]. Michael Bull puts a hard number on the split. At 50% of market value or under, Bull cash closes; at 60% to 80%, Bull wholesales through a double close or assignment. That is why 95% of the operation runs on cash closes [V4qnHYV6EVo @ 00:11:38]. The other shared point is that money is not the excuse. Healey says capital is 'not the reason you should double close' [GsUpcKZrJAQ @ 00:03:52]. Land Academy puts it harder: 'The only reason you're doing this is because you don't have the money or you don't believe in the deal' [fTJxXxQQQGs @ 00:08:04].

Everyone also agrees the window is narrowing. Seth Williams told REtipster in August 2024 that finding deals is 'harder than it's ever been.' Texting, ringless voicemail, cold calling, and even direct mail are under regulatory pressure, and 'a lot of states are making that hard' on assignments and double closings [k24QX2JK1ps @ 00:02:53]. Williams' answer is to double down now on whatever will be harder in two to five years [k24QX2JK1ps @ 00:03:22]. Land Academy reports municipalities and states restricting double closes. Title companies are pushing back on operators who look like unlicensed agents, which Jill calls 'the gray area' [fTJxXxQQQGs @ 00:10:07]. On title, the consensus is that cash land buyers are exposed. Clause Gate stresses that a lender policy 'provides zero direct legal protection' to the buyer. It covers only the loan balance and expires at payoff. The owner policy covers the full purchase price for a one-time fee and passes to heirs [cPrVIwbUYrs @ 00:02:15]. House Cashers LLC is blunter: 'Cash buyers have no lender's policy at all.' Their list of cases that call for an owner policy includes estate homes, recent family quitclaims, cash purchases, vacant property, foreclosures, tax sales, and FSBO deals [Up2OF5KmfcU @ 00:01:56].

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On the phone, McCall wants a verdict inside five minutes [YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:25:53]. The posture is the reluctant buyer or a doctor running a diagnosis. The caller fires 20 to 30 questions per call, because whoever asks the most questions stays in control [YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:11:43]. Land facts come first: county, size, utilities, flood plain, whether the parcel is listed, and other lots. Then comes motivation, asking 'why do you even want to sell it' and rating the answer 1 to 10 [YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:14:42]. Price tactics are street-grade. Drop a $5,000 anchor and follow with 'good thing I didn't offer…'. Tell agents 'he who names the price first loses.' Probe with 'is that the lowest' or 'close in seven days… five grand less' [YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:17:42]. The host's version trades speed for discount, offering 15 days instead of 30 for a bigger cut [YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:19:54]. When the seller balks, the takeaway line is 'I'm probably not the best buyer for you,' and the rule is never to sell the concept [YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:21:18]. The Apke Brothers say to state upfront that closing takes about 90 days, not 14 [LDjHRRkWVYE @ 00:18:23]. Healey warns never to tie up a seller who needs money tomorrow for three to twelve months [GsUpcKZrJAQ @ 00:01:42].

The double close itself is two standard contracts and two escrows. Each side is blind to the other's price, and escrow gets paid twice [V4qnHYV6EVo @ 00:02:27]. Bull splits the funding two ways. Transactional funding buys the parcel and resells it one to 24 hours later. Pass-through funding lets title use the end buyer's money: buy at 20, sell at 40, keep $20K [V4qnHYV6EVo @ 00:05:22]. Flip With Rick prices the drag. Double closing means twice the closing costs, roughly $5K-6K, so a $10K spread nets about $4K, and anything under $10K should be an assignment [4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:05:40]. Rick's 'reverse double closing' sidesteps the $3K-6K transactional funding fee in four moves. Sign PSA #1 with the seller at $110K and PSA #2 with the buyer at $150K. Have the buyer open escrow at your title company. The buyer funds $145K three days before closing. A title-prepared directive then releases $110K to the seller and $40K to the wholesaler [4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:10:54]. Hepler's Alabama deal shows the land math: 15 acres bought at $50K, $3.2K in costs, sold at $80K with a seven-day gap, for $24.8K net [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:12:50]. In Georgia, a 38-acre deal at $140K hit a seven-day cooling-off rule. Of eleven title companies called, the ninth took it, saving a $28K spread [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:08:08].

Sumner Advanced sets the floor at a $15,000 minimum spread and starts every contract at 120 days. There is no conversion difference between 90 and 120 days, and 'you probably need 90 days to get a buyer and then 30 days to close' [zyoO3FxrTDQ @ 00:03:23]. Buyer earnest money is always non-refundable: 'at least 500 bucks,' typically about $1,000. About nine of ten disposition offers get negotiated by conceding on price while pushing expenses onto the buyer [zyoO3FxrTDQ @ 00:02:25]. For resales inside about a year, the team buys an open title insurance policy to avoid paying for two new ones [zyoO3FxrTDQ @ 00:01:06]. The Apke Brothers pull Land Portal parcels that are not landlocked and carry a market value over $250K, then offer about 75%. They flag the costs that never disappear: earnest money, photos, and marketing [LDjHRRkWVYE @ 00:15:04]. On premiums, House Cashers LLC shows how the loan estimate misleads. Take an $1,800 owner premium and a lender premium of $350 bundled or $1,400 standalone. The estimate displays $1,400 plus $750, so the real add-on for the owner policy is $750 [Up2OF5KmfcU @ 00:01:21]. Clause Gate adds three cost levers: the simultaneous-issue discount, local custom on who pays, and state-set rates in Texas and Florida, with shopping allowed elsewhere [cPrVIwbUYrs @ 00:07:25].

callout.title: Title, Realtor, and Buyer Plays the Operators Actually Run
callout.body: These are tactical edges the double-closing operators use to keep spreads alive when title companies, cooling-off rules, or difficult buyers get in the way.
items: When a state rule like Georgia's seven-day cooling-off period blocks the back close, keep dialing title companies. Hepler's ninth call out of eleven saved a $28K spread on a 38-acre deal [Clay Hepler — IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:08:08].
Build a land-agent bench: search land listings sitting 60+ days on market, call 5 to 7 agents, test each with a small deal, and keep 8 to 10 who perform [Clay Hepler — IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:09:00].
On resales inside about a year, buy an open title insurance policy so the deal does not pay for two new policies [Sumner Advanced — zyoO3FxrTDQ @ 00:01:06].

Never switch a deal to a double close to satisfy a difficult buyer; replace the buyer instead. Ask which title companies offer blind or split HUDs, sometimes for an added fee [Flip With Rick — 4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:13:39].

sop_steps.title: Qualify the seller inside five minutes
sop_steps.action: Run 20 to 30 rapid questions on land facts and motivation, rate motivation 1 to 10, and decide whether it is a deal before minute five.
sop_steps.detail: Ask about county, size, utilities, flood plain, listing status, and other lots, then ask 'why do you even want to sell it' [Flipping Mastery TV — YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:11:43].

sop_steps.title: Present the two-offer fork
sop_steps.action: Give a quick as-is cash number and a higher number on a 90-to-120-day close, and state the longer timeline upfront.
sop_steps.detail: Hepler's script is $30K in 30 days as-is or $50K-plus in 90 to 120 days, credited with adding two deals and about $20K a month [Clay Hepler — IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:05:27].

sop_steps.title: Lock the contract with non-refundable earnest money
sop_steps.action: Pay the seller non-refundable earnest money and set the contract term at 120 days, or 120 plus a 30-day extension.
sop_steps.detail: Healey pays a non-refundable earnest money deposit on every double close as fair payment for the seller's time [Sumner Healey — GsUpcKZrJAQ @ 00:02:17].

sop_steps.title: Line up title and the funding path before marketing
sop_steps.action: Confirm the title company will handle both legs, choose pass-through or transactional funding, and have title prepare the disbursement directive.
sop_steps.detail: Rick's rule is that 'the directive comes from your title company'; the title company prepares it and the wholesaler never does [Flip With Rick — 4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:09:12].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in land double closing is whether the play deserves to exist at all. Land Academy's Steven says operators blast mass offers with six-month closes and "let 5% close," calls the pattern lying to sellers, and Land Academy brands it plainly: "this business model from start to finish is tainted and bad and slimy" [fTJxXxQQQGs @ 00:06:19] [5U1h-yosUoE @ 00:13:31]. Their alternative is blunt: own the dirt, keep full control, and when access turns out bad, renegotiate honestly to a number like $12K and close in days. Sumner Healey runs the opposite playbook on a narrow trigger, double closing only when the deal or market carries question marks such as access, topography, flood zones, wetlands, or an unfamiliar market, and cash closing every no-brainer [GsUpcKZrJAQ @ 00:03:52]. Clay Hepler widens that trigger to questionable property, questionable market, and compressed margins, and reports the "I have two offers" script adding 2 deals and about $20K per month, later 4-6 deals and $30-40K per month [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:04:50]. The one point both camps share is that capital shortage is never a valid reason: Healey calls funding "really easy" to find, and when students say "I don't have the money," Land Academy's Jill answers, "Well, I do."

The second split is over which exit structure should be the default. Flip With Rick says every contract "should 100% be assignable," pushes any spread under $10K into an assignment because a double close doubles closing costs, to $5-6K, and can shrink a $10K spread to about $4K net, and only double closes "when the seller freaks out" [4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:11:45]. Michael Bull anchors the choice to price instead: at or under 50% of market value the team cash closes, which is 95% of their business, and only the 60-80% band gets wholesaled through a double close or an assignment, with assignments suited to $2-6K deals because the fee is visible to the buyer [V4qnHYV6EVo @ 00:11:38]. The Apke Brothers push double closing upmarket, hunting $200-300K-plus parcels on the Land Portal at roughly 75% offers, averaging a buy at 200 and a sale at 280-300, finding end buyers on the MLS rather than an investor list, and pivoting to a double close only after a seller rejects a 50% flip offer [LDjHRRkWVYE @ 00:09:28]. Land Academy rejects every one of these as a substitute for ownership, arguing that 10-20 owned deals a year at $20-30K each beats a pipeline of contracts that rarely resell [5U1h-yosUoE @ 00:16:34].

Timeline, disclosure, and title-policy norms diverge just as hard. Sumner Advanced sees no conversion difference between 90 and 120 days, so the team opens at 120, with variants of 90/120 business days or 120 plus a 30-day extension, because "you probably need 90 days to get a buyer and then 30 days to close" [zyoO3FxrTDQ @ 00:03:23]. Clay Hepler takes the open-book route on the spread, disclosing the profit to sellers and reporting that 90% of them do not care, which cuts directly against the Land Academy charge that double closers keep sellers in the dark about what is happening [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:14:09]. On title protection for the flipper's own position, Kirby Williams of Shoreline Title states that a cash purchase does not require a policy and that it is lenders who demand one, while noting a title company cannot close without issuing a policy, so skipping it means closing through a law firm [z_2D2D6Cusc @ 00:03:55]. House Cashers lands on the other side for this exact buyer profile, naming cash purchases, vacant property, tax-sale, foreclosure, and FSBO deals as the moments to buy an owner policy, because cash buyers carry no lender policy at all and the title search only catches most problems [Up2OF5KmfcU @ 00:01:56].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure practitioners report is a contract that never converts. Land Academy says only "a very small percentage get resold" from the contract-at-$20K, remarket-at-$30K pattern, that the operators running it are "almost always out of business a year later," and that escrow companies are clamping down; even when a buyer appears, the seller can vanish or sell elsewhere, and suing them is not worth it [5U1h-yosUoE @ 00:10:12]. Land Academy's Jill adds that escrow gets strung along and that end buyers can skip-trace the seller and cut the middle operator out entirely, which is exactly the exposure ownership removes [fTJxXxQQQGs @ 00:12:55]. The Apke Brothers report a leak further upstream: land wholesalers sending deals with no APN, and beginners who cannot evaluate land walking straight into new laws and the "brokering" label [LDjHRRkWVYE @ 00:13:22]. Flip With Rick flags the assignment-side version of the same blow-up, where a realtor, lawyer, title company, or the seller can kill the deal once the fee is exposed, and title underwriters increasingly require that fee disclosed to the seller; Rick's fix is disclosing investor status up front so nobody is surprised at the closing table [4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:03:52].

Regulatory and title-company friction is the second trap. Seth Williams says states are restricting assignments and double closings and that "even direct mail seems like it's under attack in some places now," so the squeeze runs from lead generation all the way through closing [k24QX2JK1ps @ 00:02:53]. Clay Hepler hit it head-on in Georgia: a 38-acre deal at $140K ran into a 7-day cooling-off rule, and out of eleven title companies called, the ninth agreed to close it, preserving a $28K spread [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:08:08]. Clay also dates North and South Carolina restrictions to October 2025 and lists three workarounds: novation so end buyers can use FHA, conventional, or USDA financing, 7-14-day closing windows, and creative attorneys [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:11:26]. Jill frames the licensing exposure as "the gray area," warning that operators risk being seen as unlicensed agents while title companies and states push back on the model [fTJxXxQQQGs @ 00:10:07]. Sumner Healey's answer is pure avoidance: skip any state with a 7-day re-close wait or no pass-through funding, because the deal structure simply does not survive there, and fall back on cash closing the slam dunks.

The economics check is where thin double closes die. Rick's math shows doubled closing costs of $5-6K turning a $10K spread into roughly $4K net, while a reverse double closing with the end buyer funding three days early sidesteps the $3-6K transactional funding fee [4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:05:40]. Sumner Advanced sets a hard floor of at least a $15,000 spread, calls a double close as a first deal "hard mode," and only negotiates a flat agent rate on compressed small deals like buy 25 / sell 40 [zyoO3FxrTDQ @ 00:00:49]. Clay Hepler tells operators to avoid $3-5K margins, slam dunks, uncomfortable sellers, and self-listing, which fails, and to "save this for deals where you're going to make 10, 15, 20K at least" [IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:15:28]. On the funding side, Steve Hodgdon's worst case shows what skipped diligence costs: 29 acres near Houston bought at $200K against a partner estimate of $450K turned out landlocked after a bridge and road washed out, a $600K reassessment pushed taxes to $1,000 a month, and a seller-family lawsuit pulled a $360K sale. Hodgdon's verdict: "the people that lie in these transactions are the sellers" [8qUfThwrzAw @ 00:14:02].

callout.title: Four Checks Before Signing a Double Close
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a practitioner who lost margin, lost a deal, or watched others fold. Clear all four before the seller signs.
items: Spread floor: no double close under a $15,000 spread, because doubled closing costs and agent fees compress everything below it [Sumner Advanced — zyoO3FxrTDQ @ 00:00:49].

Title company first: call title companies before contracting until one confirms it will close both sides, as Clay did when the ninth of eleven calls saved a $28K Georgia spread [Clay Hepler — IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:08:08].
Buyer skin in the game: collect non-refundable buyer earnest money of at least $500, typically about $1,000, because legitimate buyers will pay it [Sumner Advanced — zyoO3FxrTDQ @ 00:02:25].

Access and seller-disclosure check: verify access before committing, since sellers do not disclose their problems and a landlocked Houston parcel tied up capital in taxes and litigation [REtipster — 8qUfThwrzAw @ 00:14:17].

action_checklist: Talk to 5 sellers a day, send every seller a written offer by physical mail, and re-send the same offer every 30 days [Flipping Mastery TV — YPqUHvSAZrU @ 00:26:21].
Present two offers on every borderline lead: $30K in 30 days as-is, or $50K-plus in 90-120 days [Clay Hepler — IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:05:27].
Pay the seller a non-refundable earnest money deposit on every double close to compensate them for their time [Sumner Healey — GsUpcKZrJAQ @ 00:02:17].
Build a land-agent bench by searching land listings on market 60-plus days, calling 5-7 agents, and testing each with a small deal [Clay Hepler — IRJeZQijnxU @ 00:09:00].
Have the title company prepare the closing directive that splits the end buyer's funds between seller and wholesaler; never prepare it yourself [Flip With Rick — 4Ueirfxr5Ww @ 00:09:12].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I sell land, offer seller financing legally, and present properties to buyers?
chapters.title: Selling Land: Buyers, Seller Financing, and Drone Media
chapters.subtitle: Why buyers are the real asset, seller financing under Dodd-Frank and the SAFE Act, MLO requirements and exemptions, selling notes, shooting acreage with drones, top drone shots, and scaling a real estate media business
chapters.executive_summary: Land operators report that terms, not cash, drive the business. REtipster's Seth Williams and Gokce Capital's Abhi both sell on seller financing for higher prices, interest, and fees. Abhi runs roughly 80% of sales on terms, buying around $10K and selling around $20K, with buyers putting 10% down and paying about $500 a month. Abhi treats buyers as the real asset because acquisition costs climbed from $5 to $800-$1,200 per lead, and pulls cash forward with 5% and 2.5% early-payoff cashbacks instead of selling notes. On Dodd-Frank, Seth, William Bronchick, and Seller Finance Consultants agree that vacant land sold to non-occupants sits outside the dwelling rules. They split on entity stacking, licensed originators, and Joe Crump's 'don't worry' stance. Drone shooters Matt Wood, Rob, and Wyman Gentry sell acreage, surroundings, and lot lines, pricing aerials from $125 for five photos.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus: Terms Sell the Dirt, Buyers Are the Asset
paragraphs: Land sells fastest and fattest on terms, and the practitioners who move volume say so without hedging. Seth Williams frames seller financing as the income route that brings a higher price plus interest while keeping the operator out of the landlord business. The buyer owns the parcel, so 'you're not a landlord' [JL60o3hoi_w @ 00:02:17]. Seth ties the whole model to a lending gap: banks avoid raw-land loans without a development plan. The seller who carries the paper therefore captures a higher price, a faster sale, interest, closing fees, and servicing fees on the same dirt [JL60o3hoi_w @ 00:12:45]. Abhi of Gokce Capital runs a seven-figure operation nearly 800 deals deep. Abhi sells roughly 80% on terms and 20% for cash, treats 2023 and 2024 as exceptions, and calls it 'very hard' to sustain a land business without monthly terms income [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:09:39]. The Seller Finance Consultants panel lands the same point from the lending side. No conforming loan exists over four to five acres, so large acreage moves only on cash or seller financing [gSHz85xxIz4 @ 01:48:25]. The operating consensus is blunt: the bankless buyer is the default buyer for vacant land. The note is the product being sold, and the parcel is the collateral that makes the note possible.

The second point of agreement is that the buyer list, not the parcel, carries the business. Abhi tracks acquisition costs that climbed from about $5 per Facebook lead to $800 to $1,200, with direct mail rising alongside [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:42:14]. Abhi concludes that lifetime value is the only lever an operator actually controls. A $500 acquisition cost against $5,000 of lifetime gross profit leaves $4,500 to work with [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:14:53]. Abhi's answer is a customer success program: monthly check-in calls, a birthday call, and permission-based contact that never leads with an offer. The reasoning is that in the age of AI, 'human touch is our competitive advantage' [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:49:44]. Daniil Kleyman's panel frames the same buyer pool from the pricing side. They say seller financing 'has been proven to sell properties for 15% more especially in the lower uh price point markets' [gSHz85xxIz4 @ 00:50:55]. Both camps converge on one rule. The people who cannot or will not use a bank are the market, and the premium they pay for access to terms is the margin. Once leads stop being cheap, the real work is keeping those borrowers paying, referring, and coming back. Abhi estimates repeat buyers at roughly a fifth of sales, a share nobody on the team formally tracks yet.

On compliance, the practitioners working vacant land reach the same practical baseline. The heaviest Dodd-Frank rules hang on an owner-occupied dwelling, and a bare parcel is not one. Seth Williams reads Regulation Z Subpart E as limited to a consumer's principal dwelling, defined as a one-to-four unit residential structure. Seth concludes that 'vacant land seems to be excluded' from its originator, balloon, and ability-to-repay restrictions, and says more than one attorney agreed [m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:09:01]. The Seller Finance Consultants panel states flatly that vacant land and investor buyers are exempt, and that the real test is owner occupancy [gSHz85xxIz4 @ 01:15:07]. William Bronchick has been an attorney since 1990 and has closed more than 1,000 owner-finance deals. Bronchick confines Dodd-Frank to residential sales to owner-occupant buyers, mobile homes included. Investor sales, commercial deals, and short lease-options fall outside it [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:07:19]. The shared trap is the buyer who moves onto the land. Bronchick warns that coverage can reach raw land and contracts for deed when the buyer occupies within one year [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:03:45]. The practical consequence for a land seller is simple. Whether a note sits inside or outside the dwelling rules depends on who ends up living on the ground and when, not on what the deed says.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Abhi's unit economics are the cleanest template for terms deals: buy around $10,000, sell around $20,000, and never go above $50,000 [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:55:43]. Loans average $14,000 to $19,000. The typical buyer puts 10% down and pays about $500 a month [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:48:02]. Instead of selling notes or borrowing from funders, Abhi pulls cash forward with an early-payoff cashback on four-year loans. Borrowers get 5% back for paying off within six months, or 2.5% within twelve. About 10% of borrowers take it, and Abhi calls it cheaper than borrowing [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:11:17]. A higher down payment earns a lower rate. Against competitors advertising '$1 down, $199 a month,' the script is that such a structure takes ten years to become a landowner. Seth Williams shows why big down payments matter on cheap dirt. On a parcel bought for $500 and sold for $8,000, the down payment alone recovers the cost, which changes how much risk the seller is willing to carry [m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:22:58]. Abhi's sales floor runs on speed. Leads get a response within 60 seconds, phones stay open 9am to 9pm, and a typical sale is a seven-call close. Each call aims for a hard yes or a hard no, because a maybe counts as failure.

The paper itself gets engineered around the dwelling trigger. Seth Williams recommends loan documents that require payoff before the buyer improves the property. Seth repeats the clause for RESPA, which exempts vacant-land loans unless a structure or manufactured home goes on the land within two years using loan proceeds [m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:17:36]. Bronchick's version is a one-year no-residence clause on raw land [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:26:56]. Advertising is where Seth treats the rules as live, because Regulation N reads 'real property or a dwelling.' An ad quoting 5% interest, $2,000 down, and $499 a month locks those terms at closing. The workaround is a vague line: 'seller financing may be available on this property, contact the owner for more information' [m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:27:41]. On privacy, Seth keeps intake to name, address, and phone, which stays clear of nonpublic personal information. Collecting an SSN, driver's license, or passport pulls that information in, and sharing it then requires an opt-out disclosure. Pulling a credit report only needs the FTC's no-opt-out form, which Seth calls fairly easy to fill out. When a deal does touch an owner-occupant, Bronchick paid a licensed loan originator $500 and added the fee to the buyer's closing costs [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:25:25]. The paper stays in the seller's hands, and the compliance cost lands on the buyer.

Drone media is where the parcel gets sold visually, and the shooters agree the asset is the acreage, not the house. Matt Wood was shooting 35 acres with a lake. Wood starts with Google Earth, FAA restrictions, and a survey, then sets D-Log, ISO 500, shutter around 120, ND16, Sunny white balance, AEB 5, 24fps, and 4K [ZU1aoe6pwQI @ 00:03:23]. Wood keeps two-thirds horizon in frame. The flight pattern is two orbits, the second 50 to 100 feet higher, followed by low-and-slow passes that combine three simultaneous movements. Wood reviews the footage before leaving the property [ZU1aoe6pwQI @ 00:08:05]. Rob of Next Move runs one battery through four jobs on the Mavic 4 Pro. The 28mm wide lens is the 'map,' shot with a high push and a quarter orbit. The 70mm is the portrait lens, and the 168mm shoots from a distance to stay off the neighbors. Rob finishes with roughly ten-second vertical 9:16 clips and sells the bundle as a premium 'triple lens listing pass' [HrG-12X_ds8 @ 00:03:10]. Wyman Gentry prices aerials as an add-on: $125 for five photos and $225 for ten. The shoot takes about five minutes and requires Part 107 certification. Gentry steers clients away from drone shots when the neighbors are junky or a freeway sits next door [ItWPpkhNHto @ 00:03:51].

callout.title: What the Volume Sellers and Shooters Do Differently
callout.body: These are the small operating edges that separate high-volume land sellers and acreage shooters from the rest: timed cashback nudges, deal-count workarounds, synthetic balloons, and long-lens distance from hostile neighbors.
items: Time the cashback nudges. Abhi's team sends early-payoff reminders in months 4-5 and 9-11 of the loan to trigger the 5% and 2.5% windows before they close [REtipster — HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:20:04].

Stack entities for deal count. Bronchick figures three LLCs could give about 9 owner-occupant deals a year under the three-per-entity exemption [William Bronchick — MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:20:23]. Seller Finance Consultants calls multiple entities 'a blatant attempt to evade' [Seller Finance Consultants, Inc. — SB_vfxPYuF8 @ 00:00:43].
Build a synthetic balloon. Escalating rates of 6, 8, 10, then 12% make buyers 'cry uncle' and refinance, which mimics a balloon where balloons are barred [William Bronchick — ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:23:53].
Shoot long to avoid neighbors. Rob uses the 168mm lens from a distance to stay off adjacent properties, citing a drone that was shot down in Athens, AL [Next Move with Rob — HrG-12X_ds8 @ 00:07:06].

sop_steps.title: Screen the Parcel Before Listing
sop_steps.action: Run the land due-diligence checklist before any marketing goes live.
sop_steps.detail: Verify road access (landlocked parcels exist), utilities, flood zone and wetlands, cliffs and steep slope, and zoning approval, and confirm what the local body allows [REtipster — JL60o3hoi_w @ 00:09:26].

sop_steps.title: Shoot the Acreage
sop_steps.action: Plan the flight, lock the settings, fly orbits plus low passes, and review on site.
sop_steps.detail: Research the site on Google Earth, check FAA restrictions, and pull the survey [Matt Wood — ZU1aoe6pwQI @ 00:02:26]. Open with the wide lens as the map, then shoot 70mm portraits and 168mm distance shots, ending with 9:16 vertical clips [Next Move with Rob — HrG-12X_ds8 @ 00:03:10].

sop_steps.title: Advertise Vague, Respond Fast
sop_steps.action: List with non-specific financing language and answer every lead within 60 seconds.
sop_steps.detail: Use the line 'seller financing may be available on this property, contact the owner for more information' to avoid locked-in Regulation N terms [REtipster — m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:27:41]. Respond to every lead within 60 seconds [REtipster — HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:23:16].

sop_steps.title: Write and Service the Paper
sop_steps.action: Add a no-build-before-payoff clause, structure the terms, and run retention.
sop_steps.detail: Require payoff before the buyer improves the property [REtipster — m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:09:52]. Then offer the 5% and 2.5% early-payoff cashback and run permission-based monthly check-ins [REtipster — HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:11:17].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether Dodd-Frank touches a vacant-land note at all. Seth Williams of REtipster breaks with the early land-investor line that the law simply does not apply, then lands on a narrow reading: the Subpart E balloon, originator, and ability-to-repay rules key off a consumer's principal dwelling, defined as a one-to-four unit residential structure, so 'vacant land seems to be excluded from all of these special rules listed out in subpart E' [m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:09:01]. The Seller Finance Consultants broker panel agrees from the licensing side, stating flatly that vacant land and investor buyers sit outside the rules [gSHz85xxIz4 @ 01:15:07]. William Bronchick draws the line by occupancy rather than property type: if the buyer moves onto the property within one year, the rules can reach raw land and installment contracts for deed [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:03:45]. Joe Crump sits at the far end, telling viewers the act is mainly focused on securities and private money, that ethical disclosure already satisfies it, and not to worry, while still adding 'I'm not saying don't comply' [mtE3-cvmAN0 @ 00:00:41]. For a land operator, every comfortable reading above depends on the buyer never occupying the parcel while the note is open, which means the loan documents, not the operator's hopes, have to carry that restriction.

The second fault line is whether to engineer around the deal limits or pay a licensed originator on every owner-occupant sale. William Bronchick teaches the counting game: one free pass per year for a natural person, estate, or trust, three per year for any entity under the eight-part test, and roughly nine deals a year for an operator running three LLCs [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:20:23]. Seller Finance Consultants calls that structure 'a blatant attempt to evade,' putting multiple entities, forbearances, lease options, and land-trust titling in the same bucket [SB_vfxPYuF8 @ 00:00:43]. Their broker panel also brands the three-loan exemption a 'worthless exemption' because it bans the balloon, and Daniil Kleyman explains the cost: the plan is to season a note a few months and sell it, and that resale needs a balloon [gSHz85xxIz4 @ 00:37:12]. Their fix is routing every deal through an MLO, since an MLO can create a balloon that a non-MLO seller cannot, while the buyer pays the fee, so the seller should 'take the free insurance' [SB_vfxPYuF8 @ 00:02:45]. The split is not about cost, since both camps push the originator fee onto the buyer; it is about whether the note must survive a resale.

Practitioners also split hard on what to do with the paper after closing. Abhi of Gokce Capital, whose sales run roughly 80% terms across nearly 800 deals, deliberately does not sell notes [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:13:32]. Instead, the team pulls cash forward with an early-payoff cashback on a four-year loan: 5% back if paid off within six months, 2.5% within twelve, taken by about 10% of borrowers, which Abhi treats as cheaper than borrowing [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:11:17]. The Seller Finance Consultants model runs the opposite direction: the San Diego case resold at $437,500 with 30% down on an 8% note amortized over 30 years and due in five, then sold that note after three payments at a 12-15% investor yield for a $49,277.63 profit [gSHz85xxIz4 @ 01:01:58]. The Seller Financing, Real Estate & Note Investing channel splits the difference, declaring the old flip of 10% down and dumping the 90% note at 94 cents dead, and backing a 12-36 month partial sale that keeps the tail, with paper seasoned six to twelve months first [X6Bv1fbSvBk @ 00:03:06]. The choice tracks the business: a land shop selling $10,000 parcels for $20,000 lives on monthly terms income, while a house flipper carrying a $218,000 note needs the capital back to fund the next acquisition.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The Dodd-Frank downside is concrete in the numbers practitioners quote. The Seller Finance Consultants panel puts it bluntly: 'the penalty is the recision of the note and interest forgiven,' meaning an operator can lose the 10-30% down payment plus every payment collected, with licenses also at risk [gSHz85xxIz4 @ 00:47:31]. They add a resale hit before any lawsuit: a badly written $200,000 note facing a 30% discount is a $60,000 loss [gSHz85xxIz4 @ 00:36:36]. William Bronchick stresses that Dodd-Frank is not regulatory, so the threat is a private civil action rather than arrest, but the clock runs longer than it looks: the statute of limitations is three years, yet a buyer can raise the violation as a foreclosure offset ten years later [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:13:40]. In the webinar version, Bronchick frames the bet as losing less than 1% of the time versus complying 100% of the time, and says no reported cases have surfaced [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:28:37]. A Houston investor Bronchick describes sells about 40 houses a year at around $60,000 and would simply give the house back if challenged. The economics check is blunt: the exposure lands exactly when an operator needs the note most, during default and foreclosure.

Land operators carry traps of their own. Seth Williams warns that the vacant-land exclusion from the dwelling rules evaporates if the buyer builds, so the loan documents should require payoff before the buyer improves the property [m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:09:52]. William Bronchick reaches the same place from the occupancy side with a one-year no-residence clause on raw land [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:26:56]. Advertising is the quieter trap: Regulation N reaches 'real property or a dwelling,' so a listing promising 5% interest, $2,000 down, and $499 a month locks those terms in, and changing them at the closing table is the violation; the escape is a vague line that seller financing may be available [m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:26:44]. Data collection is the third decision point. Name, address, and phone carry no nonpublic personal information, but an SSN, driver's license, or passport does, and sharing it triggers opt-out paperwork; Seth weighs that friction against margin, and on a $500 buy resold for $8,000 where the down payment alone repays the cost, the risk is 'not a big deal' [m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:22:58]. Bronchick's clause, Seth's payoff clause, and vague ad copy cost nothing to add and close the three easiest doors to a claim.

The operating failures are about cost and speed more than law. Abhi reports customer acquisition cost climbing from about $5 per Facebook lead to $800-$1,200, with direct mail rising too, which is why Gokce Capital leans on lifetime value instead of cheap leads [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:42:14]. Speed is the other leak: a weekend voicemail delay lost a sale when the buyer spent the money on a Walmart TV instead, which backs the team's 60-second lead-response rule and 9am-9pm phone coverage [HpkNhY7WclQ @ 01:06:48]. Media agencies report the same pattern in people and paperwork. ACRE Partner says the agency lost its best creatives six to eight times and now hands members hiring templates, interview scripts, and SOPs to rebuild faster [x1a5YxEWplQ @ 00:07:22]. It also warns that brokerage partnerships launched without paperwork or clear expectations cost tens of thousands of dollars [x1a5YxEWplQ @ 00:06:36]. The common thread is that the first collapse point in both businesses is response capacity, not lead supply: Abhi added three hires to cover 150-200 active loans, and ACRE pushes owners at $20-40K a month to hire before they can reach $50-100K. Underfunded follow-up and undocumented handoffs leak margin faster than any market shift.
