callout.title: Pre-Close and Pre-Flight Gate
callout.body: Run these four checks before signing a terms deal or flying a listing; each one maps to a loss a practitioner reported firsthand.
items: Lock the parcel as vacant: add a no-build-before-payoff clause, because RESPA's land exemption fails if a structure or manufactured home goes on within 2 years using loan proceeds [REtipster — m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:17:36].
Count owner-occupant deals per person, not per LLC, against state RMLO thresholds of Texas 5, Colorado 3, and California 0 before writing the next note [William Bronchick — ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:08:25].
Run the high-cost test on APR, not the note rate, and stay under it: 'Just don't have a high-cost mortgage' [William Bronchick — MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:28:44].
Before any acreage flight, research the parcel with Google Earth, FAA restrictions, and the survey so the lines and airspace are known [Matt Wood — ZU1aoe6pwQI @ 00:02:26].

chapters.pull_quote: "What this means is we are in a place where you need to become the bank." — Seller Finance Consultants, Inc. (gSHz85xxIz4 @ 00:08:26).
action_checklist: Before listing any parcel on terms, verify road access, utilities, flood zone and wetlands, slope, and zoning approval [REtipster — JL60o3hoi_w @ 00:09:26].
Write a payoff-before-improvement clause into every land note so a buyer who builds cannot convert the parcel into a dwelling mid-loan [REtipster — m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:09:52].
Either advertise exact terms you will honor at closing or keep the listing vague with 'seller financing may be available' [REtipster — m1GoTr9J5TM @ 00:27:41].
On owner-occupant deals, pay an RMLO roughly $500 and add the fee to the buyer's closing costs [William Bronchick — MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:25:25].
Answer every buyer lead within 60 seconds and pitch the 5%/2.5% early-payoff cashback to pull cash forward [REtipster — HpkNhY7WclQ @ 00:23:16].
Shoot acreage with two orbit heights 50-100 ft apart, then low and slow passes combining three movements, and review footage before leaving [Matt Wood — ZU1aoe6pwQI @ 00:08:05].

chapters.question_prompt: What alternative uses like RV parks, solar leases, and battery storage can make raw land more valuable?
chapters.title: Alternative Land Uses: RV Parks, Solar, and Battery Storage
chapters.subtitle: RV park vs. mobile home park investing, RV storage lot economics, buying a first RV park, RV lot ownership vs. renting, rising RV park costs, the solar and energy storage lease process, solar farm construction, BESS components and sizing, and planning and zoning for battery storage
chapters.executive_summary: Operators across RV hospitality and energy leasing converge on one thesis: land earns most when it is repositioned into a use that zoning and capital keep scarce. Heather Blankenship and Dr. Jeff Anzalone hunt mom-and-pop RV parks, stack propane, golf carts, cabins and dynamic pricing, and Anzalone buys at 9-11+ caps to sell at a lower cap. The Owner's Math shows RV storage swinging from roughly 12% cash-on-cash to about 1% purely on site layout. On the energy side, LandGate's Dan prices solar leases at $300-$2,000 per acre per year with a 2% escalator and storage sites bought outright at $30,000 per acre. The fights: American Fault Lines frames corporate RV repricing as a squeeze on fixed-income residents, and the Financial Times hears that Texas batteries 'eat their own lunch.'

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every RV operator starts from the same frame: an RV park is a hotel, a mobile home park is an apartment building. Texas Land Hub's Vima puts it bluntly, warning that RV parks need 'quite a bit more amenities and quite a bit more staff,' charge daily, weekly and monthly rates, and run seasonal, but earn more per lot and, above 80% capacity, sell for more than an equal mobile home park [bwY6HXq0w4g @ 00:00:05]. Heather Blankenship, with 12 years in parks and $30M+ in real estate, files RV parks under outdoor hospitality and mobile home parks under affordable housing [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:00:27]. Commercial Property Advisors scores the yield and cap-rate round to RV, pointing to Airbnb-style dynamic pricing that can 'double your revenue,' while handing stability and agency financing to mobile home parks because Fannie and Freddie loans do not cover RV parks [ek2QTeZlqCY @ 00:09:26]. Dr. Jeff Anzalone runs parks the same way, with an Airbnb-style check-in app and a standing ask for honest guest reviews, and notes RV parks carry lower expenses and insurance because tenants roll in with their own structures [tZwHEMuaXiQ @ 00:02:19]. The tradeoff is consistent: more labor and seasonality in exchange for per-lot revenue an apartment-style asset cannot match.

The second point of agreement is where the deals sit: off-market, with aging owners who never built a digital footprint. Commercial Property Advisors' insider data says 34% of mobile home park owners are roughly 70 or older, over 50% hold title individually rather than in an LLC, 80% run no website, 45% have no findable phone and 65% have near-zero internet presence, with 75% of parks sized at 7 to 100 pads [ek2QTeZlqCY @ 00:03:26]. Supply of mobile home parks stays capped because cities refuse new ones, while the RV industry climbs from $10.7B in 2023 toward $11.4B by 2028 across 11M RV-owning households and pad supply lags [ek2QTeZlqCY @ 00:02:07]. Blankenship puts mom-and-pop ownership of RV parks above 88%, says one deal took 3 years of monthly calls, and pairs cold calling with direct mail [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:10:51]. Anzalone shows what happens when an under-marketed park gets worked: the Vicksburg property sat at 200 sites and 50% occupancy until Anzalone marketed directly to workers at a nuclear plant 5 miles away and pushed it to 90% [5o06VeN0Gak @ 00:04:27]. The shared conclusion is that neglect, not scarcity of parks, is the edge a buyer is paying for.

On the energy side, the speakers agree that storage now moves as fast as solar and that money, not ideology, is the engine. LandGate's Dan reports there are as many storage deals as solar deals hitting landowners, with developers locking sites under 4-to-5-year exclusive options because nobody spends that long working an interconnection queue, power purchase agreements and transmission lines without exclusivity [Uaymin1wo40 @ 00:07:27]. The Financial Times reporting from Texas calls batteries a 'pure economic play,' quoting the line that 'all of the batteries being deployed in the state are because they can make money,' with operators charging mid-morning on depressed solar prices and discharging into evening peaks [QwCGBQ0n2tM @ 00:03:18]. Brian Ross of the Great Plains Institute counts 650 GW of battery projects in the interconnection queue in 2022 against 1,200 GW of total national generating capacity, driven by renewables growth, falling costs, IRA credits that now reach standalone storage, and mandates in 12 to 14 states [A84PRdZGcoE @ 00:14:51]. The land footprint is modest: EltonDP's Elmbrook solar build covers less than one third of its 36 acres with panels, and the battery sits in a shipping container set on pads by crane [sM7ge9ahsGY @ 00:03:46].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Blankenship's acquisition playbook starts with a 150-mile demand radius drawn around a target and a state or region, not a single city, as the hunting ground; Blankenship expects 20-30% down, wants expansion land for an institutional-grade exit, and runs 30-90 days of due diligence plus 30 days to close, verifying merchant reports against bank statements and collecting website logins, vendor access and every water shutoff location [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:05:45]. Commercial Property Advisors steers buyers toward 7-to-50 or 7-to-60 pad parks that stay off the institutional radar, pointing to a student, Tiffany, who bought a 7-pad and a 13-pad park [ek2QTeZlqCY @ 00:05:02]. On structure, the same channel scores seller financing a tie with a slight edge to RV and says long-time owners want income at 5-6% spread over 4-5+ years [ek2QTeZlqCY @ 00:13:18]. Blankenship's own entry is the leverage extreme: at 26 Blankenship bought a bankrupt park on a $3.2M non-recourse loan with no money down, swallowed an $18,500 first payment and a roughly $20,000 first electric bill, and now runs a park worth $13M with about 30 staff from 900 miles away [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:29:28]. The repeatable lesson across both channels is to verify cash, keep expansion room, and negotiate terms as hard as price.

Once a park is bought, the revenue mechanics are specific. Blankenship runs dynamic pricing and occupancy optimization inside the reservation software, stating 'my price increases 10% every 10% of occupancy' on the first park, and layers online booking with industry-specific PPC; that park averages 500 guests, 3-day stays, 10+ revenue streams and $2.5M+ a year [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:17:25]. Anzalone stacks propane, ice, golf carts, laundry, cabins, birthday parties and chuck wagons, keeps parks pet-friendly, fills vacancies off a waitlist, and is adding 37 sites to a 52-site park at full occupancy, some under canopies charged at a premium, with one-way traffic flow [5o06VeN0Gak @ 00:01:44]. Anzalone also splits tenants into three layers: nightly guests at the highest rate, monthly workers such as crews building an Amazon fulfillment center, and permanent residents, with golf carts and propane tank swaps as side income [tZwHEMuaXiQ @ 00:01:16]. American Fault Lines quantifies why operators push transient stays: nightly rates of $75-90 equal $600-800 a week, while a $500-a-month resident pays under $17 a night, and upgrading 50 sites to 50-amp service runs $150-250k [BQMMvL0zywU @ 00:15:23]. The arithmetic pushes every operator toward short-stay, high-amenity pricing power.

Land-lease mechanics on the energy side are equally hard-numbered. LandGate's Dan says solar contracts run 35-40 pages, an option agreement with a 30-year lease attached as an exhibit, paying $2,000-$35,000 a year in option money at the start of each year, terminable by the developer at any time, then $300-$2,000 per acre per year with a 2% escalator once the lease kicks in [Uaymin1wo40 @ 00:03:04]. Storage is different: 5-15 acre sites are bought rather than leased because the substation is deeded to the utility, with one offer paying $10k for two option years, $15k for three more, then $30,000 per acre, or $450,000 [Uaymin1wo40 @ 00:09:18]. Dan's closed 400-acre Brown County, Ohio deal stepped option payments from $10k to $30k over five years before a $1,050-per-acre lease, a stream worth $17M over 30 years that Craig could sell in year one for 40-45% of face [Uaymin1wo40 @ 00:11:33]. The Owner's Math runs the RV storage version: 240 spaces at $110 on a $2M build yields about $190k NOI, about 9.5% yield on cost, and roughly $82k of cash flow after $108k of debt service on $1.3M, about 12% cash-on-cash [xjNh4eemKCs @ 00:16:42].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is which asset to buy. Commercial Property Advisors scores stability and financing for mobile home parks, flatly noting Fannie and Freddie loans do not cover RV parks, but hands the yield round to RV, where Airbnb-style dynamic pricing can “double your revenue” [ek2QTeZlqCY @ 00:09:26]. Texas Land Hub frames the same split as hotel versus apartment: RV parks need “quite a bit more amenities and quite a bit more staff,” run seasonal, but earn more per lot, and at 80%-plus occupancy an RV park sells for more than an equal mobile home park [bwY6HXq0w4g @ 00:01:25]. Dr. Jeff Anzalone goes all-in on the RV side, buying at 9 to 11-plus cap rates while apartments trade at 3 to 4, then raising NOI and selling at a lower cap [tZwHEMuaXiQ @ 00:03:05]. Heather Blankenship draws the line differently: RV parks are outdoor hospitality, mobile home parks are affordable housing, and her first park pulls $2.5M-plus a year off 10-plus revenue streams [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:00:39]. The playbook choice therefore maps to operator profile. Commercial Property Advisors routes the wealth preserver, value-add beginner and retiree into stabilized mobile home parks and reserves RV parks for the active operator willing to run a hospitality desk [ek2QTeZlqCY @ 00:14:32].

Repricing is where operators and resident advocates collide. Anzalone treats long-term residents as an asset, noting they can become the majority and build waitlists, and he fills vacancies off that list [5o06VeN0Gak @ 00:04:11]. Blankenship runs the other side of the dial: at her first park, “my price increases 10% every 10% of occupancy” [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:17:25]. American Fault Lines reports what that math does to full-timers: lot rent of $350 to $500 now runs $900 to $1,500-plus, and one couple's shelter cost going from $450 to about $1,175 is “more than a 150% increase on the exact same plot of gravel” [BQMMvL0zywU @ 00:05:44]. The same channel lays out why operators chase transients: $75 to $90 nightly equals $600 to $800 a week, versus under $17 a night from a $500-a-month resident [BQMMvL0zywU @ 00:15:23]. On lot ownership, Elegment Land argues buying beats renting because it delivers customization, community, equity and rental income [JkPCf6kuMu0 @ 00:08:07]. American Fault Lines counters that zoning caps stays at 14, 28 or 60 days with 30 days out, and that living in an RV on your own land is usually illegal, with fines of $50 to $100 a day [BQMMvL0zywU @ 00:10:25].

On the energy side, Dan of LandApp by LandGate splits the land play in two: solar is leased for 30 years at $300 to $2,000 per acre with a 2% escalator, while storage sites of 5 to 15 acres are bought outright because the substation is conveyed to the utility by deed; his sample storage deal paid $30,000 per acre, or $450,000 [Uaymin1wo40 @ 00:08:46]. Whether the storage boom holds is contested. The Financial Times reports Texas batteries are a “pure economic play,” charging on depressed mid-morning solar and discharging into the evening, yet “batteries do eat their own lunch” by lowering high prices and raising low ones; the counterview is that population growth, data centres and electrification leave “a lot more room” [QwCGBQ0n2tM @ 00:05:31]. Hardware camps split as well. Keith of Sunsynk prefers air cooling over liquid because it is easier to service, and he pushes back on anyone claiming expert status, since LFP is fairly new and “there's very few experts” [VZWhkHs1sXA @ 00:04:15]. Gaurav J of TheElectricalGuy instead walks through liquid cooling with pumps at the bottom as the fit for compact units, with HVAC as the alternative, holding cells in a 20 to 40 degree band to keep heat from tipping into thermal runaway [GNmL-gBPe3g @ 00:13:07].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The Owner's Math runs the cleanest stress test on RV storage. A 240-space lot at $110 grosses about $285,000 at 90% occupancy, nets roughly $190,000 after 30 to 35% opex, and throws off about $82,000 of cash flow, or 12% cash-on-cash, on a $2M build with $1.3M of debt [xjNh4eemKCs @ 00:16:42]. Botch the geometry and the same site converts only 40% of its land into 160 spaces, NOI drops to about $115,000, and cash-on-cash falls to “roughly one” percent [xjNh4eemKCs @ 00:18:13]. Paving carries its own trap: “Pave the lot and you may lose 10 or 15% of your rentable area to a hole in the ground that stores water for 2 hours a year” [xjNh4eemKCs @ 00:05:19]. A bad year with a competitor 30% cheaper and 78% occupancy cuts NOI from $255,000 to $115,000, a $140,000 gap worth about $2M of value [xjNh4eemKCs @ 00:19:55]. Ground leases bring a different risk: “You can be evicted by success, someone else's” [xjNh4eemKCs @ 00:15:53]. On RV parks, American Fault Lines tallies $150,000 to $250,000 to upgrade 50 sites to 50-amp service, insurance up 30 to 70%, and $2,000 to $4,000 per abandoned rig removal [BQMMvL0zywU @ 00:13:53]. Commercial Property Advisors adds that Fannie and Freddie loans do not cover RV parks [ek2QTeZlqCY @ 00:11:40].

Blankenship's own scars are specific. She bought a bankrupt park at 26 on a $3.2M non-recourse loan with no money down, then met an $18,500 first payment and a first electric bill of about $20,000 [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:29:28]. She was audited in 2013 over work campers, who must be paid and charged for their site, and she now over-hires: “Typically, I hire 20% more than I actually need when I'm hiring work campers” [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:22:16]. A glamping student of hers was shut down for 6-plus months, which is why zoning and permitting come first [FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:32:00]. Anzalone warns buyers to know their tenant demographics and get a mentor before wiring money [5o06VeN0Gak @ 00:06:40]. On energy leases, Dan of LandGate flags that the long-term lease may not cover all optioned acreage, citing a 415-acre example and noting a developer won't build a 100 MW project “if they can only sell 60 megawatts” [Uaymin1wo40 @ 00:02:28]. Option payments of $2,000 to $35,000 a year are not a predictable revenue stream because the developer can terminate at any time during the option; only lease payments count [Uaymin1wo40 @ 00:05:18]. That stream can still be sold: the 400-acre Brown County, Ohio deal totals $17M over 30 years, and Craig could sell it in year one for 40 to 45% of that figure [Uaymin1wo40 @ 00:11:33].

BESS hardware carries failure modes no land deal can paper over. SpeedFreakLS1, an electrician with at least five or six BESS builds, warns that emergency circuits open only the inverter while the batteries stay energized: “You cannot de-energize batteries.” A fire can burn the whole skid and spread to neighboring skids, and on his site a camera sat in a blind spot behind a pole [tBKeO4d6hqc @ 00:08:46]. Gaurav J of TheElectricalGuy flags two single points of failure: if the PCS fails there is no charging or discharging, and a mis-timed arbitrage schedule in the EMS loses money [GNmL-gBPe3g @ 00:16:44]. Alex of Fortress Power on the RENVU webinar lists the sizing errors: undersizing triggers shutdown and “over promising and under delivering,” oversizing risks inrush BMS trips, capacity should be added within one year, models should not be mixed, cold is worse than heat across a 32 to 113 degree Fahrenheit range, and charging should be scaled back above 10,000 feet [CLwCvBlXLA4 @ 00:24:55]. On siting, the PlanningWebcastSeries panel puts the record at 22 battery fires since 2012 and 7 in 2023, against 7.8 grain silo explosions per year, and Jared Newton of Connexus Energy's lesson was to meet planners early and give the fire chief a tour [A84PRdZGcoE @ 01:24:07].

callout.title: Four Checks Before Wiring Money
callout.body: Each check below comes from a loss, a shutdown, or a busted pro forma the practitioners hit or measured themselves.
items: Model site conversion before buying RV storage land: 55 to 65% usable on a good layout versus 40% on a poor one is a 60% inventory gap [The Owner's Math — xjNh4eemKCs @ 00:06:07].
Clear zoning and permitting before building glamping units; one student was shut down for 6-plus months [Heather Blankenship — FY9TF9ZkLwk @ 00:32:00].
Match lease acreage to optioned acreage and underwrite only lease payments, since the developer can terminate during the option [LandApp by LandGate — Uaymin1wo40 @ 00:05:18].
Size storage from backup loads to daily usage to bank size, and never mix battery models in one bank [RENVU Solar Equipment Distribution — CLwCvBlXLA4 @ 00:24:03].

Pitch long-time owners seller financing at 5 to 6% over 4 to 5-plus years of income [Commercial Property Advisors — ek2QTeZlqCY @ 00:13:18].
